en: Now begins the first chapter.
At the beginning of his work, the author invokes the presiding deity to dispel obstacles:

"Victorious is the speech of the poet, which brings forth a creation free from the constraints imposed by destiny, consisting solely of bliss, independent of anything else, and rendered beautiful by the nine poetic sentiments. (1)

That which is determined by the power of destiny (*niyati-śakti*), possesses a fixed form, has pleasure, pain, and delusion as its inherent nature, is dependent upon auxiliary causes such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and karma, and consists of the six tastes— which are not exclusively pleasant— such is the creation (*nirmiti*) or emanation (*nirmāṇa*) of Brahmā. However, the creation of the poet’s speech is of a different character from this.
For this very reason, [the word] "conquers" (jayati) is used;
and by the sense of "conquering," a salutation is implied, so that it is understood: "I am bowed down before her."
Here, he states that the subject matter is accompanied by its purpose:
"Poetry [leads] to fame, to the attainment of wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, and to the warding off of misfortune."
It leads to immediate supreme bliss, and because it is like a beloved woman, it is suited for instruction.
[It provides] fame like that of Kālidāsa and others; wealth like that of Dhāvaka and others [attained by] Śrīharṣa and others; knowledge of the appropriate conduct toward kings and others;

the warding off of misfortune like that of Mayūra and others [attained by] Āditya and others; and, as the crown of all purposes, the bliss arising immediately from the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasa), in which all other objects of cognition have dissolved—[a bliss] distinct from the Vedic scriptures and others, which prioritize words comparable to a master.

Poetry—which, unlike the Purāṇas and Itihāsas that aim at the welfare of friends, is distinct from them in its treatment of word and meaning because it is inclined toward operations that serve as limbs of rasa—is the work of a poet skilled in extraordinary description. Like a beloved woman, it draws the poet and the connoisseur toward itself by producing aesthetic relish (*sarasatā*), and imparts instruction as appropriate: "One should behave like Rāma and others, not like Rāvaṇa and others."
Since it acts [in this way], one must strive toward that in every respect.
Having thus stated its purpose, he states the cause:
"Power, proficiency through the study of the world, the sciences, and poetry, and practice under the instruction of those who know poetry—these are the causes for its production. (3)
*Śakti* is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāraviśeṣa*) in the form of the seed of poetic genius,
without which poetry would not emerge, or even if it did emerge, [it would be flawed].
It would be an object of ridicule for the world— that is, for the conduct of the world consisting of both the stationary and the moving—

as well as for the scriptures, namely the treatises on prosody, grammar, lexicography, the arts, the four aims of life, and the manuals on the characteristics of elephants, horses, swords, and so forth.
And proficiency arises from the study of poems related to great poets, as well as histories, by virtue of including the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
Furthermore, there is the repeated engagement in both composing and analyzing poetry through the instruction of those who know how to do so; these three taken together [constitute proficiency].
Indeed, none of these taken individually is the cause for the arising, the creation, or the manifestation of that poetry; rather, they are the causes [collectively].

Having thus stated its cause, he declares its essential nature: (Sūtra 1) "The word and its meaning are free from defects; they may possess qualities and, moreover, in some cases, be without ornaments.
Defects, qualities, and ornaments will be explained [later].

By the phrase "in some places" (kvāpi), he means this: that while [poetry] everywhere possesses ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), there is no loss of its status as poetry even when, in certain instances, there is an absence of manifest ornamentation.
For example: "He who took away my youth is indeed the same bridegroom; those same nights of Caitra; and those same mature breezes from the Kadamba trees, fragrant with blossoming Mālatī flowers."
And yet, I am that very same person; nevertheless, my heart yearns for that place on the bank of the Revā, beneath the cane tree, during the playful performance of amorous dalliance. 1.
In this case, there is no clearly manifest figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*);
and because the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is predominant, it does not constitute a figure of speech.
He now states its varieties in sequence (Sūtra 2).
When the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) excels the expressed meaning (vācya), this is called "suggestion" (dhvani) by the wise. // 4 //
"This" refers to poetry.
By learned grammarians, the term *dhvani* was applied to that word which manifests a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of the *sphoṭa*, which is the primary element.

Subsequently, others who follow that doctrine have likewise applied it to the pair of word and meaning (*śabdārthayugala*) capable of manifesting a suggestion in which the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is subordinated.

"O messenger who speaks falsely, you have gone from here to the pond to bathe, and not to that base man; for your breast-slope is entirely stripped of sandalwood paste, your lower lip has its redness rubbed away, your eyes are completely devoid of collyrium, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation—yet you do not know the pain that comes to your kinsfolk. (2)
In this context, it is primarily through the word "lowest" (adhamapada) that the suggestion is made: "You have gone to his very presence to dally."

(Verse 3) When it is not of that [highest] kind, it is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (of subordinate suggestion); however, when the suggested meaning is not superior to the expressed meaning, it is of the middle rank.
Just as the complexion of a young woman's face becomes increasingly pale when she sees a village youth with a fresh *vañjula* blossom held in his hand. (3)

Here, the suggested meaning—that she did not come to the appointment made at this *bañjula* creeper-cottage—is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), because the expressed meaning alone possesses greater aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*) in comparison to it.
(Verse 4) But that which possesses verbal beauty or denotative beauty, yet lacks suggestion, is considered inferior. (Verse 5)
"Citra" means endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*). "Avyaṅgya" means devoid of a clearly perceived suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*).
"Avara" means inferior.

May the Mandākinī, whose swelling pride is thickened by the great waves surging from the heights of the trees on its banks—trees that are long and impoverished of fruit—dispel your sluggishness; she who, for the sake of the daily bath performed by the great sages whose delusions have vanished, brings forth masses of water that are clear as they gush freely from the hollows of her pure banks. 4.
Upon hearing that he had emerged from his own palace even by mere chance,
Amarāvatī— its bolt cast down in haste by Indra in agitation— seemed to close its eyes in fear.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Kāvyaprakāśa, titled "The Determination of the Purpose, Cause, Nature, and Distinctions of Poetry. // 1.1 //
Now begins the second chapter.
He states the essential nature of word and meaning in sequence—(Sūtra 5):
"In this context, a word may be denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or suggestive (*vyañjaka*); thus it is threefold.
Here, "in this context" refers to poetry.
Their essential nature will be explained.
(Verse 6) The expressed and so forth would be its objects; namely, the expressed, the indicated, and the suggested.
(Verse 7) The intended meaning [of the sūtra] is also present in some [commentaries]. // 6 //

The view of the proponents of abhihitānvaya (the theory that the meaning of words is already expressed before their connection) is as follows: through the force of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), compatibility (yogyatā), and proximity (saṃnidhi), when there is a syntactic integration of word-meanings whose specific natures will be described below, the sentence-meaning—the intended meaning (tātparyārtha)—emerges as a distinct entity, even though it is not itself the meaning of any individual word.
The proponents of the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna-vāda) maintain that the meaning of a sentence is nothing other than what is directly expressed.
(Verse 8) It is generally accepted that all meanings also possess suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*). Among these, an example of the suggested meaning (*vācya*) is as follows:
"Mother, you have indeed said that there is no visiting the house today; so tell me, what should be done? The day does not stand still like this. (6)

In this case, it is suggested that she desires to wander at her own will. An example of the indicated (lakṣya) meaning is as follows: "O friend, while making my beloved happy, you have become distressed at every moment on my account; indeed, you have acted in a manner consistent with true affection and what must be done out of love. (7)
In this case, the literal meaning (*lakṣya*) is: "By you, while delighting my beloved, enmity has been practiced.

And by that, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is the manifestation of her culpability regarding the lover. An example of the suggested meaning is as follows: "Look, the crane shines motionless and still upon the lotus leaf!"* *The literal sense suggests she is so still she is like a painting; the suggested sense is that she is so motionless because she is hiding from her lover.*
She is like a pearl necklace resting upon a vessel of pure emerald. //8//
Here, by means of being motionless,
there is the state of being refreshed,
and by that, the absence of people.
Therefore, this is said by someone to someone else: "This is the place of our appointment.
Or rather, it is suggested: "You speak falsely; you have never come here before."
He states the definitions of the denoter (*vācaka*) and the others in their proper order:
(Sūtra 9) That which directly expresses the intended object is the denoter (*vācaka*). (7)

Since there is no cognition of a word's meaning for one who has not grasped its convention, a word conveys a specific meaning only with the assistance of convention; therefore, that [word] for which a convention is grasped without mediation in relation to a certain [object] is the designator of that [object].
(Sūtra 10)
The conventional [object] consists of four types, beginning with the genus (*jāti*), or it is the genus alone.

Although it is indeed the individual (*vyakti*) that is fit for engagement and withdrawal because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), nevertheless, due to its infinity and variability (*vyabhicāra*), it is not appropriate to establish a convention (*saṃketa*) with respect to it.

Thus, since the distinction between the objects of such expressions as "cow," "white," "dog," and "Ḍittha" would not otherwise be possible, the convention (*saṃketa*) must reside precisely in their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, the adjunct is of two kinds: that which is an inherent property of the object (*vastudharma*), and that which is imposed by the speaker's whim (*vaktṛyadṛcchāsaṃniveśita*).
The property of the object is also twofold: established (*siddha*) and to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Even the established (siddha) is of two kinds: that which bestows life upon a category-meaning (padārtha) and that which is the cause of imparting a specific quality. Of these, the first is the genus (jāti); for it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "A cow is neither a cow by its own nature nor a non-cow; rather, it is a cow through its connection with cowness (*gotva*)."
The second section:
For an object whose existence has been acquired through [qualities] such as whiteness is qualified by them;
the thing to be accomplished (sādhya) consists of parts occurring in a temporal sequence and is of the nature of an action (kriyā).

The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of words such as *ḍittha*, which is grasped by the final cognition and in which the sequence [of phonemes] has been withdrawn, is applied by the speaker at will (*yadṛcchayā*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to objects such as *ḍittha*. This very thing, being of the nature of a name (*saṃjñārūpa*), is of the nature of arbitrariness (*yadṛcchātman*).
Thus says the author of the Mahābhāṣya: "In cases such as ‘cow,’ ‘white,’ ‘dog,’ and ‘ḍittha,’ there is a fourfold application of words."
However, because atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth are recited among the qualities (*guṇa*), their status as qualities is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*).
Although qualities, actions (*kriyā*), and proper names (*yadṛcchā*) are in reality of a single nature, they appear as if distinct due to the difference in their substrates (*āśraya*),
just as a single face appears different depending on whether it is reflected in a sword, a mirror, oil, or other surfaces.

Others maintain that for all words, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). For instance, among the various instances of "white" and so forth—which are ultimately distinct based on their substrates such as snow, milk, or conch shells—that by virtue of which the non-distinct designation and cognition "white, white" arises is the universal "whiteness" (*śuklatva*).
Similarly, there is "cooking-ness" (*pākatva*) and so forth in the cooking of molasses, rice, and the like.

Furthermore, even though the words "Dittha" and so on are uttered by children, the elderly, parrots, and others, and thus differ at every moment, or though the referents "Dittha" and so on differ at every moment, there exists "Dittha-ness" (*ḍitthatva*) and so forth; therefore, the universal alone is the ground for the application of all words.

Some have stated that the meaning of a word is either the possessor of that [exclusion] or the exclusion itself; however, this has not been demonstrated here for fear of making the text too cumbersome and because it is not relevant to the present subject.
(Verse 11) That is the primary meaning; the primary function [of the word] toward that is called "denotation" (*abhidhā*).
"He" refers to that which is directly designated;
"of this" refers to the word.

(Verse 12) When the primary meaning is sublated, yet there is a connection with it— whether by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)— another meaning is indicated; that is *lakṣaṇā*, a figurative operation.

In cases such as "skilled in ritual action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*), because the grasping of *darbha* grass and so forth is impossible; and in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), because the Gaṅgā and other such things cannot possibly be the physical locus of a hamlet and so forth— thus, when the primary meaning is sublated, and since the conventional usage is well-established through the relationship of proximity in the sense of being a "discriminator" (*vivecaka*) and so forth, [the secondary meaning arises].
Likewise, from such usages as "a cowherd settlement on the bank of the Gaṅgā," for those who do not have such a cognition [of the primary meaning],

the secondary meaning is indicated by the primary meaning— both because of the properties such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*) and because of the purpose consisting in the communication of that [secondary sense]. This superimposed verbal operation, which rests upon an intermediate object,
is *lakṣaṇā*.
(Verse 13) For its own establishment, there is the implication of another; for the sake of another, there is the surrender of itself.
Thus, it is said that pure indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is of two kinds: appropriation (*upādāna*) and indication (*lakṣaṇa*).

In expressions such as "the spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*) or "the staffs enter" (*yaṣṭayaḥ praviśanti*), persons who are in conjunction with the spears and so forth are implied for the purpose of establishing the entry of the self [of the spears] through those spears.
Therefore, this is *upādāna-lakṣaṇā*.
In such cases as "A cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), the individual (*vyakti*) is implied by the genus (*jāti*) so that the binding enjoined by the Veda may be accomplished for oneself;

however, it is not denoted by the word itself, according to the maxim: "The denotative power (*abhidhā*) does not extend to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as its capacity is exhausted in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* should not be cited [as a separate type].
For there is no purpose here, nor is this a conventional usage;
rather, because it is invariably concomitant with the individual, the individual is implied by the genus,
just as when one says "let it be done," the agent is implied.
In the case of "Do it," the object is [the action];
in "Enter the house" and "Eat the cake," [the objects] are the house and the cake, respectively; and in "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," [the implied object is food].

And in this case, eating at night is not indicated by presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) or by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because that [latter] has a different scope.
In the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word *Gaṅgā* surrenders its own primary meaning in order to establish that the bank is the locus of the hamlet.
In such cases as these, this indication (lakṣaṇā) is by means of a definition;
and this [indication] is of two kinds, and it is pure because it is unmixed with metaphorical usage (upacāra).
In these two cases, there is no form of neutrality (*tāṭasthyam*) consisting of a difference between the indicated object (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaka*).
For when banks and the like are conveyed by words such as "Ganges," it is through the apprehension of their true nature (*tattva*) that the intended purpose is understood.

But if only the mere connection with the Ganges were perceived, what difference would there be from the primary expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Ganges" (*gaṅgātaṭe ghoṣaḥ*)? In that case, it would simply be a matter of denotation (*abhidhāna*). Therefore, [the function] is indeed indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
(Verse 14) But another [type of] superimposition (sāropā) is said to occur where the object of description (viṣayin) is expressed as being like the actual object (viṣaya).

When that which is being superimposed and the object of superimposition are indicated through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) without their difference being denied, that is the definition of *sāropā* (superimpositional) indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
(Verse 15) When another [object] is internalized as the subject, that [metaphor] would be *sādhyavasānikā* (of the nature of identification). // 11 //

When the subject of attribution (the *viṣayin*) has internalized— that is, swallowed up— the other object of attribution (*āropaviṣaya*), it would be *sādhyavasānā* (metaphor with complete identification).
(Verse 16) These two types of difference are to be understood as being figurative and primary, respectively, due to similarity and another kind of relationship.
These two types of superimposition (*āropa*) and determination (*adhyavasāna*), caused by similarity, occur respectively in the cases of "The Vāhīka is a cow" and "This is a cow.

For in these instances, certain scholars maintain that the qualities such as dullness and sluggishness— which coexist with the primary meaning of the word "cow"— even while being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*), serve as the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "cow" when it denotes the other object.

Others hold that by means of the non-difference from the qualities associated with its own meaning, only the qualities residing in the meaning of another are indicated (*lakṣyante*), and the meaning of another is not directly denoted (*abhidhīyate*).
Still others maintain that by virtue of being the locus of common qualities, the meaning of another itself is indicated.
And it has been stated elsewhere: "Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is defined as the cognition of that which is invariably connected with the expressed meaning."
"Metaphorical usage (gauṇatā), however, is accepted as arising from the connection with qualities perceived [in the primary object].

Here, "inseparable relation" (avinābhāva) refers to mere relationship in general, and not to necessary concomitance (nāntarīyakatva). For if it were the latter, [the metaphorical expression] "the platforms are crying out" would be impossible.

In such cases, there would be no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, it has been stated that since the desired meaning is established through mere implication (*ākṣepa*) even in the absence of a literal sense, there is no utility for figurative indication— as in the expressions "clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*) or "this is indeed life" (*āyurevedam*).
And in such cases as these, there is another relationship— such as the relation of cause and effect— which is distinct from similarity;
and in instances like these, the superimposition and determination are preceded by characteristics such as the relation of cause and effect.

In this context, although there is a difference between the two types of secondary (gauṇa) distinctions, their purpose is the cognition of identity and the complete comprehension of non-difference. However, in the case of pure (śuddha) distinctions, the purpose is the capacity for causal efficiency and so forth, characterized by distinction from others and by invariable concomitance. In some instances, figurative usage (upacāra) occurs for that very purpose.
For example, a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra.
In some cases, this occurs due to the relationship between property and owner;
for example, a king's servant is called "the King."
In some cases, [the name is applied] because of the relationship between part and whole;
for example, in the case of "hand-tip" (*agrahasta*), the term "hand" (*hasta*) is applied to the part that is merely the tip.
In some cases, it is due to performing that function (*tātkarmyāt*).
For example: "one who is not a carpenter is a carpenter."
Therefore, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of six kinds. (Sūtra 17) // 12 //
Together with the two initial divisions.
And that [conventional meaning] is devoid of the suggested sense in the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), but it is accompanied by it in the case of a specific purpose (*prayojana*);
for a purpose is indeed accessible only through the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*).
(Verse 19) And that [suggestive meaning] is either hidden or unhidden;
"that" refers to the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).

The face is hidden by a blossoming smile; the glance is mastered with a graceful curve; the gait is surging with amorous playfulness; the mind has cast aside all reserve; the chest is covered by budding breasts; and the hips are prominent with the fullness of their curves—oh, how the emergence of youth rejoices in the body of this moon-faced maiden! 9.
As an example of the non-hidden [meaning]: "Even the dull-witted become conversant with the conduct of the clever through familiarity with beauty;
it is the very intoxication of youth that instructs amorous women in their graceful charms. (10)
Regarding this, it is taught as follows:
Thus, this has been described as threefold. (Sūtra 20) // 13 //
It is either without a suggested meaning (*avyaṅgyā*), with a concealed suggestion (*gūḍhavyaṅgyā*), or with an unconcealed suggestion (*agūḍhavyaṅgyā*).
(The phrase) "the word *tadbhūlakṣaṇika*" is to be construed [with the preceding].
It belongs to that [level] and has that as its support.
In that context, the operation consists of manifestation (*vyañjanā*).
Why is this so? He says: (Sūtra 23)
Metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is employed in order to produce a cognition of that [which is not directly expressed]. // 14 //
In this case, where the fruit (the result) is accessible solely through the word, there is no function other than suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

Where a word is employed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the desire to convey a specific purpose, the cognition of that purpose does not arise from anything else, but rather from that very word itself;
and in such a case, there is no operation other than suggestion.
For instance (Sūtra 24):
there is no primary denotation because of the absence of convention;

in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," those qualities such as sanctity which are perceived in the bank and so forth are not qualities for which the word "Gaṅgā" and the like have been conventionally established.
(Verse 25) Because of the absence of a cause, there is no defining characteristic. 15.
The triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning is the logical reason.

And thus: (Sūtra 26) "The indicated meaning is not primary here, nor is there sublation; there is no connection with a result, nor is there a purpose in this, nor does the word have a faltering application. (16)

Just as the word "Ganges," being obstructed in its primary sense of the river current, indicates the bank, so too, if it were obstructed even on the bank, it would indicate a further purpose. However, the bank is not the primary meaning here,
nor is there any obstruction in this context.
Furthermore, there is no connection between the bank—the referent of the word "Ganges"—and the qualities such as sanctity that are to be indicated;
nor is there any purpose for the purpose itself when it is the indicated object; nor is the word "Ganges" incapable of conveying the purpose, in the same way that it conveys the bank.
(Sūtra 27) Even so, there would be an infinite regress that destroys the very root.

If, even in this way, a purpose is perceived, it must be by means of another purpose, and that [other] purpose by yet another; thus, because the original subject matter remains unestablished, there would be an infinite regress.
But surely, it is the bank itself, endowed with qualities such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*), that is indicated;

since the cognition of an additional meaning from the expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Gaṅgā" is also the purpose, why is there a need for *vyañjanā* (suggestion) when indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs in respect to the qualified [object]? To this, he replies:
(Verse 28) It is not logical that the object to be characterized exists together with its purpose.
Why is this so? He says:
(Sūtra 29) "The object of knowledge is one thing, and the fruit is said to be another.
For perception and the like, blue and other such objects are the object, whereas the fruit is either manifestation or consciousness."
(Verse 30) It has not been explained in this way that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of a qualified [referent].
The specific qualities would exist in that which is characterized. (Sūtra 31) // 18 //

Those specific qualities such as sanctity and the like, which reside in the riverbank and so forth, must be understood through a function other than denotation (*abhidhā*), intentionality (*tātparya*), or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And that function, which is denoted by terms such as "suggestion" (*vyañjana*), "resounding" (*dhvanana*), or "illumination" (*dyotana*), must necessarily be admitted.
Thus, suggestiveness based on the literal meaning has been explained.
Regarding the basis of denotation, however, it is said: (Sūtra 32) "When the denotative capacity of a word with multiple meanings has been restricted..."
The coloring [of the mind] is the activity that produces the cognition of an inexpressible object through conjunction and other means. // 19 //
“Conjunction, separation, association, opposition,
purpose, context, indicative mark, and the proximity of another word.”
“Capability, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth,
are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise indeterminate.”
According to the direction thus stated: "Hari with the conch and discus" refers to Acyuta; "Hari without the conch and discus" [refers to another];
"Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa" refers to the two sons of Daśaratha;
and "the course of Rāma and Arjuna" refers to Bhārgava and Kārtavīrya.
"Worship Sthāṇu for the cutting off of worldly existence"—this refers to Hara;
"The God knows everything"—this is used in the sense of "you"; "The one whose banner is the sea-monster is angry"—this refers to Kāma.
"Of the god who is the destroyer of the cities"—this [is used] when there is an assembly; "the cuckoo is intoxicated by honey"—this [is used] in spring;
"may the face of your beloved protect you"—this [is used] when facing one another.
"The Supreme Lord shines here" refers to the king with respect to the country in the form of the capital;
"the rainbow shines" refers to the sun during the day and to fire at night;
"a friend shines" refers to a well-wisher.
In the case of "the sun shines as Mitra," and in expressions such as "Indra's enemy" (indraśatru), [the compound is formed] only in these instances,
not in poetry.
The *sveḥ* (the suffix *sva*) produces a specific understanding;
by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), [it includes examples such as:
"She whose breasts are this large, whose eyes are this wide, whose state is this much—[all] in this many days" (11).
In such cases, [the means are] gestures and so forth.

Thus, although the capacity of a word with multiple meanings to denote another meaning has been ruled out by conjunctions and other factors, when that word nevertheless conveys another meaning in certain instances, that is not *abhidhā* (denotation), because its scope is restricted;
nor is it *lakṣaṇā* (indication), because there is an absence of the sublation of the primary meaning and the other necessary conditions.
Moreover, the function [of a word] consists precisely in its primary meaning (vyañjana) and its secondary meaning (añjana).
As it is said: "The trunk of that noble elephant, whose nature was auspicious, whose body was difficult to assail, who rose high upon a vast lineage, who had mastered the collection of arrows (or:
who had gathered bees), and whose gait was never faltering—his trunk was always made beautiful by the sprinkling of the water of his rut (or: the water of his gift). (12)
(Sūtra 33) The word that manifests [the meaning] is endowed with that; it is endowed with the manifesting [phonemes]. (Sūtra 34)
In that case, when it is associated with another meaning, that meaning also is considered to be a manifestor by way of being a cooperative cause. // 20 //
"So be it," said the manifester.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of Word and Meaning," in the Kāvyaprakāśa.
Now begins the third chapter.
(Verse 35) The meanings have been previously stated; their [respective] meanings are the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Of those [factors], namely the seed, the characteristic mark, and the manifestor.
The manifestation of meaning is now described.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: (Sūtra 37)
[The meaning is determined] from the speaker, the person to be addressed, the intonation, the sentence, the expressed meaning, and the proximity of other factors. // 21 //

For those possessed of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), that operation which—due to the particularity of the introductory context, place, time, and so forth—serves as the cause for the cognition of another meaning from a given meaning, is indeed nothing other than manifestation (*vyakti*). (22)
That which is to be understood is that which is to be established.
*Kākū* is a modification of the tone of voice.
*Prastāva* is the context or occasion.
Examples of meaning (artha), consisting of the expressed, the indicated, and the suggested, follow in order:
"Having taken a large water-jar, I have come quickly, my friend."
I rest for a moment, my inhalations and exhalations equalized like the flow of water. //13//
And here, the concealment of secret love-making is expressed:
"The downcast eyes, the physical weakness, the anxiety, the languor, and the sighing—alas, my friend, these belong to me, the unfortunate one, yet they afflict you as well! (14)
Here, the enjoyment of her lover by the messenger-maiden is suggested. [The messenger says:

"Having seen the daughter of Pañcāla in such a state in the royal assembly, having lived for a long time in the forest with hunters while wearing bark garments, and having stayed in the residence of Virāṭa while concealing an unbecoming occupation—even now my preceptor feels grief for me who am exhausted, but not for the Kurus. (15)
Here, it is revealed through intonation (*kāku*) that "grief is not appropriate for me, but rather appropriate for the Kurus.

Nor should one suspect that this is a case of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), on the grounds that the intonation is merely an auxiliary factor for establishing the literal meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*); for the intonation finds its rest in the mere act of questioning itself.
At that time, you did not turn your gaze away from my cheek;
now I am the same and those cheeks are the same, but that gaze is no more. //16//
"Beholding you, as you gazed at my friend reflected in her cheek, your gaze was one thing; but when she moved away, it became something else entirely—oh, what a hidden lustfulness of yours!
Thus it is suggested.
This is a spot on the Narmadā that surpasses the beauty of rows of succulent plantains, where the charms of beautiful women blossom forth through the excellence of its groves.
Moreover, O slender one with firm breasts, what winds are blowing here, before which the Mind-born God proceeds, having assumed the anger of a blooming blue lotus? //17//
Here, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is: "Enter for the sake of sexual pleasure.
"My mother-in-law, whose mind is unshaken, assigns me to the burden of the household;
yet, if only for a moment at twilight, there might be—or perhaps not—rest. (18)
In this context, a certain woman suggests to a neutral bystander that he is a maker of appointments at twilight:
"Your beloved will arrive today in just one watch;
why then do you stand here? Friend, prepare what must be done. (19)
A certain woman is being dissuaded by another who says it is not proper for her to set out to meet her lover here:
"O friends, you go elsewhere and gather flowers; I shall do so here.
For I am not able to wander far; please be gracious, here I offer this salutation with joined palms. (20)

"Here is a secluded place; let the secret lover be brought to you"—thus does one woman inform a trusted friend. "O beloved, subject as you are to your elders, what can I say to you, unfortunate as I am?"
Today you are going on a journey; go, for you yourself shall hear what must be done. //21//
In this context, it is suggested that if you depart now during the season of spring, then for my part I shall remain, but as for your destination, I do not know;
this is implied by the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), which refers to gestures and the like.

Regarding gesture (*ceṣṭā*), an example is as follows: while I was standing close to the edge of the doorway, she, with the splendor of the essence of beauty, caused her pair of thighs—tightly pressed against one another—to quiver.
The veil was brought before her face, her flickering eyes were cast downward, the flow of her speech was checked there, and her two vine-like arms were drawn back in contraction.
Here, by means of a gesture (*ceṣṭā*), a particular intention (*ākūta*) on the part of a lover who is concealing his identity is suggested (*dhvanyate*).
It is cited again and again because it provides a complete understanding and because its occasion has arrived;
[it occurs] when vowels and consonants are joined together, categorized as dyads and so forth.
In this sequence, the suggestiveness of both the expressed (lakṣya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) meanings should be illustrated.
(Sūtra 38) Since an object known through the means of verbal testimony manifests another object,
that [manifestation] constitutes the word’s state of being a cooperative cause for the manifestation of the object. // 23 //
Regarding the word "sound":
for an object cognizable by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be a manifestor.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Suggestiveness of Meaning," in the illustrious *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Although the nature of defects, merits, and ornaments must be stated once the determination of word and meaning has been made, nevertheless, since the status of qualities as things to be abandoned or adopted is understood only when the substratum has been demonstrated,
he first states the divisions of poetry.
(Sūtra 39)
In that [type of] dhvani where the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed (avivakṣitavācya), the expressed meaning is either transmuted into another meaning or completely set aside. (24)

It should be understood as "dhvani" because of the restatement: "that in which the expressed meaning is not intended [as primary], provided that there is a predominance of the suggested meaning based on the literal sense.
Thus, it is known as *dhvani*.
In that regard, it must be stated that in some cases, because [the literal meaning] is not applicable, it is transformed into another sense.
For example: "I speak to you; here stands an assembly of the learned. Relying upon your own judgment, establish your position here accordingly. (23)
In this context, speech and so forth transform into the form of instruction and so on; in some cases, however, they do so by way of being logically untenable.

It has been utterly disregarded. For example: "Much has been done for you there; what more can be said? You have displayed supreme goodness toward me. O friend, by always acting in this very way, may you live happily for a hundred autumns. (24)
Someone says this with respect to a wrongdoer by means of an ironic definition (*viparītalakṣaṇā*).

(Verse 40) That [poem] in which what is intended to be expressed is subordinate to another [meaning] is the other type; "subordinate to another" means being focused on the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
And this is another [type of] sequence of the suggested and the suggested (lakṣyavyaṅgyakrama), which is distinct from the sequence of the unmanifest and the manifest (alayavyaṅgyakrama). // 25 //
Regarding the term *alakṣya*:
rasa is certainly not merely the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*);
rather, it is by means of these that rasa [is manifested].
Such is the sequence of the "existent" (astikrama);
however, it is not perceived due to its brevity.
In this context (Sūtra 42), the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the emotion (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*), and so forth, exist as the non-sequential;
they stand distinct from the ornaments of *rasa* and the like, by virtue of being the objects of ornamentation (*alaṃkārya*). // 26 //

From the very beginning, there exist the emergence of a state, the transition between states, and the variegation of states. That in which rasa and the like reside as the primary element is the *alaṃkārya* (the object of embellishment),
as will be illustrated by examples.

But in other cases, where the sentence-meaning is the primary element and rasa and so forth are subordinate members, there are the figures of speech known as *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, *samāhita*, and others, which belong to the category of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinated).
These will be illustrated under the discussion of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
Regarding that, he states the essential nature of rasa (Sūtra 43):
"If those causes, effects, and auxiliaries which exist in the world for the stable emotion (*sthāyin*) such as love (*rati*), are present in drama and poetry," [then rasa arises]. (27)
The determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), and those transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are thus described.
That permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva), when manifested by those [determinants] and the others, is known as aesthetic flavor (rasa). // 28 //
For it has been stated by Bharata: "The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin).
They explain this as follows:
"By means of the determinants—such as women, gardens, and so forth—which serve as the objective and the inciting causes..."
“Emotion (*bhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and the like, is first produced;

it is then rendered capable of being perceived through the *anubhāvas*—effects such as side-long glances and the casting of arms—and further intensified by the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as despondency (*nirveda*) acting as auxiliary factors.

Thus, rasa is that which is primarily manifested in the original character (*anukārya*) such as Rāma, and is perceived even in the actor (*naṭa*) because of the identification with that [original] form. So say Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others.

"This is indeed Rāma; this is Rāma himself"—this [cognition] "This is Rāma" is distinct from the cognitions of correctness (*samyak*), error (*mithyā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*), such as the subsequent sublation "This is not Rāma," or "This might be Rāma or he might not," or "This is similar to Rāma"; rather, it is like the case of a painted horse and so forth.

Through the power of dramatic representation, as the actor is perceived as the object [of the emotion]: "This mistress of my life, who is a spray of nectar upon my limbs, a probe of pure camphor for my eyes, the embodied glory of my heart's desire, has come within the range of my vision. (25)
"By fate, today I have been separated from her, whose eyes are large and tremulous; and this season has arrived, with its dense and shifting clouds. (26)

Through the power of contemplating such poetry and by manifesting his own body through the practice of training, the actor reveals the causes, effects, and auxiliary factors— even though they are artificial— by designating them with the terms *vibhāva* and so forth, while not conceiving of them as such. Although [the rasa] is inferred from their "conjunction"— that is, from the relationship of the signifier and the signified— it is distinct from anything else that is inferred, because it is experienced as a relish (*rasanīyatva*) by the force of the beauty of the reality itself.

The venerable Śaṅkuka holds that a state such as love (rati), which is capable of being conceived as a stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), even if not present [in the actor], is called "rasa" when it is relished by the audience through their latent impressions (vāsanā).
Rasa is neither perceived as something external (tāṭasthyena) nor as belonging to oneself (ātmagatatvena); it is neither produced nor manifested.

Furthermore, Bhaṭṭanāyaka maintains that in poetry and drama, the stable emotion (sthāyin), being brought into being by the second operation— namely, the "enjoyer-function" (bhāvakatva-vyāpāra) consisting of the universalization of the excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth— is enjoyed through an experience characterized by a repose in consciousness consisting of the manifestation of the intensification of that [emotion] and bliss.

In the world, for those possessed of proficiency through practice in inference based on stable [perceptions], these same [factors]—which in poetry and drama function as excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth by abandoning their status as causes and the like—are designated by the term "extraordinary" (*alaukika*). Thus, they are not thought of as "these belong to me alone," "these belong to my enemy alone," or "these belong to a neutral person alone"; nor are they thought of as "these do not belong to me alone," "these do not belong to my enemy alone," or "these do not belong to a neutral person alone."

Thus, because there is no determination regarding the rules for accepting or rejecting specific relations [with particular individuals], the stable emotion (*sthāyin*)— such as love (*rati*) and so forth— which exists as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the spectators and is manifested through these [emotions] perceived in a universal manner, although it resides in a restricted subject,

by the power of the universal means [of aesthetic presentation], comes to possess an immeasurable state that is free from contact with other objects of knowledge, due to the temporary dissolution of the limited state of the subject.

By the cognizer—who participates in the common consensus of all sensitive hearts—it is perceived as if non-different from his own mental form through a process of universalization; having relish (*carvaṇā*) as its sole life-breath, with its existence limited by the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, it is relished according to the analogy of a blended beverage (*pānakarasa*). Thus, appearing as if right before one’s eyes, entering as if into the heart, embracing as if every limb, obscuring everything else as if it were nothing, and causing one to experience as if the taste of Brahman itself.
The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), such as the erotic and so forth, produces a transcendental wonder;
furthermore, it is not an effect,
because it would follow that it could still exist even after the disappearance of its determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.
Nor is it something to be made known, because that [rasa], being already established, cannot be produced;
rather, it is to be relished as manifested by the excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth.
If it is asked, "Where else has anything been seen other than a product or a thing made known? [the answer follows].
The fact that it is not seen anywhere is an ornament, not a defect, for the establishment of its supramundane nature.
Since its production occurs through the completion of *carvaṇā* (relishing), let it be called "produced" in a figurative sense.

It is the object of a supramundane self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that is distinct from worldly perception and other means of knowledge, from the detached cognition of those limited by the senses, and from the knowledge of yogis; it is devoid of contact with any other cognizable object and is restricted solely to one's own self, being unlike the limited consciousness of other yogis.
Thus, let it be stated in response as well:
that which apprehends [the rasa] is neither non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because its primary function is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the *vibhāva* and other factors;
nor is it conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because that which is being relished—which consists of supramundane bliss—is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

The venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda maintains that even the dual nature of that whose essential form is the absence of both [subject and object] leads, as before, to its supramundane character rather than to contradiction.

Tigers and the like are determinants (*vibhāva*) for the Furious sentiment as they are for the Heroic, the Marvellous, and the Terrible; tears and the like are consequents (*anubhāva*) for the Pathetic and the Fearful as they are for the Erotic; and mental anxiety and the like are transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) for the Heroic, the Pathetic, and the Fearful as they are for the Erotic. Because these are not restricted to any single sentiment individually, they are specified in the Sūtra in combination.
The sky possesses the beauty of clouds whose bellies are dark with water like a swarm of bees, while the quarters of the horizon are filled with the warbling of bees and cuckoos.
The earth is marked with the beauty of fresh sprouts; be gracious, O charming one, toward your beloved who is intent on prostrating before you.
In such cases as this: "Her limbs are withered like crushed lotus stalks; yet, through the entreaties of her attendants, she somehow manages to engage in her duties.
And her cheek, as lovely as a fresh slice of ivory, bears the beauty of the stainless moon. (28)

When her beloved has committed an offense, oh, how the eye of the proud woman becomes so adept at manifold expressions: eager from afar; turned upward as he approaches; wide-open when he speaks; reddened as he embraces her; knitting its creeper-like brows when she seizes his garment; and filled with tears of water upon the act of bowing at her feet. 29.

And although in such cases there exists only the excitants (*vibhāva*), the ensuants (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*)—namely longing, bashfulness, joy, anger, envy, and serenity—nevertheless, because these are uncommon [to other rasas], they imply two others; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
He states their specific divisions:
(Sūtra 44) "The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the odious, and the marvelous—these are remembered as the eight aesthetic sentiments (rasas) in drama. // 29 //
In that regard, there are two divisions of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*): union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).
Of these, the former—consisting of mutual gazing, embracing, sipping the lower lip, kissing, and so forth—is considered as one alone, being indivisible due to its infinite variety.

Just as a young woman, having observed that the bedchamber was empty, rose slightly and slowly from her couch; and having gazed for a long time at the face of her husband who had feigned sleep, she kissed him confidently. Seeing the horripilation on the surface of his cheeks, her face bowed with shame, she was kissed for a long time by her laughing beloved. (30)

When her beloved said, "O lovely-eyed one, you possess such captivating beauty even without your bodice," and touched the knot of its fastening, the circle of friends— who had been seated near the bed and were delighted by the festival of their friend's eyes— slowly withdrew under the pretext of some false excuse.
Another [type of love-in-separation] is fivefold, having as its causes longing, absence of desire, jealousy, sojourn abroad, and a curse.

The examples follow in order: "May those various gestures of the lovely-eyed one—moist with love, touching upon affection, arising from familiarity into the surge of intense passion, and naturally sweet—be directed toward me;
for even when merely imagined through longing, they bring about in an instant a dense absorption of bliss that obstructs the functioning of the external senses within the heart. (32)
"Is he going elsewhere? What talk can there be of such a thing? Nor is there any friend of his who does not wish for me and yet has not come. Alas, alas!
What is this course of fate?"—thus, her heart swallowed by these and other manifold imaginings, the young woman tosses about within her chamber at night and finds no sleep.
This is the maiden longing in separation.
At the time of her son’s first offense, she did not know how to indicate her feelings through the turning of her graceful limbs or through indirect speech, lacking the instruction of a friend;
with her lotus-eyes cast down and tears falling from the base of her clear cheeks, the young girl simply weeps, her trembling locks of hair rolling about as they mingle with the tears.
The bracelets have made their departure; the dear friends, the tears, have gone away incessantly; not for a moment has it been stayed by fortitude; the mind has resolved to go on ahead.
When the beloved one has made up her mind to go, everyone sets out together. O Life, since we must depart, why is this caravan of dear friends being abandoned?
Having painted you upon a stone with mineral pigments while feigning anger out of love, I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
yet before I can do so, my vision is repeatedly obscured by gathering tears. Cruel Fate does not tolerate our union even in that [portrait].
An illustration of the comic (hāsya) and the other rasas in sequence: "Contracting her impure hand, the courtesan struck me on the head with drops of consecrated water at every step;
with a loud cry and a resounding *thūtkṛta*, Viṣṇuśarman weeps, saying, 'Alas, alas! I am ruined! (37)

"O Mother! Where are you in such haste? What is this? O deities! Where are your blessings? Fie on my life! A thunderbolt has fallen; your limbs are burnt and your eyes are consumed!"—with such cries, choked with piteous sobs, the voices of the city women break even painted figures into tears and shatter even walls into a hundred pieces. (38)

"By those beast-like men who, devoid of all restraint and with weapons raised, have committed, approved, or witnessed this heinous crime against their preceptor—for them, along with Bhīma and Arjuna, and together with the Enemy of Naraka, I shall now offer a sacrifice to the quarters with their blood, fat, and flesh. (39)
"O base monkeys, abandon this terror! These arrows, which have crushed the temples of Indra’s elephant, feel great shame as they fall upon your bodies."
"O son of Sumitrā, stay back; you are not a fit vessel for my wrath. Surely I am Meghanāda! I seek out Rāma, who by the mere playful movement of his eyebrows has restrained the ocean."

With his gaze fixed upon the chariot following him, he makes it beautiful by the way he repeatedly turns his neck; through fear of the falling arrow, he draws most of his body forward while half his rear remains hidden.
His path is strewn with half-chewed grass falling from mouths opened by exhaustion; behold, because of his high leaps, he travels much further in the air and but little upon the earth.

Having repeatedly torn away the skin, and having first devoured the vast quantities of flesh— abundant in thickness and easily accessible from parts such as the shoulders, buttocks, and the muscles of the back—
the wretched *preta*, afflicted, with rolling eyes and bared teeth, calmly eats the raw meat remaining on the skeleton, even that which clings to the bones within the hollows of the skull.
How wonderful! Oh, what a great incarnation this is! Where is such beauty, and where this entirely novel grace?
What extraordinary fortitude, what marvelous power, and what an indescribable form—this is a truly new creation! (4.3)

He states the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*) of these [rasas]: (Sūtra 33) "Love (*rati*), laughter (*hāsa*), sorrow (*śoka*), anger (*krodha*), energy (*utsāha*), fear (*bhaya*), as well as disgust (*jugupsā*) and wonder (*vismaya*)—these are proclaimed as the stable emotions. //30//
This is clear.
He states the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*): (Sūtra 46)—despair, exhaustion, apprehension, as well as envy, intoxication, and fatigue.
Laziness, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude; //31//
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness, pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy. //32//
Sleep, awakening, indignation, dissimulation, and then ferocity; intelligence, disease, as well as madness, and likewise death. //33//
Fear and reflection are to be known as transitory mental states;
these thirty-three states have thus been fully enumerated by name. (34)

Although *nirveda* (disgust/disillusionment), being for the most part inauspicious, is not to be adopted at the outset, its inclusion here is for the purpose of designating it as a *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion), even though it is variable (*vyabhicārin*).
By this [sūtra 47], there exists a ninth rasa, the *śānta* (quiescent), which has *nirveda* as its *sthāyibhāva*.

Whether it be a snake or a pearl necklace, a bed of flowers or a stone slab, a jewel or a clod of earth, a powerful enemy or a well-wishing friend, a blade of grass or a woman—my days pass with an equal eye toward all these as I utter "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva" while dwelling in some sacred forest. (4.4)
(Verse 48) Love directed toward objects such as gods and the like, as well as a transitory emotion similarly manifested, [are also rasas]. //35//
The state [of love] has been described;
by the word "etcetera," it refers to objects such as sages, gurus, kings, and sons,
while when directed toward a beloved woman, it is manifest as the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
An example: "O Lord, even the Kālakūṭa poison resting in the corner of Your throat is for me a great nectar;
yet even the nectar I have received does not please me if it exists as something distinct from Your body. (4.5)

The sight of you removes sin in the present, is the cause of future welfare through auspicious deeds performed in the past, and reveals the spiritual fitness of embodied beings throughout all three periods of time.
In this manner, other examples may also be cited.

An example of the "apparently non-deviant" (*añjitavyabhicārī*) is as follows: "I know that today in a dream I saw my beloved with her face turned away in anger; weeping, she began to move forward, saying, 'Do not touch me with your hand!
But before I could embrace my dear one and comfort her with hundreds of endearments, O brother, I was robbed of my sleep by that deceitful Fate. (4.7)
In this context, there is dissatisfaction regarding the prescribed rule.
(Sūtra 49) Its semblances are those set in motion by impropriety.

These are the semblances of rasa (*rasābhāsa*), the semblances of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsa*), and the semblances of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*). Among these, the semblance of rasa is as follows: "Whom shall we praise, O fair-eyed one, without whom you do not find delight even for a moment? Who gave up his life at the front of the sacrifice of battle, whom you seek out? In what auspicious conjunction was he born, O moon-faced one, whom you embrace by force? Whose is this glory of asceticism, O city of Love, whom you meditate upon? (4.8)
Here, the phrase "we praise her longing directed toward many lovers" and so forth reveals the employment of numerous activities that follow from this state.
An example of the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) is as follows: "She has a face like the full moon, tremulous and long eyes, and limbs whose graceful movements ripple with budding youth.
What shall I do? How can I establish a friendship here? What indeed might be the means for the process of winning her favor? (4.9)
In this case, there is the fault of *cintā* (inconsistency), which arises from impropriety (*anaucitya*).
Other examples of this kind should also be cited accordingly.
(Verse 50) The quiescence, the arising, the junction, and likewise the variegated state of an entity. //36//
An example in sequence: "Is your chest, marked with the seal of the embrace from her firm-smeared breasts, being concealed under the pretext of bowing at her feet?
When this was said, she cried out, "Where is that? and suddenly embraced me with impetuosity to wipe it away; and due to the pleasure of that embrace, the slender one forgot all else. (50)
Here is an example of anger (*kopa*):
On a single bed, while her rival women were being embraced, the beloved began to offer endearments; yet, immediately distressed by her assumption of pride, she rejected him out of agitation.
As he remained silent for that moment, she turned her neck repeatedly and looked back again, thinking: "Let it not be as if he has fallen asleep. (51)
Herein lies the state of longing:
on one hand, both my love for the company of the virtuous and the impetuous leap of heroic zeal draw me toward the arrival of that exalted treasure-house of ascetic power and prowess;
yet on the other hand, this embrace of Vaidehī—delightful, cool and smooth as Haricandana sandalwood and the moon, and causing my consciousness to repeatedly fade away—holds me back.
Herein lie agitation and joy:
"Where is the misdeed of the moon-crested one, and where is my noble lineage? Might she be seen once more to pacify our faults! Ah, her face is lovely even in anger;
what will the sinless and wise say [of me]? She is difficult to obtain even in a dream; O heart, attain composure! What fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lower lip? (53)
Herein, there is a variegation of initial thought, longing, intelligence, memory, doubt, dejection, fortitude, and reflection;
however, the establishment of the aesthetic emotion (bhāva) has already been stated and illustrated.

(Verse 51) Even when they are the primary rasa, those— namely, the emergence, subsidence, and so forth of the transitory emotions (bhāvas)— sometimes attain the status of being the dominant element (aṅgin).
The state of being the principal [factor] is like that of a servant who has set out for a wedding following his king.
(Verse 52) But that [suggestion] which exists as something whose sequence is imperceptible, appearing like an echo, is [the second type]. //37//
That *dhvani* is said to be threefold, arising from the power of both word and meaning:

that which has as its suggested content (*vyaṅgya*) the resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word; that which has as its suggested content the resonance rooted in the power of the meaning; and that which has as its suggested content the resonance rooted in the power of both. Thus it is of three kinds.
In that regard, where either an ornament or the very subject itself appears through the words [of the sentence], [that is *dhvani*]. //38//
(Sūtra 53) That [suggestion] arising from the power of words is to be known as twofold by virtue of its predominance:
namely, that which is the thing itself (*vastu*).

The first [type] consists of the mere subject matter (*vastumātra*) without ornament (*alaṅkāra*). For example: "By that Lord, who raised aloft the great cloud of his dark sword-blade and uttered a mature, powerful roar, the entire blazing majesty of his enemies in the three worlds was extinguished in battle by the waters of its stream. (54)

In this context, lest the sentence be charged with expressing an unrelated meaning, one must conceive of a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the contextual and the non-contextual; thus, the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

"O Lord, you shine forth—possessing a splendor as lovely as the sun, acting as the creator of night for the moon [or: possessing a splendor as lovely as the moon], charming in your play, wise, acting according to reality, and leading the foremost of both sides at every step. (55)
In this verse, there is an apparent contradiction (virodhābhāsa) because each word can be split into two words:
"O Lord, giver of joy, you are immeasurable due to the excellences attained from battles;
you are not hostile [to the good], but accompanied by the fame of the virtuous, and you are the destroyer of the wicked. (56)
Here too, there is an apparent contradiction:
"Obeisance to that wielder of the trident, who, praiseworthy for his artistic skill, unfolds the variegated world-picture upon a wall-less surface, without any accumulation of material causes. (57)
Here there is a figure of speech by way of contrast (*vyatireka*).
Even that which is the object of adornment may function as an ornament according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the row" (*brāhmaṇa-śreṇi-nyāya*).
An example of a mere fact (*vastumātra*) is: "O traveler, there is no bedding here in this village, the ground of which consists only of stones."
If you wish to dwell having beheld her full, swelling breasts, then indeed dwell there. 58.
In this context, it is implied: "If you are capable of enjoying [this], then sit down.
O King, he upon whom you are angry—whether he be a thunderbolt or not a thunderbolt—is struck down violently by that very thunderbolt.
Wherever you are pleased, that person shines forth as both noble and ignoble. (59)

It is suggested that even though they are not in conflict, they perform a single action for the sake of following your lead. (Sūtra 54) Furthermore, a meaning arising from the power of the literal sense (*arthaśaktyudbhava*) that is possible by its own nature (*svataḥ sambhavī*) is also suggestive (*vyañjaka*). [Kārikā 39]

Whether established through mere bold assertion (prauḍhokti) by the poet or by his creation, and whether it be a matter of fact (vastu) or an ornament (alaṃkāra), this [suggestion] has six varieties according to what it manifests. //40//
Alternatively, this [suggested meaning] consists of twelve types through its vastness and ornaments.

It is not merely "inherently possible" (*svataḥsaṃbhavī*)—meaning established by mere verbal expression—but is also that which is conceivable as being possible even externally through propriety. Furthermore, there are two other types: that which is created by the poet’s mere imagination even though it does not exist externally, and that which is expressed by a speaker fashioned by the poet; thus, it is threefold.
The suggester (*vyañjaka*) is sixfold—either a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
Since its suggested counterpart (*vyaṅgya*) is likewise either a fact or an ornament, there are twelve varieties.
This is *dhvani* arising from power (*śaktyudbhava*).
The examples in order: "O daughter, he is the foremost of rogues, lazy, bald-headed, and possessed of great wealth.
When this was said, Nāgāṅgī’s eyes blossomed wide with joy. (60)
In this instance, one thing is suggested by another: "This is for my enjoyment alone.
"O friend, you are blessed, for you can speak hundreds of confident, amorous flatteries during the intervals of love-play when meeting your beloved.
But as for me, O friends, I swear that I do not recall even the slightest thing once my lover’s hand was placed upon the knot of my garment. (61)
In this context, the poetic figure is *vyatireka* (contrast), as it implies: "You are unfortunate here, whereas I am fortunate.
[His] luster is crimson with thick blood, flowing from the frontal globes of scent-elephants blinded by pride, which have been struck down as they fell upon the surface of his broad chest.
In battle, his sword—its luster reddened by fury—was beheld by the heroes like the side-glance of Kālī held in her hand.
In this instance, by means of the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), the fact (*vastu*) is suggested that the entire army of enemies will be destroyed in an instant.

"He who, in the midst of the agony caused by the deep wounds from the teeth of his beloved, bit his own lower lip in rage during battle, thereby freeing the coral-like lips of the wives of his enemies from the peril of being bitten by their husbands' teeth. (63)

In this instance, through the figure of contradiction (virodhālaṃkāra), it is suggested by the figure of equal pairing (tulyayogitā) that the enemies were destroyed at the very moment the lower lip was bitten; furthermore, the notion "may the injury of another be averted even by my own injury" is poetically imagined, thus constituting the figure of poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
In these examples, the suggester is inherently possible (svataḥsaṃbhavī).
On the first peak of Kailāsa, hearing his fame being sung by the jewels among the gods to the accompaniment of the resonant melodies of flutes,
the elephants of the quarters— casting down their sidelong glances and suspecting it to be the stalk of a lotus from a lake— wave their trunks upon the sandy banks of their ears.

In this instance, by means of the literal subject matter (*vastu*), the following fact is suggested (*dhvani*): "Your fame produces such wonder even in those who possess no comprehension of meaning, by generating such a cognition.
"Having seized her by the hair with force, he took the Glory of Victory (*Jayashrī*) from him in battle; so that the enemies were firmly established in his throat within the mountain caves. (65)

Here, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) suggesting that the caves, as if their passion were kindled by the seizing of hair and the sight [of the enemy], embrace those who are distressed by him around the neck. Furthermore, because his enemies, having seen defeat in a single battle, flee and remain in caves, there is the poetic figure of "poetic cause" (*kāvyahetu*).
It is not that those enemies have fled elsewhere; rather, it is because they anticipate defeat from him that the caves do not abandon them—this is an instance of *apahnuti* (concealment).
When the lover approaches with the intimacy of a firm embrace, the pride of proud women quickly slips away from their hearts, as if afraid of being crushed. (66)
Here, by means of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the act of embracing in return and so forth is manifested; thus, this is a *vastu* (a suggested fact).
"She who, laughing like an old man, having fixed her residence upon the lotus of the poet, makes the circle of the world appear as if it were something else—victory to that Speech! (67)
Here, through poetic fancy (utprekṣā), the Goddess seated upon the non-insentient throne creates a world that is ever-new, which is the sole cause of aesthetic wonder;
thus, there is a figure of contrast (vyatireka).
In these instances, the suggestor is brought about solely by the bold assertion (prauḍhokti) of the poet.

Those Malaya breezes, which had previously fallen into poverty while attempting to swallow the rows of hoods—thickly expanded in fear—of the serpents exhausted by the amorous play of Urvaśī on the slopes of Mount Laṅkā, have now suddenly become full of the vigor of youth, thick with the contact of the sighs of women separated from their lovers. 68.
In this passage, by means of the fact that "the winds, having attained sovereignty through sighs, do what they will," one thing suggests another thing (*vastunā vastu vyajyate*). For:
"Having created confidence in me by his steadfastness while I was maintaining my pride, he suddenly vanished at the very moment when my heart was distracted by the sight of my beloved. (69)

Here, even though no request has been made, she is pleased; this is the figure of speech *vibhāvanā*. Or, it may be a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy): "The power of the good fortune of one whose sight is dear cannot be endured through fortitude.
With hands dripping wet with tears, [she] has bestowed [her gaze] upon your eyes.
The red garment was cast down in anger, yet these two were not stepped upon. // 70 //

In this passage, by means of the figure of speech *uttarālaṃkāra* (the answer), the following fact is conveyed: "Why do you bear such angry eyes?"—namely, that you are not only concealing the fresh nail-marks, but have even become the recipient of their favor.
"O fortunate one, she, finding no room in your heart already filled with thousands of women..."
Day after day, performing no other work, she makes her already slender body even more emaciated. // 71 //

Here, by means of the figure of speech *hetvalaṅkāra* (the ornament of cause), there is the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (the statement of a specific effect despite the absence of its cause), expressed as: "Even though your body has been emaciated, [love] does not reside in your heart. In these cases, the suggestor (*vyañjaka*) has its form established solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker created by the poet.
Thus, there are twelve divisions.
(Verse 55) There is one [type of suggestion] which consists of both word and meaning,
as in: "Adorned with the tireless moon, awakening the god of love..."
Whom does that dark-complexioned woman, tremulous as a star, not fill with joy?
Here, the simile is suggested (vyaṅgya).
Its divisions are eighteen. (Sūtra 56) //41//
"Of this" refers to the sound.
Now, one might ask: since *rasa* and the other [qualities] have many subdivisions, how can there be eighteen? To this he says:
(Sūtra 57) "Because *rasa* and the others are infinite, their subdivisions are counted as only one."
"Because it is infinite. For instance, there are nine rasas; among them, there are two varieties of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa.
There are two types: union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).

Union also has many subdivisions, such as mutual gazing, embracing, kissing, and so forth, as well as the gathering of flowers, water-sports, the setting of the sun, the rising of the moon, and descriptions of the six seasons.
Regarding separation, longing (*abhilāṣa*) and the other [stages] have been described.
For these two as well, there is a variety of determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Within those, there is the nature of the two protagonists as being superior, middling, or inferior;
and within those too, there are distinctions of place, time, situation, and so forth—thus, even for a single rasa, there is infinity.
What need is there to mention others?
However, by relying on the commonality of the "imperceptible sequence" (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), the various types of suggestion (*dhvani*) such as *rasa* and so forth are counted as only one.
(Verse 58) In the case of a sentence, "arising from both" (*dvayuttha*) refers to that which is rooted in the power of both word and meaning.
(Verse 59) Others [hold that it occurs] even in a word;
because of the word "even," it also occurs in a sentence.

Just as a loving woman shines by means of an ornament placed on a single limb, so too does speech (bhāratī) shine even when its suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is conveyed through a word, though it is actually manifested by the sentence as a whole.
Regarding its manifestation by a word, here are examples in sequence: "He whose friends are truly friends, and whose enemies are truly enemies;
he who is worthy of compassion is compassionate—he alone is truly born, and he alone truly lives. (73)

(1) Here, the second [instance] of words such as "friend" (*mitra*) have their literal meanings transferred (*saṃkramita-vācya*) to signify qualities such as being trustworthy, being restrained, and being a worthy object of affection.
"Though the practices of the wicked appear cruel, nevertheless, the undertakings of the steadfast—highly esteemed by the heart-friend [the intellect]—do not falter. (74)
(2) Regarding the phrase "here they are bewildered":
That loveliness, that radiance, that form, and that sequence of speech—then it was a source of nectar, but now it is a great fever. (75)
In this context, objects that are accessible solely through direct experience are revealed by words such as *tat* (that) and so forth.
For example: "O innocent one, why do you begin to spend all your time in mere innocence? Assume pride, maintain your composure, and cast away your straightforwardness toward your beloved!
O friend, speak thus; for surely my lord of life, dwelling within my heart, will hear it. (76)

(3) Here, by the phrase "with faces terrified," the propriety of the rule for reciting in a low tone is understood. Since there is no greater aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) when states of being (*bhāva*) and so forth are manifested by words, they are not cited as examples here.
O King, with your mace-like arms made formidable by swords adorned with streams of blood,
and your forehead instantly furrowed with a frown, you appear truly terrifying.

(4) Here, Bhīmasena serves as the point of comparison for that which is terrifying: "To whom does the True Tradition (sadāgama)—which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation and is intent upon providing exclusive instruction—not grant a continuous flow of bliss? (78)

(5) A certain woman praises the one who gave her the rendezvous in this way, using the primary sense [of the words]: "The evening bath has been performed, my limbs have been anointed with unguents from the great sacrifice, and the sun, the jewel of the sky, has gone to the crest of the western mountain; you have come here with full confidence. How wonderful is your delicacy, for by it you are now utterly exhausted that your pair of eyes is unable to remain open! (79)
(6) Here, by means of the expressed matter (*vastu*), the matter "you are exhausted from having cultivated intimacy with men" is manifested as being illuminated by the word *adhunā* ("now").
[She is one] whose entire stock of sins has been dissolved by the great suffering of not attaining him.
Likewise, those whose store of merit was exhausted by the immense joy of reflecting upon that [teaching]. // 80 //
Another cowherd girl, meditating upon the source of the universe who is the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman,
attained liberation through the cessation of her breath.

(7) Here it is stated that the fruits of misdeeds and good deeds, which would otherwise have to be experienced over thousands of births, are instead experienced through the sorrow of separation and the joy of reflection.
Thus, there is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) illuminated by the word *caya* (accumulation).

O Hero, when you turn your back upon your enemies, the night becomes no longer a night, the forest ceases to be a forest, and calamity is no longer a calamity; indeed, for your foes, everything has turned its face away.

(8) Here, by means of the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) based on the element of contradiction rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), the fact illuminated by every word is: "Even the Creator follows you.
"In the morning, your lover's lip was like a withered lotus petal."
That young bride, having heard it, speaks her words face-to-face with the buffalo. // 83 //

(9) Here, by means of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), it is suggested that you kissed this [lip] so repeatedly that it became withered; thus, the poetic figure of "poetic cause" (*kāvyaliṅga*) is expressed through words such as *mlāna* ("withered"). In these cases, the suggester (*vyañjaka*) is inherently possible (*svataḥsaṃbhavī*). [The verse: *“On nights white as the moon, having gracefully drawn back the bow...”* (Note: This fragment corresponds to the opening of the famous verse from the *Gāthāsaptaśatī* describing a lover's skillful seduction.)
Exerting his power, he makes the sovereignty over the world as if under a single umbrella. // 84 //

(10) Here, by means of the *vastu* (the literal fact), it is revealed that for those lovers for whom this king is Cupid, there is not even one who turns his back on his command; thus, they pass the night remaining awake and solely intent on enjoyment—this being the *vastu* illuminated by the word *bhūṣaṇarājya* (sovereignty over the world).
"In the interval between youth and old age, the bodiless god, with the thought of his sharpened arrows, entrusts his own strength to the eyes of the fair-eyed woman."
In whichever direction she falls, there the various states of being arise, having encountered a total upheaval.
(11) Here, by means of the subject matter, there is a contradiction (*virodha*) illuminated by the word "intermingling" (*vyatikara*), wherein even mutually contradictory states arise simultaneously:
"Though repeatedly restrained by her heart—which was distressed by longing and which was a dear friend to her breasts—the necklace of pure birth does not move. (86)

(12) Here, by means of the figure of speech *hetvalaṃkāra* characterized by the purity of his birth, the fact that the necklace remains constantly unshaken is expressed; this is the *vastu* (fact) illuminated by the word *ṇa calai* ("does not move").
He, with his face dark as a fresh lotus, his hair braided, and his body adorned with playful ornaments—
Having seized strength from her shoulders, the arrow triumphs in the battle against the gods. // 87 //
