(13) Here, through the metaphor (*rūpaka*), the mass of hair reaches the shoulders by being repeatedly pulled back;

thus, even when the pleasure has ceased, the lover’s desire does not subside. This is a *vibhāvanā* (poetic cause) suggested by the word "shoulders" (*khaṃdha*). In these cases, the body [of the figure] is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet.
O fortunate one, tell me truly: who are you to me, like the full moon of the new harvest, or like the night of the full moon, endowed with all the splendor of beauty? 88.

(14) Here, by means of the *vastu* (the expressed fact), another *vastu*—namely, that "you were not [there] at first even in another woman as you were in me"—is suggested, as illuminated by words such as *ṇava* ("new") and *paosa* ("passion").
"For there, on her lap which was like a newly wedded bride and crowded with her circle of friends, the necklace seemed to be warded off as it rose up; so how could she have enjoyed herself? (89)

(15) Here, by means of the factual matter (*vastu*), it is implied through the word "how" (*kahaṃ*) that after the breaking of the necklace, quite another kind of pleasure must have necessarily occurred; tell me, what was it like? This is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast). "Entering the door of the house, having looked at the path with a face turned back, and taking the jar upon her shoulder, you cry out, 'Alas, alas! It is lost! O friend, why do you weep? (90)

In this instance, by means of the figure of speech *hetu* (causation), the suggested fact (*vastu*) is: "Having seen him going to the place of their assignation, if you wish to go there yourself, then take another jar and go"—this is what is illuminated by the word *kiṃti*.
Or, for example: "O friend, having seen you stumbling along the path with eyes darting restlessly..."
Under the pretext of touching the water, he has fallen and been shattered, thinking that the self is heavy. // 91 //

(16) Here, on the riverbank in the thicket of creepers, you saw that he had not arrived at the time appointed for entering the house; seeing him return from the pasture, you intentionally broke the water-jar with a display of agitation under the pretext of knocking it against the door so as to make him go back to the river—this is what I have inferred. So why do you not take heart? Go, for the sake of accomplishing his desired purpose.
"I shall explain everything to your mother-in-law"— this is a *vastu* (the actual matter) concealed under the pretext of touching the door.
She, whose mind is eager for her youth that has faded by the sweet wine of the *joṅkā* flower...
Even though she is old, like a newly-wed bride, this wife of another—alas!—captivates your heart. // 92 //

(17) Here, by means of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), there is a *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) expressed through the word "another's wife" (*paravadhū*), stating that it is impossible to describe your conduct—namely, that you abandon us and pursue an elderly woman belonging to another.

In these cases, the body [of the figure] is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker fashioned by the poet. As for those manifested by the sentence, an example was given previously. However, since that which arises from the power of both word and meaning (*śabdārthobhayaśaktyudbhava*) is not manifested by a single word, there are thirty-five varieties [of *dhvani*].
(Verse 60) Even in a continuous composition, [the suggested meaning] arises from the power of the sense. //42//
As in the dialogue between the vulture and the jackal, and so forth:
"Enough of staying in this cemetery, crowded with vultures and jackals, filled with skeletons, terrible, and a source of fear for all living beings. (93)
And here, no one who has lived ever escaped the law of time;
whether beloved or hated, such is the destiny of all living beings. (94)
Thus spoke the vulture, who was powerful by day, with these words aimed at sending away the men:
"O fools, the sun still stands; show affection now!
This moment is fraught with many obstacles; perhaps he might yet live. (95)
O fools, why do you so recklessly abandon this child, who possesses the luster of gold and has not yet reached youth, merely because of the words of a vulture? (96)
Thus, the statement of the jackal howling at night, which aims at turning away the people, is well known as a literary composition (*prabandha*).
However, the other eleven varieties have not been illustrated here for fear of excessive prolixity; they should be followed by oneself according to their definitions.
By the use of the word "also" (*api*), [these varieties apply] to both words and sentences.
(Verse 61) Even in the letters that constitute a portion of a word, there exist aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like.
In that regard, by way of nature: "Victory to the third eye of Rudra, which was kissed by Pārvatī while his two eyes were blocked by his sprout-like hands as he reclined during amorous play. (97)
Now, [the expression] "it conquers" (jayati) is not appropriate, and so forth.
For even though the act of concealing is the same, its covering occurs only through a supermundane operation; therefore, that alone is superior.
Or, for example: "That beloved, having been dismissed with oaths by his mistress after prostrating at her feet, being full of longing, does not go more than two or three steps from the bedchamber."
On the contrary, she ran forward and, as if having already offered her salutation, grasped him with her hands while the knot of her lower garment was slipping; oh, how strange is the course of love!

In this context, it is "steps" (*padāni*) and not "doors" (*dvārāṇi*). This is like the distinction between the *tiṅ* and *sup* suffixes; for example: "On every path, there are sprouts as beautiful as the beaks of parrots; in every direction, the wind is the dancer of the creepers.
Upon every man, the flower-bowed God (Kāma) swiftly scatters his arrows; in every city, the practice of pride among haughty women has ceased. (99)

In this context, by the verb *kirati* ("scatters"), the state of being in process (*sādhyamānatva*) of the scattering is indicated; by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the state of completion (*siddhatva*) of the turning away (*nivartana*) is expressed; and even there, by the *kta* suffix in *avanataḥ*, the state of having already occurred (*atītatva*) is illuminated.
Or, for example: "Drawing lines on the ground outside, the lover dearer than life sits with his face cast down; the friends have abandoned food, their eyes swollen from constant weeping;
the parrots in their cages have given up all laughter and recitation; and your condition is such as this—O hard-hearted one, abandon your pride now! (100)
In this context, it is "writing" (likhan) and not "writes" (likhati); likewise,
it is "sits" (āste) and not [the finite verb].
"Seated" (*āsita*) means that he remains until the limit of serene confidence;
"on the ground" (*bhūmim*) means not "upon the ground" (*bhūmau*), for he does not draw anything else intentionally— this is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) of the verbal and nominal case endings.
Regarding the relationship [of the speaker], as in: "I am one who mounts the cow; I dwell in the village; I do not know the ways of the city.
I take away the husbands of the city women; I am whoever I may be. (101)
In this context, the genitive case in "nāgarikāṇām" (of the citizens) [expresses the agent],
while in "ramaṇīyaḥ kṣatriyakumāra āsīt" (the prince was delightful), it expresses time.

For this is the speech of Bhārgava, enraged at the son of Daśaratha who had broken the bow of Maheśvara: "O beautiful one, such has become the end of those words, of those appreciations of virtue, of those longings, and of that love. (102)

Here, by mentioning the multiplicity of the "grasping of qualities" (*guṇagrahaṇa*) and so forth, the singularity of love (*preman*) is illuminated. As for the change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*), it is as follows: "O mind, you whose desire is captivated by the tremulous eyes [of that woman], why do you dance upon seeing this deer-eyed one, abandoning the majesty of steady love? What, do you think, will you sport with? Alas! Abandon this wretched inner hope. This [woman] is indeed a stone placed at the edge of your throat in the ocean of worldly existence. (103)
Here is the irony:

Regarding the rule of prior placement [of words in a compound], even those who are esteemed for their very weakness of arm—relying almost exclusively on the methods of mere policy—are they truly fit to be lords of the earth?

But as for those whose sequence of conduct is beautiful in its adoption of both valor and statesmanship, such as you, O Indra among kings, there are at most two or three pure ones like you in the three worlds. (104)

In this verse, the preeminence of valor is understood through a specific grammatical case-ending: "O King, on that day you fought for the entire day against enemies who were formidable in battle and who maintained the sound of firm bows; yet by that very day, O Lord of Men, you attained a state of being praised as virtuous by those whose words are established by destiny. (105)
In this context, the instrumental case ending in *divasena* indicates the attainment of the result through completion.

Seeing Mādhava wandering again and again along the streets of the nearby city, Mālatī—standing at the high window of her palace’s turret—though she was Love incarnate, grew weary like a newlywed bride with limbs utterly distressed by intense longing. (106)

Here, due to the occurrence of compassion—expressed through the suffix *karuṇa*—there arises a certain transformation within that is beyond all definition, outside the scope of every word, and which has never before entered the path of experience in this birth; dense with the great delusion accumulated from the destruction of discernment, it both numbs the inner being and causes torment. (107)
In this matter, the prefix *pra-* has been elided [in the word *praharṣita*].
You have already directed your mind toward pride; what else remains? Our enemies are thus struck down.
For darkness persists only so long as the sun does not reach the crest of the mountain of sunrise. (108)
In this context, the particle "ca," which indicates *tulyayogitā* (juxtaposition), [is used as follows]:
"That Rāma has attained supreme fame in the worlds through the quality of his valor; it is only due to the reversal of our own fortune that Your Majesty does not know him."

This man is like a bard singing his praises with tears, for he utters the seven notes produced from the hollows of the massive palm trees that have become a single row due to being struck by a single arrow.

In this [verse], the use of the pronouns "atrāsau" (here he), "bhuvaneṣu" (in the worlds), and "guṇaiḥ" (by virtues)— which are [respectively] a pronoun, a nominal stem, and a case-ending— is not [intended] for "tvat" (you) or "mat" (me); rather,
it is for "asmad," which implies everyone, and which expresses the reversal of fortune by way of its failure to come to pass, and not by way of its mere absence.
While youth imparts its first arts to her eyebrows, which are like the bow of the God of Love,
this girl with eyes as tremulous as those of a startled doe now dwells upon the crest of all women.

In this regard, although [the locative] is identical to those ending in *tvā* and so forth—such as "in the state of youth" for the nature of the *imanij*, *avyayībhāva*, object, or locus; "near the bow"; and "dwelling on the head"—it is distinct.

Regarding their status as denoters (*vācaka*), there exists a certain specific quality of the word-form itself which produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*); that very quality attains the status of a suggester (*vyañjaka*).
This should be understood to apply to other cases as well.
The suggestiveness of phonemes and compositions will be illustrated in the definition of the nature of the *guṇas*.
By the force of the word "also" (*api*), this applies to entire compositions such as the *vājaka* and others.
Thus, there are six varieties of *rasa* and the rest, including the two previously enumerated divisions.
(Verse 62) Thus, the fifty-one divisions have been explained.
And when these are joined with one another, [the result is as follows]. //43//

Not only do there exist fifty-one pure varieties alone, but through threefold *saṃkara*— namely, *saṃkara* of three types, *saṃsṛṣṭi* of one type, and their own fifty-one sub-varieties by way of being objects of doubt, the relationship of the assisted and the assister, and the entry into a single suggester (*ekavyañjakānupraveśa*)— there are further divisions.
And by multiplying with the fourfold combination consisting of a single mode of association that is mutually independent,
[the result is] "Vedas, sky, oceans, sky, and moon" (40404).
(10404) together with the pure Vedas (4), [the result is] 10455, which is [the sum of] arrows (5), darts (5), yugas (4), and moons (1). //44//
In this regard, a mere indication of the direction is given by way of example:
"O brother-in-law, the momentary guest, your wife has said something to you; she is weeping in the upper chamber of the back house—go and console that poor woman. (111)

In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether the "affection" (*anunaya*) has been transferred to another object characterized by enjoyment, or whether, according to the principle of resonance (*anuraṇana*), it is the suggester (*vyañjaka*) of enjoyment itself as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The sky is smeared with the glossy, dark luster of clouds, in which cranes wheel about; the winds are laden with spray, and the sweet warbling of peacocks—the friends of the clouds—is joyous.
Let these things be as they may; I, Rāma, am of a heart so firm that I endure it all. But how will Vaidehī fare? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast. 112.

Here, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two types of *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the literal meaning is completely set aside), namely "stained" (*lipta*) and "of the friends of the clouds" (*payodasuhṛdām*).

Together with these, there exists a relationship between the *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* (where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense) expressed as "I am Rāma" and the *rasadhvani* (suggestive power of aesthetic flavor) where the literal meaning is transferred; this occurs through the relation of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāva*), as well as by the mutual entry of the single suggester (*ekavyañjaka*) characterized by the word "Rāma."
This is a confusion;
in this same manner, other examples may also be cited.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of Dhvani," in the Kāvyaprakāśa.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Thus, having determined the nature of *dhvani*, he states the subdivisions of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*:

(Sūtra 66) "The non-concealed (*agūḍha*), that which is a subordinate element of another (*aparasyāṅga*), that which is a subordinate factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*), and the indistinct (*asphuṭa*)."
When there is doubt or equal prominence [of the suggested meaning], that which is implied by intonation (kāku) is considered "not beautiful" (asundara). //45//
Thus, eight varieties of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) have been recorded.

Like the jar-like breasts of a lovely woman, the *gūḍha* (concealed) suggestion produces aesthetic charm; however, the *agūḍha* (unconcealed) suggestion, being too obvious, becomes merely the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and is therefore indeed subordinate.

An example of the unhidden (*agūḍha*) [suggestion]: "Since my enemy, having come here, pierces my ears with the torment of heated needles in the form of insults, I am that very person who was once the loom for weaving the string of his girdle; yet now, though living, I am no more—what can I possibly achieve? (113)
In this verse, the word "living" (*jīvan*) is an example of the suggested sense where the literal meaning is transmuted into another.
"With their limbs reddened by the pollen of full-blown red lotuses, bees hum sweetly in the long ponds of the house;
and here shines the orb of the sun, kissing the peak of the Eastern Mountain, with the luster of a fresh bandhujīva flower. (114)
In this instance, the literal meaning of the "kiss" is completely subordinated.
"Here was the act of binding with the serpent-noose upon your brother-in-law as he was struck deeply in the chest by Śakti; here Hanumān brought the Droṇa mountain;
here Indrajit was sent to the other world by the divine arrows of Lakṣmaṇa; and here, O deer-eyed one, the forest of the Lord of Rākṣasas' throats was cut down by someone. (115)
(1) Here, the reading "tasyāpy atra" is appropriate, referring to that which consists of a resonance rooted in the power of meaning, expressed as "by someone here."

Or, rasa and so forth may be subordinate to another [element], whether it be rasa and so forth that is directly expressed (*vācya*)— that is, having become the meaning of the sentence— or that which consists of resonance (*anuraṇana*).
Just as this hand of his, which draws up the girdle, presses upon her full breasts, touches her navel, thighs, and hips, and loosens the knot of her garment. (116)
In this instance, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) subordinates the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).

"May that radiance of the toe-nails of the Mountain-Daughter (Pārvatī), upon which the appearance of red lac was produced by the light from the forehead-eye of the Lord whose abode is Kailāsa, always protect you—she by whom the splendor of [Śiva’s] eyes, though firmly rooted as if through a flourishing rivalry, is instantly cast aside, its beauty once so charmingly imitating the *kokanada* lotus. (117)
In this case, the sentiment (*bhāva*) is *rasa* (the aesthetic flavor).
"The mountains rise exceedingly high on all sides, and the oceans likewise stretch far and wide; yet you, bearing even these, are not at all weary—homage to you!
While I was thus repeatedly offering praise out of wonder, I was suddenly reminded of your arm as it supports the earth, and my words were then silenced. (118)
In this instance, the emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the earth is subordinate to the emotion of love directed toward the king:

"O King, having taken captive the deer-eyed wives of your enemies, your soldiers embrace them, bow down before them, seize them, and kiss them on all sides as they gaze upon their beloved husbands. By our merits, you have fallen within the range of our vision, O ocean of propriety; thus, all our calamities are destroyed. In this way, you are praised by those adversaries. (119)
In this context, the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) and the semblance of sentiment (*rasābhāsa*) are illuminated by the first half and the second half [of the verse] respectively:
"By means of frequent trembling of their foreheads, frowns, threats, and roars, the intoxication of your enemies was seen; yet upon seeing you, it vanished somewhere in an instant. (120)
In this case, there is the subsiding of an emotion (*bhāva-praśama*).

When you, O Lord, were engaged with your enemies in the sport of drinking wine together with those fawn-eyed women, someone there uttered your name—though it was addressed to another—and it brought about a state of distress;
here, there is the arising of fear (*trāsodaya*).

May the Destroyer of Smara grant you joy— he who, unable to endure the asceticism that so suddenly manifested its innate power, yet being a connoisseur of the intimate conversations of the Mountain’s Daughter during their moments of repose, was simultaneously beset by both haste and hesitation when removing his disguise as a false young brahmin.
Herein is the juncture (saṃdhi) between agitation (āvega) and fortitude (dhairya).
"Look at me! O fickle one, O restless one, what haste is this? I am a young maiden; give me a hand to hold! Alas, alas! What a transgression—where are you going?
Thus does a certain maiden, living in the forest as an enemy of you, the lord of the earth, speak while gathering fruits and tender shoots.
Here, there is a variegation (*śabalatā*) of doubt, envy, fortitude, memory, fatigue, dejection, awakening, and eagerness;
and these are indeed the figures of speech known as *rasavat* and so forth.

Although the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasaṃdhi*), and the variegation of emotions (*bhāvaśabalatva*) are not [traditionally] classified as figures of speech, [they are included here].

Nevertheless, it has been stated thus so that someone might say [something further]. Even though there is no such subject matter where a commixture (*saṃkara*) or a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the suggested meaning subordinate to sound (*dhvani*) with its own subdivisions and so forth does not exist, designations nevertheless occur according to what is predominant; thus, usage is made in certain cases by means of certain [terms].
In Janasthāna, my mind blinded by the golden deer-illusion, I wandered; at every step, with tears welling up, I prattled the name "Vaidehī.
I performed the various maneuvers of the face of the Lord of Alakā; I attained the state of Rāma, yet I did not achieve the status of being the father of Kuśa and Lava. 124.

In this instance, a simile consisting of a resonant suggestion (anuraṇana) based on the power of the words—where Rāma functions as the object of comparison—is made subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācya*). "O slender-limbed one, behold! Having spent the night elsewhere, the thousand-rayed sun now arrives at dawn and, with his body faltering from the pain of separation, slowly propitiates this lotus plant by prostrating himself at her feet. (125)

(2) Here, the narrative of the hero, which is based on the power of the literal meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) and takes the form of a factual event (*vastu*), exists solely through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the independent narrative of the sun and the lotus.

An example of a factor that contributes to the establishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*) is as follows: "The poison produced by the serpent-cloud forcibly brings about whirling, restlessness, dejection of heart, dissolution, fainting, darkness, physical exhaustion, and even death for women separated from their lovers. (126)

In this case, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is *hālāhala* (poison), which serves to establish the literal meaning (*vācya*) of the serpent-form. Or, for example: "Shall I go, O Acyuta? What satisfaction could arise from seeing you? Yet, while we two remain thus in solitude, wicked people would imagine otherwise.

May Hari protect you—he whose body bristles with horripilation as he embraces the cowherd girl, who is languid with the weariness of her futile standing, as indicated by the tone of his address. (127)
(3) Here, the suggested meaning— such as "the state of being Acyuta" and so forth— is subordinate to the expressed meaning, such as the act of addressing;
and this occurs in a single instance,
by virtue of residing in a single speaker.
The distinction between these two lies in the fact that in the former case, [the emotion] resides in a different speaker.
An example of the indistinct (*asphuṭa*) is as follows: "When you are not seen, there is longing to see you; when you are seen, there is fear of separation.
Neither by being unseen nor by being seen can happiness be obtained from you. (128)

(4) Here, the *kliṣṭa* (defiled) type occurs when one thinks, "I shall act in such a way that you are not seen [by others] and that the fear of separation does not arise. An example where the predominance [of the figure] is doubtful is as follows: "But Hara, his composure slightly shaken like the ocean at the onset of moonrise, cast his eyes upon Umā’s face, whose lower lip was like the bimba fruit. (129)
(5) Here, there is a doubt as to whether the suggested sense—that he desired to kiss her—is primary, or whether the expressed action of the movement of the eyes is primary.
An example of equal prominence (*tulyaprādhānya*) is as follows: "The avoidance of transgressing against Brahmins will lead to your very prosperity;
Paraśurāma is your friend, otherwise he becomes displeased. (130)

(6) Here, in the case of the descendant of Jamadagni [Paraśurāma], there is an equal prominence of both the suggested meaning—that he will bring about the destruction of all the Rākṣasas in an instant, just as he did for all the Kṣatriyas—and the expressed meaning. An example of what is implied by intonation (*kāku*) is as follows: "Shall I not, out of anger, crush a hundred Kauravas in battle? Shall I not drink the blood from the chest of Duḥśāsana?"
I shall crush Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace; let the king make peace with you on this condition.

(7) Here, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—namely, "I am indeed churning"—exists in conjunction with the negation of the expressed meaning (*vācya*). An example of the "inelegant" (*asundara*) is as follows: "While listening to the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of *vāṇīra* reeds, the limbs of the young woman, busy with her household chores, grow weary. (132)

(8) Here, because of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that "someone who has received a secret signal has entered the thicket of creepers," the expressed meaning (*vācya*) "my limbs are sinking" becomes possessed of aesthetic charm (*sacamatkāra*).
The subdivisions of these should be understood, as appropriate, to be as previously described. (Sūtra 67) //46//

Regarding the phrase "according to the case": following the direction stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*—namely, "When figures of speech are manifested by a mere matter (*vastumātra*), they certainly possess the status of being a constituent of *dhvani*, because poetic function (*kāvyavṛtti*) rests upon them"—where a figure of speech is manifested by a mere matter, there is no status of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
(Sūtra 68)

"And their connection with suggestive expression (dhvani) through combination (saṃsṛṣṭi) and commingling (saṃkara), along with figures of speech (sālaṃkāraiḥ). By "along with figures of speech" is meant: both by those very same figures and by those [suggestive expressions] joined with figures.

As it was stated by the author of the Dhvanyāloka: "That [suggestion] shines forth in many ways again, together with its own varieties consisting of those in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) along with figures of speech (sālaṃkāra), and further through the two modes of combination (saṃkara) and commingling (saṃsṛṣṭi)."
Thus, (Sūtra 69):
"From the mutual combination [of these] alone, the number of divisions would become exceedingly great. //47//
In this manner,
when counting the intermediate subdivisions, the enumeration becomes exceedingly vast;
for instance, even in the case of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment alone, there is infinity in the enumeration of its divisions and subdivisions.
What need is there to count all of them? In summary, however, this sound (dhvani) has three varieties,
because the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) possesses three forms.
To explain: some [objects] tolerate being expressed [directly], while others do not.

Among these, those that tolerate being expressed are of two kinds: non-variegated (*avicitra*) and variegated (*vicitra*). The non-variegated consists of the mere thing (*vastumātra*), whereas the variegated takes the form of a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
Although that [poetic figure] is primarily the object to be embellished, it is nevertheless described as such according to the analogy of the "Brahmin and the ascetic.
However, the meaning characterized by rasa and so forth must not be expressed even in a dream;
for that would mean it is denoted either by the word *rasa* or by words such as *śṛṅgāra*.
Nor is it directly expressed;

for even when that [word] is employed, if the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are not employed, it is not apprehended, whereas even when that [word] is not employed, if the excitants and so forth are employed, it is apprehended. Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that it occurs solely through the medium of the expression of the excitants and so forth; therefore, it is exclusively suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Since there is no sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) and so forth, it is not to be indicated (*lakṣaṇīya*) again.

It has been established previously that in the cases of "transferred" (*arthāntarasaṃkramita*) and "completely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛta*) denotations, indication itself would not even occur without a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of a mere fact (*vastumātra*).
However, in the case of [suggestion] rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*),...

Since there is no restriction on denotation, it is beyond dispute that another meaning not directly expressed, as well as figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*) associated with it, are suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Even in the case of that variety [of suggestion] rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), it is not appropriate to establish a convention for specific instances;

therefore, where the mutual connection of word-meanings—which exist in a general form—arises by virtue of expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, resulting in a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) that is a specific form not itself a word-meaning (*apadārtha*), what [role remains] for the theory of "the connection of already-expressed meanings" (*abhihitānvayavāda*)?
Regarding the claim that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is actually the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*):
those who say, "In this context, one perceives directly the word, the elder [speaker], and the denoted object;
and one perceives the listener's comprehension through inference based on his activity," [are refuted as follows].

But by means of presumption (*arthāpatti*), based on the impossibility [of the effect] otherwise, one should understand the twofold power of cognition; one should understand the relationship as being established by three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*). //2//

In the manner thus established, when an elder (the *uttamavṛddha*) utters a sentence such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," and thereby causes a middle-aged person (the *madhyamavṛddha*) to lead an object possessing a dewlap and so forth from one place to another,
[the child] thinks: "From this very sentence, such an object was understood by him."

Thus, having inferred that [the child] through their behavior, and having ascertained the relationship characterized by the signifier-signified (vācya-vācaka-bhāva) between those two—the indivisible sentence and the sentence-meaning—by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), the child becomes proficient in that regard. Subsequently, [he hears such commands as]: "Caitra, bring the cow; Devadatta, bring the horse; Devadatta, lead the cow."
In the employment of such sentences, one ascertains the respective meaning of each respective word;

since, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is the sentence alone that brings about engagement and withdrawal and is thus fit for usage, the convention (*saṃketa*) is grasped precisely for words situated within a sentence as being already connected with their meanings as connected [to others].
Thus, the sentence-meaning consists solely of the word-meanings as qualified [by one another].

But it is not the specific relationality (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the word-meanings [that is grasped]. Even though these very words are determined by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyaya*) when they are employed in other sentences as well, the word-meaning that is the object of convention (*saṃketa-gocara*) is that which is related merely to another word-meaning.

Nevertheless, the proponents of the theory that words denote related meanings (anvitābhidhānavādins) maintain that this [meaning] is understood precisely as a particular form, though delimited by a universal, because things that are interconnected exist in such a state.

Even in their view, the object of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is a word-meaning consisting of both universal and particular forms; therefore, that which is an extreme particular, being included within the sentence-meaning, is indeed inexpressible because it has not been made the subject of convention. Thus, when a word-meaning is understood in such a case, it is far removed from the scope of expression.
In cases such as "niḥśeṣacyuta... and so forth, there is a discussion regarding injunctions and the like concerning that which has become a different meaning (arthāntarabhūta).

In the theory of Abhihitānvaya, a meaning that is unconnected [to others] is connected merely with other word-meanings; however, in the theory of Anvitābhidhāna, it is precisely the specific connected meaning that is unexpressed. Thus, according to both systems, the sentence-meaning is indeed not a word-meaning at all.

As for what is said, "Signs (nimitta) are conceptualized in accordance with their effects (naimittika)," in that regard, the status of being a sign for a word must be either its capacity as an agent (*kārakatva*) or its capacity as an indicator (*jñāpakatva*). Since a word is a manifestor (*prakāśaka*), it does not have the status of an agent. As for its status as an indicator: how could that which is unknown [indicate]? And its state of being known occurs only through convention (*saṃketa*), and that convention applies only to that which is already associated [with its meaning].

Thus, as long as the necessity of the cause (*nimitta*) has not been ascertained, how can there even be a cognition of the effect (*naimittika*)? Therefore, the statement that "causes are postulated in accordance with the effects" is an unexamined assertion.
As for those who maintain that "this is like the very long-reaching operation of an arrow," [that too is untenable].
Thus, according to the principle that "the meaning of a word is that toward which it is directed," the injunction alone is what is expressed here;
yet those who claim this while being ignorant of its true purport are merely "beloved of the gods" (fools).
For it is said: "When there is the mention of both what has been and what is to be, that which has been is taught for the sake of that which is to be.

Thus, the meanings of the words denoting factors (*kāraka*)—when construed with the meaning of the verb—are brought to a state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyamānatā*) through their connection with their own actions, which bring about the principal action.
Consequently, according to the maxim of "burning what is not yet burned," whatever has not yet been attained is enjoined as long as it remains unattained.

Just as when the performance by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is established through another means of knowledge, in the statement "the priests perform [the rite] wearing red turbans," only the state of wearing red turbans is the thing to be enjoined;
and since the act of offering (*havana*) is established from elsewhere, in cases such as "he offers with curd," only the instrumentality of the curd and so forth is the thing to be enjoined.
In some cases there is a prescription of both; in others, even a prescription of all three.
For example, in such expressions as “weave a red cloth,” and so forth.
Whether it be of one kind, two kinds, or three kinds, it follows that "the purport (tātparya) lies only in that which is to be enjoined";

thus, the purport resides only in the meaning of the word actually employed, and not in whatever is merely perceived. For instance, [in the case of the sentence] "The frontman runs... [the purport does not lie in the mere perception of the frontman].
In such cases as these, there may sometimes be an intention (*tātparya*) even toward a secondary meaning (*aparārtha*).
As for the statement, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house," [the intended meaning is] "One must not eat in this man's house."
If it is argued that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here is that this alone constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), we reply:
in that case, the particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Furthermore, there is no relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) between two verbal sentences; thus, the sentence regarding eating poison cannot be considered a subordinate part of the friend’s statement. Therefore, [the meaning is]: "This eating at home is even more wicked than eating poison."
In the statement "Do not eat in his house under any circumstances," the intended meaning (tātparya) pertains precisely to the sense conveyed by the word as it has been employed.
If the function of a word were restricted solely to denotation (*abhidhā*) regarding as much meaning as is obtained immediately following the hearing of the word,
then how [could one explain] such cases as: "A son has been born to you, O Brāhmaṇa," or "Your daughter-in-law is pregnant, O Brāhmaṇa"?

In such cases, even joy, sorrow, and the like are not the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Furthermore, why would there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even regarding the indicated meaning (*lakṣaṇīya*), since its comprehension is established solely through the operation of expression (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) that is increasingly extended? Moreover, since it is established that among direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each preceding one is stronger than the succeeding, the suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*) of the injunction (*vidhi*) is proven even under the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*). Furthermore: "Produce desire... [etc.]
Thus, how can there be defectiveness when the order of words is reversed within a poem? For in this case, an indecent meaning is not connected with other word-meanings;
therefore, it is simply not expressed at all.
Such [faults] as these would become unavoidable.

Furthermore, if the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifester (*vyañjaka*) is not accepted as distinct from the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), then the distinction made— namely, that defects such as ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) are permanent (*nitya*) while defects such as vulgarity (*saṣṭatva*) are non-permanent (*anitya*)— would be untenable.
It may be so;
yet it is not untenable, because everything indeed appears as distinct.

However, if one resorts to the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) rather than the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), then—given the manifold nature of the manifested—a systematic distinction is indeed possible, as it occurs appropriately in specific instances for specific [manifestors].

"In this pair, both have now become objects of pity by their longing for union with the Skull-Bearer (Śiva)"—in such passages, why is it that words like *kapālin* are more suitable for poetry than words like *pinākin*?
Furthermore, the expressed meaning (*vācya-artha*) is common to all understanders; [but the suggested meaning is not].
This [literal meaning] is fixed as being of a single form;
for the expressed meaning in such cases as "the sun has set" never becomes otherwise.
The suggested meaning, however, assumes multiplicity by virtue of its dependence on various specific factors, such as the particular context, the speaker, and the listener.
And likewise, from the statement "the sun has set," one understands:
"this is the opportunity to launch a surprise attack against the enemy," "let us commence our pursuit," "our beloved is almost within reach," or "let us desist from our labor."

"Let the twilight ritual be commenced," "Do not go far away," "Let the cows be brought into the house," "The heat is no longer oppressive," "Gather up the goods for sale," "My beloved has not yet arrived"— such is the endless suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) that manifests itself in each respective instance.
In the verse beginning with "niḥśeṣa" and so forth, the relationship between the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) consists of a negation and an injunction; [as in]:
"O noble ones, casting aside envy and deliberating upon what ought to be done, speak with propriety:
are the hips of the mountains to be resorted to, or rather those of playful women smiling with passion? (133).
In such instances, [the figure of speech] takes the form of a certainty that has emerged from within a doubt that was previously suspected; as in:
“O King, how can you take pride in this, that the Fortune of your enemies was seized by them even as their heads were severed by the edge of your sharp sword?
Surely, even though their enemies have been slain by you, has not their beloved Fame been carried off to the third heaven by these very men, whose limbs have now departed [from their bodies]? (134)

In such cases, there is the apprehension of the *svarūpa* (essential form) through the medium of censure or praise; of *kāla* (time), by way of its manifestation as preceding or following; and of the *āśraya* (substratum), namely sound, by virtue of its being the locus of words, parts of words, their meanings, phonemes, and syntactic structures—and this apprehension occurs through the knowledge of grammatical science (*śabdānuśāsana*), accompanied by the purity of intuition (*pratibhā*) aided by context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors.

Thus, because the cause (nimitta) brings about the designation of being merely a cognizer or being clever, as well as the mere perception or the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), there is [an absence] of number (*saṃkhyā*) in the effect—according to the method demonstrated in examples such as "The sun has set"—and [in the verse]:
"Who would not feel anger upon seeing the bitten lip of his beloved? [...]"* *Note: The second half of the verse is missing from the provided text.*
O you who smell the lotus with its bees and who are perverse in rejecting my words, endure this now! // 135 //

In such cases, even though there is a difference in the object—such as its being located in a female friend or her lover—if they were nonetheless identical, then no distinction whatsoever would exist between blue, yellow, and so forth.
For it has been said: "This alone is indeed the difference, or the cause of difference, namely, the attribution of contradictory properties and the difference in causes.
Thus, while denoters depend upon their objects, suggesters do not; therefore, the power of suggestion is not identical to the power of denotation.

Furthermore, in cases such as "vāṇīrakuḍaṅge... (in the bower of reeds), where the expressed meaning rests solely upon its own form after having manifested the suggested meaning, that is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion). In such instances, one might ask: "To what operation does that meaning—which, though not the primary purport (*atātparyabhūta*), is not denoted by its own word, yet enters the path of cognition—become the object? Is it not the case, for example, in the verse: "I am Rāma; I endure everything"?

Thus, in such instances as "By Rāma, who holds his life dear, an act was done toward his beloved that was unbecoming of love," or "That very Rāma has attained supreme renown in the worlds through the quality of his prowess," the indicated meaning (*lakṣya-artha*), though manifold, becomes the cause for specific designations; and its comprehension depends upon both word and sense, while being contingent upon context and other factors— what, then, is this?
The "newly perceived" is what is called the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*).
It is said: even though the indicated object may have multiple aspects, it possesses a fixed nature, just like the denotation of a word with multiple meanings.
Indeed, by its primary meaning, an indeterminate relation cannot be indicated;
however, that which is being understood through the force of specific factors such as context possesses a determinate relation,
whereas an indeterminate relation is manifested as a "relation of the related" (saṃbaddhasaṃbandha).
And [she said]: “The husband lies here; look well here by day, O traveler blind at night, lest you sink into my bed. (136)
In such cases, in the *dhvani* where the intended meaning is other than the expressed (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), there is a sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
How, then, can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here?
It has already been established that even in the case of indication, suggestion (*vyañjanā*) must necessarily be resorted to.

And just as denotation (abhidhā) depends upon convention (samaya), so too does indication (lakṣaṇā) depend upon a specific convention consisting of the triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning;
for this very reason, they say that indication is the "tail" of denotation.
And suggestion is not of the nature of indication alone, because it is observed to follow that [indication];
nor is it exclusively following that,
because it exists even by relying upon denotation.
Nor is it only that which follows both [meaning and sound],
for it is observed even in accordance with phonemes that are not expressive;
nor is it only that which follows the word.

Since that [function] is well-established even as occurring in such things as a glance with a third part of the eye, which is non-linguistic in nature, the function synonymous with *dhvanana* (suggestion) and others—which transcends the three functions consisting of denotation (*abhidhā*), intentionality (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is indeed undeniable.
In this regard, there is a fixed relation in cases such as "The lover is here," and so forth; and in cases such as "Whose anger would not arise? and so forth.
An indefinite connection:
“When Lakṣmī saw Brahmā seated upon the lotus of the navel, she, filled with passion, quickly covered Hari’s right eye. (137)
In such cases as this, there is a "connection of the connected" (*saṃbaddhasaṃbandha*).
For here, by the word "Hari," the right eye is suggested to be of the nature of the sun; by its closing, the setting of the sun is suggested;
and by that, the closing of the lotus.

Then, because Brahman was present there, the limbs of the cowherd girls were not visible; thus, their amorous dalliance was unrestrained. "The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) alone is the expressed meaning (*vācya*), which is to be grasped by an undivided cognition."

Even for those who assert that "the sentence alone is the expressive [unit]," since they too have fallen into the realm of ignorance (avidyā), they must necessarily employ the conceptualization of words and word-meanings; thus, even according to their view, in the aforementioned examples and others, the injunction (vidhi) and so forth are indeed suggested (vyaṅgya).

Now, it cannot be that something unrelated to the expressed meaning (vācya) is cognized, because that would lead to the absurd consequence of any object whatsoever being cognized from anything whatsoever.

Thus, since the relationship between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifestor (vyañjaka) does not necessarily exist in the absence of a connection, it results in having the same nature as inference (anumāna)— which is the cognition of the probandum (liṅgin) from a three-featured logical mark (liṅga) characterized by pervasion and subsistence in a specific locus (niyatadharmin).
For instance: "Roam about, O pious man, with confidence; that dog has been killed today by a fierce lion dwelling in the thicket on the bank of the Godāvarī river. (138)
In this case, the wandering [of a person] in this house, established by the absence of dogs, leads to the inference of non-wandering on the banks of the Godāvarī due to the perception of a lion.

For whatever wandering belongs to one who is timid is preceded by the perception of the absence of the cause of fear; yet, on the banks of the Godāvarī, a lion is perceived. This is the "perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).
To this it is replied: even a timid person might wander there by the command of a teacher or a master, or out of affection for a beloved.
Furthermore, because [the person] wanders even when such a cause of fear exists, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);

because one might fear a dog yet not fear a lion due to being a hero, it is also contradictory (*viruddha*); and the presence of a lion on the banks of the Godāvarī is not ascertained through either perception or inference.

Moreover, it is not from the mere statement [that inference occurs], for there is no validity in a statement because it lacks a necessary connection with the actual object; thus, since [the reason] is unestablished, how can the probandum be proven by such a reason?
Likewise, in the verse beginning with "niḥśeṣacyuta," those things such as the falling of sandalwood paste that are presented as indicators could also arise from other causes.

Therefore, since these have been stated here specifically as being for the purpose of ritual bathing (*snāna*), they are not invariably restricted to mere enjoyment; thus, [the reasons adduced] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the proponent of the theory of manifestation (*vyaktivādin*) has stated that these possess the power of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) when accompanied by the word *adhama*.

Furthermore, since inferiority (*adhamatva*) is not established here by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be an inference? For the proponent of *vyakti* (manifestation), it is not a flaw to argue that such a meaning is revealed from such a meaning, even in the absence of logical necessity (*upapatti*).
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Kāvyaprakāśa, titled "The Determination of the Subdivisions of Dominant, Subordinate, and Interblended Suggestive Poetry. //5//
Now begins the sixth chapter.

(Verse 70) Regarding the two types of poetry previously illustrated as "wondrous in word" and "wondrous in meaning," therein the word and the meaning exist according to the predominance of their respective qualities. //48//
But it is not the case that when there is verbal ornamentation (*śabdacitra*) the meaning lacks ornamentation, or when there is semantic ornamentation (*arthacitra*) the word lacks it.
Thus it has been said: "Metaphor (*rūpaka*) and other ornaments have been described by others in many ways for that [poetry];
yet even the face of a woman does not shine, though beautiful, if it is devoid of adornment."
Others declare that external ornament consists of figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and the like;
they desire that the derivation of nouns (*sup*) and verbs (*tiṅ*) constitutes the ornament of speech.
Regarding this, they say: "This is merely verbal elegance; such is not the true mastery of meaning.
However, we accept both, namely, the distinction between verbal ornaments and the ornaments of the expressed meaning."
Thus it is said.

An example of verbal ornamentation (*śabdacitra*) is as follows: At first, the moon rises with a reddish glow; then it possesses a golden luster; then it takes on the hue of the surface of the cheek of a slender woman languishing in separation;
and thereafter, at the onset of night, the deer-marked one rises, capable of destroying the darkness, with the brilliance of a freshly cut section of a juicy lotus root. (139)
An example of variety in meaning (*arthacitra*) is as follows: "Whom do the locks of hair of the long-lashed women not agitate here, even when they have merely fallen before one's eyes?
And so too the wicked men—who, ever clinging to deceitful falsehoods with playful charm, never abandon their blackness, just as they never abandon their crookedness. (140)
Although in all poetry, ultimately,
the conclusion arrives at the form of the *vibhāva* and so forth, nevertheless, because a manifest rasa is not perceived, these two types of poetry are said to be "without suggestion" (*avyaṅgya*).
And herein, there are many subdivisions based on the distinctions between word-ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) and meaning-ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*).
And these will be determined in the *Alaṃkāranirṇaya*.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of Verbal and Semantic Figures," in the Kāvyaprakāśa.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Having defined the nature of poetry, he states the general definition of defects (Sūtra 71): "A defect is that which destroys the primary meaning; since Rasa is the primary [meaning] and the expressed (vācya) is its substratum, words and other elements are useful for both. Therefore, that [defect] exists in them as well. (49)
The removal of the [objection regarding] the elephant;
[the phrase] "sound and so forth" includes the arrangement of phonemes by virtue of the inclusion of "and so forth.
He states the definition of the particularity: (Sūtra 72).

A defective word is one that is harsh to the ear, corrupt in its grammatical formation, unidiomatic, or semantically incapable; it may also have its meaning obscured, convey an inappropriate sense, be redundant, fail to express the intended meaning, or be indecent in three ways. (50)

[The defects of a compound are: ambiguity, unintelligibility, vulgarity, lack of clarity of meaning, obscurity, failure to distinguish the predicate portion, contradiction, and excessive prolixity. (51)

(1) "Harsh to the ear" (*śrutikaṭu*) refers to that which is faulty due to its harsh-sounding phonemes, as for example: "When will he attain his heart's desire, embraced by that slender-limbed woman with her side-glances rippling like waves, which are the very temple-houses of the god of love? (141)
In this context, it is called "the state of having achieved the goal."

(2) “*Cyutasaṃskṛti*: Lacking the characteristics of grammatical refinement, it is as follows: ‘Alas! This pair of breasts, with their dark centers like slightly ripened *tinduka* fruits and pale edges, appears fit for the touch of the hands of a handsome Pulinda; O daughter of the village chief, that elephant herd, distressed by their plea for safety from the frontal lobes, entreats you—do not cover your pair of breasts with leaves! (142)

Regarding this, it is said: "He entreats" (*anunāthate*). Just as in examples such as "he entreats for ghee" (*sarpiṣo nāthate*), the Ātmanepada ending is prescribed for the root *nāth* specifically in the sense of a benediction, according to the rule "the root *nāth* [takes the Ātmanepada] in the sense of a benediction" (*āśiṣi nāthaḥ*).
In this context, however, the meaning is "to beg";
therefore, it should be read as "he entreats the pair of breasts."
(3) "Improperly employed": likewise,
even that which has been handed down by poets is not accepted if it is perceived as being consistently of a cruel nature, as in this case.
Thus I think that, by the power of fate, he must be either a Piśāca or a Rākṣasa.
In this context, although the word *daivata* is recorded as masculine in the rule "the [words] *daivata* etc. are [masculine] or [neuter]," it is not employed by anyone in the masculine gender.
(4) "It is incapable."
That which is recited for a certain purpose, yet he has no power over it—for example:
"Having acquired merit by bathing at other sacred fords, he now respectfully destroys [the sins] of this river with its beautiful current. (144)
In this context, the word "strikes" (hanti) has the sense of "goes."
(5) "With its meaning frustrated" (*nihatārtha*): that which is employed when both meanings are [intended] but the intended meaning is not established.
For example: "By her lover, whose hair was stained with blood from a blow of a foot moistened with liquid lac-dye..."
Seeing him, she was startled by fear; yet, she was suddenly kissed. 145.
In this case, by the word *śoṇita* (blood), which has the conventional meaning of "blood," its intended sense of being "made radiant" is obscured. (6) "Inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārtha*):
For example—That which is obtained with great effort by ascetics after a long time, and which is desired by those performing sacrificial sessions;
Those illustrious ones, having become sacrificial animals in the horse-sacrifice of battle, swiftly attain that goal.
In this context, the word *paśu* (beast) reveals cowardice; thus, it is an instance of "inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārtha*).
(7) "Meaningless" refers to an initial word whose purpose is merely to fill out the meter (*pādapūraṇa*);
for example: *utphullakamalakesaraparāgagauradyute mama hi gauri*.
O Blessed One, may my desired wish be fulfilled through your grace. // 147 //
For here, the word "hi" (indeed) [is used].

(8) “Inexpressible”: For example—“Embodied beings become submissive of their own accord to one who does not bind his anger and who destroys calamities; but toward a person who is devoid of indignation, neither affection nor respect for an enemy arises. (148)
In this context, the word *jantu* (creature) is intended to mean "one who does not give," yet it is not directly expressive of that meaning.

Or, for example: "Alas! That moon-faced woman, so dark [in complexion], was indeed seen by me; the day since she was seen has been rendered like a night of darkness due to the pain of separation from her, and has become as if scorched.
What can we do? The Creator is always adverse toward our welfare; otherwise, why would my world of living beings now consist entirely of nights? (149)

In this context, the word *dinam* (day) is non-expressive (*avācaka*) when its intended meaning is "that which consists of light. Furthermore, that which has shifted to another meaning due to association with a prefix (*upasarga*) is also non-expressive;

for example: "The [leg] whose stalk is the thigh, formidable with a row of filaments shining with the rays of the toenails, possessing young sprouts in the form of the spreading luster of fresh lac-dye, and where the charming anklets are the bees..."

Victorious is the fresh staff-like foot of Bhavānī, which, in its imitation of her husband’s dance, creates the beauty of a lotus born from the pond of the natural, translucent loveliness of her own body. 150.
In this context, the word *vidadhat* has the meaning of *dadhat*.

(9) "The indecorous" (*aślīla*) is of three kinds, because it manifests shame, disgust, or inauspiciousness. For example: "He possesses a most formidable means [of power] such as is not seen in anyone else;
what other person could withstand the arched brow of that wise man? (151)
(1) Struck by a lotus in play, his lower lip bitten by another woman without his knowledge, a certain man stood with his eyes closed as if his vision were impaired by the filaments of the flower.
There, a charming girl stood blowing air upon him with her face like a bud; whether through delusion or through guile, she was incessantly kissed by him without her bowing down. 152.
(2) Disturbed by a gentle breeze due to the destruction of my beloved, this peacock’s plumage has today become unrivaled in its deep luster.
While the beautiful-haired woman still possesses her mass of hair, loosened by passion and laden with flowers, whom could this bird captivate? 153.
(3) Among these, the words *sādhana*, *vāyu*, *vināśa*, and *śabda* suggest embarrassment and so forth.

(10) “Ambiguous”: for example—“The venerable one has been embraced by the glory of victory in the next world; therefore, placing a venerable succession of blessings at my ear, please show me compassion. (154)
In this case, there is a doubt as to whether she is a woman abducted by force who should be reviled, or one who is worthy of salutation.
(11) "Unfamiliar" (*apratīta*) refers to that which is well-known only within a specific treatise.

For example: "For one who possesses a mind whose latent dispositions have been shattered by the great light of right knowledge, even this [action] being performed would not become a bond of karma. (155)
In this context, the word *āśaya* is a synonym for *vāsanā*, used specifically in works such as the Yoga Śāstra.

(12) “Vulgar” (*grāmya*) is that which exists only in common worldly usage; for example: “Your face, having received the splendor of the full moon, and your waist, possessing the beauty of a slab of refined gold, captivate the mind. (156)
In this context, it is the waist.
(13) “[Regarding] ‘of interpretable meaning’: ‘Some figurative indications (*lakṣaṇā*) have become established through their capacity, like primary denotations;
some are currently being employed, while others are not at all due to incapacity.’”
Thus, that which is prohibited is the figurative (lākṣaṇika).
For example: "O slender one, your face makes the beloved of the full-moon night, shining forth in the autumn season, a recipient of a slap. (157)
In this case, being defeated by the striking of a palm is indicated.
Now, the connection is that only that which occurs within a compound is defective;
the other [type of defect] is both independent and occurring within a compound.
(14) "Afflicted" (*kliṣṭa*): because the comprehension of the meaning is obstructed,
as [in the case] of those illuminated by the rising light produced from the eye of Atrī.
O protector of the earth, your conduct is exceedingly worthy and shines with great splendor.
The meaning is: by means of the night-lotuses (kumuda) shining with the rising light of the moon born from the three eyes [of Śiva].

(15) “*Avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśam*” means that in which the *vidheyāṃśa* (the element to be predicated) is not clearly indicated (*avimṛṣṭa*) as being primary. For example: “Of those whose false greatness born of victory over the world was acquired through the grace of the Lord’s feet—which were washed by streams of blood flowing incessantly from their throats after their heads had been severed and tossed up—”

What fruit is there in these arms of theirs—proud with surging arrogance that betrays their desire to make Mount Kailāsa tremble—if they must now exert themselves merely to protect this city? // 159 //
In this case, the "false majesty" (mithyāmahimatva) is not the subject of restatement (anuvādya), but rather that which is to be predicated (vidheya).

Or, for example: "She repeatedly lowered from her hips the girdle of kesara flowers, which was like a second bowstring deposited there by Smara, who knows the proper place, as he prepared to draw his bow. (160)
In this case, it is merely the state of being "second" that is to be imagined;
"maurvīṃ dvitīyām" (the second bowstring) is the appropriate reading.
Or, for example: "The body whose birth was indicated by the eye of Virūpākṣa, and wealth revealed by the state of being Digambara..."
O fawn-eyed one, is that which is sought among desirable things even partially present in the Three-eyed Lord? (161)
In this case, it should have been stated as "unperceived birth.
Or, for example: "The ocean of bliss, the sole abode for binding the heart characterized by extreme restlessness—she who was never for even a moment released by you;
yet now, the anxiety concerning her news spreads exhaustion over you. Fie, fie upon us! (162)

In this case, the negation "she is not liberated" (*na muktā*) is what is to be predicated. For example: "This is a newly formed rain-cloud, not a haughty night-stalker; this is a rainbow drawn far back, not his bow."
This too is a sharp downpour of rain, not a succession of arrows; this is lightning, glistening like gold on a touchstone, not my beloved Urvaśī.
In this passage, nothing else is enjoined by way of restating his state of liberation (amuktatā), as in:
"He protected himself, undaunted; he practiced dharma, free from ailment."
Free from greed, he acquired wealth; unattached, he experienced happiness.
In this context, by way of restating [the state of] being terrified and so forth, there is the concealment of the self.
(16) "Creating a contradictory impression"; for example: "He whose conduct is as skillful as the rays of the moon—how can we describe that sole friend of misdeeds? (165)
In this case, what is intended to be expressed is "a friend without [common] purpose," yet the cognition that arises is "a friend for an improper act."
Or just as a beloved woman, bestowing the joy of sight after a long time, suddenly embraces her lover around the neck. 166.
In this case, one should have said "embracing by the neck" (*kaṇṭhagraham*).

Or, for example: "If [the bow] was not broken out of fear—since the soul of the Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, is pacified by a continuous stream of compassion for all beings—then why has Skanda been forgotten?
He who, as the son of that Lord, brought joy to the whole world by slaying Tāraka, who was blinded by pride; or else, how could he have forgotten me, his dear disciple, like Skanda himself? (167)

May that beloved of Ambikā protect you—he who, though the husband of Bhavānī, conveys the notion of being the husband of another Bhavānī; and who, though the lion of the Mountain-Daughter’s mount, has attained the state of being her own vehicle, yet remains free from egoism in her presence. (168)
In this context, the phrase "beloved of Ambikā" gives rise to a contradictory notion.
“Harshness of sound” (*śrutikaṭu*) occurring within a compound is, for example: “She is far away, her eyes rippling with thick nectar;
this time has arrived, which is fit for the cry of a peacock. (169)
In this same way, other [cases] should also be understood.

(Verse 47) Having set aside [the defects] of corrupted euphonic combination (*cyutasaṃskāra*), incapacity (*asamartha*), and meaninglessness (*nirarthaka*): these same defects exist in a sentence as well, and some of them also occur in a portion of a word (*pada*). //52//
Some [verbs], but not all;

here are examples in order: "He studied the Vedas, he worshipped the gods, he gratified the ancestors, he honored his kinsmen, he conquered the group of six [internal foes], he delighted in policy, and he destroyed his enemies by the roots. (170)
May he grant you a succession of those who are free from envy;
and may he sever those who are unworthy by means of defects such as deafness and dumbness.
In this context, *duścyavana* means Indra;
*aneḍamūka* means one who is both mute and deaf.

O King, your fame shines most brilliantly, radiant with the luster of the moon, belonging as it does to one whose arm has the arrow for its companion and who has subdued the lords of the earth under the banner of the fish-emblemed god of love. 172.
In this context, words such as *sāyaka* and others are well-known as synonyms for sword, ocean, earth, moon, and fame, respectively, while retaining their conventional meanings of arrow and so forth.
O Lord, you are indeed a weaver who weaves a multitude of virtues on all sides; these naked ones sing of your fame in every direction.
Nevertheless, your glory—beautiful with its every limb clearly manifest, white as the autumnal moonlight—wanders here without any covering.
In this case, the word *kuvinda* (weaver) conveys a different meaning that reveals the disparagement of the person being praised; thus, it is an instance of "inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārtha*).
"Having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, which is as radiant as a mass of clouds, this Sun (the one with seven horses) causes the thousand-petaled lotuses to fall asleep, intent on flight. (174)

In this verse, the words *prābhrabhrāṭ*, *viṣṇudhāma*, *viṣama*, *aśva*, *nidrā*, and *parṇa* are non-expressive (*avācaka*) of the meanings "excellent cloud," "sky," "seven horses" (the sun), "contraction," and "petals," respectively.
As she approached the king, the tremulous-eyed maiden,
filled with the zeal for various weapons, brought about his infatuation.
In this context, words such as *upasarpaṇa* (approaching), *praharaṇa* (striking), and *mohana* (deluding) are indecorous because they evoke shame.
Those poets whose activity consists in grasping other meanings consume what has been vomited by others and eat the excrement of others. (176)
In this matter, words such as "vomiting," "excretion," and "discharge" evoke loathing.
"I shall go to that abode of my ancestors along with my retinue, where, in the lineage of the Fire-god, my heart shall instantly become free from the thorn of grief. (177)
In this context, when "the father's house" and so forth is intended, the perception of a cremation ground and the like results in an inauspicious meaning.
Devoted to the splendor of the abode of the gods, having attained sufficient trembling, intent upon seeking [the goal], and possessing radiant ashes—let this one be beheld. (178)
In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether words such as *surā* and so forth refer to divine armies, arrows, and splendors, or whether they refer to liquor and so forth.
O friend, that effort of yours, which was grounded in firm resolve and characterized by intense urgency and superior skillful means, has now borne fruit upon the attainment of what you desired.
In this context, terms such as "excessive means" (*adhimātropāya*) and so forth are unfamiliar because they are employed exclusively within the treatises on Yoga.
This man, with his cheeks full of betel, prattles nonsense;
yet he always eats and drinks exactly as he pleases.
In this context, words such as *galla* and others are considered vulgar.
With feet of vaidūrya set in cloth, she has completely suppressed the dust of the earth;
steady and composed, she now perceives the battle of the eyes. 181.
Here, by the venerable Ratnapāda, darkness has been destroyed and the earth made firm; yet the command "awaken the pair of eyes" is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha).

Upon beholding the beauty of Dhammilla’s hair, whose eyes were like those of a young fawn, whose mind was unacquainted with such a novel arrangement, who would not be filled with intense longing? 182.
In this case, there is the fault of "clumsiness" (kliṣṭatva) because the connection—"Whose mind does not become impassioned upon beholding the beauty of Dhammilla?"—is obscure.
This indeed is my humiliation: that my enemies remain there; and even he, that ascetic, stays right here slaughtering the race of Rākṣasas—alas, Rāvaṇa still lives!
Fie, fie upon Indrajit! And what is the use of Kumbhakarṇa, who has merely been awakened? What is the use of these arms, puffed up in vain for plundering the petty village of heaven?
In this case, it should have been stated as "this very thing is an insult";
furthermore, only the swelling itself is the subject of the restatement (anuvādya),
not that which is qualified by futility.

In this case, because the arrangement of words has been made in reverse order, it is a defect of the sentence itself, not of the sentence-meaning. Or, for example: "O fortunate lady, he who has arrived [for you] spreads across your eyes a ripple-like movement reaching the outer corners, a playful arching of the brows at their curved ends, and a spreading mantle of horripilation over your body. (184)

In this context, the two words "yo" (who) and "asau" (that) are the subjects of the restatement (*anuvādya*), which effect the cognition of the object here. For instance, a word beginning with *tat* (such as *saḥ*)—referring to an object that has been introduced, is well-known, or has been experienced—does not require the employment of a word beginning with *yat*. Examples follow in order: [Example 1: Referring to what has been introduced] "Having seen that [person] who was previously mentioned... (*yaḥ pūrvaṃ prakrāntaḥ tam dṛṣṭvā...*) [Example 2: Referring to what is well-known] "...that [sun] which is well-known in the world... (*loke yaḥ prasiddhaḥ sa sūryaḥ...*) [Example 3: Referring to what has been experienced] "...that [elephant] which was experienced by me... (*mayā yo 'nubhūtaḥ sa gajaḥ...*) Thus, the use of the demonstrative pronoun (*asau*) is established without depending on the relative pronoun (*yaḥ*).
"Pure policy is cowardice; valor is the behavior of a beast of prey.
Therefore, he sought success through the combination of both. (185)
Now both have fallen into a state of pitiable wretchedness through their longing for union with the Skull-bearer:
she, the radiant digit of the Moon, and you, the moonlight for the eyes of this world.
Trembling, with the hem of your garment slipping away in fear, casting your distressed eyes in every direction—
you were not seen by that cruel fire, which, blinded by its own smoke, suddenly consumed you in its ferocity.

However, when the word *yat* (which) is employed as following the subsequent sentence, it does not require the employment of the word *tat* (that) which follows the preceding sentence by virtue of its inherent power (*sāmarthya*).
For example: "By the lotuses, a fine thing was done for the moon, which already abounds in loveliness, that they closed their eyes;
yet, when the victorious face of the beloved rose up, they committed a further act of rashness. (188)
However, a word beginning with *ya-* that has been previously employed remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) without the employment of a word beginning with *ta-*,
as occurs here in this very verse through the transposition of the first two quarters.
However, when both are mentioned, their lack of mutual expectancy is well-established.
Even when neither is explicitly mentioned, both are understood through implication in certain cases;
for example: "As for those who spread contempt toward us here, they know something [of our intent]; this effort is not directed toward them."
"Someone of equal nature to me will arise; for time is infinite and the earth is vast. (189)
In this context, "that which will arise" refers to what is to come;
thus, if the word *tat* (that) were not employed, there would be a sense of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Nor does the word *asau* (this) express the meaning of *tat*.
With its lovely filaments kissed by the breeze, led by the bright orb of the moon,
and gazed upon by the eyes of women distressed at being separated from their lovers, the spring season has arrived like Hanumān.

For in this case, there is no comprehension of the meaning of that word [“he”]. Or, if there were such comprehension: “He who, assisted by arms formidable as thunderbolts, was the peerless champion in battle against Arjuna—were he to be employed by the king in this matter, then the task would indeed be accomplished. (191)
In this case, the word "he" (sa) would be redundant.

Now, O Lord, for one who perceives this entire circle of objects as non-conceptual and as Your own body—when the world is filled with his own side [of allies] and enemies alike—whence can there be fear for him who is eternally happy? (192)
It is said that, just like the word *idam*, the word *adas* denotes the referent of the word *tat*; therefore,
its mention is appropriate here in this other sentence, but not there in that very same one.
For a word situated in proximity to the relative pronoun *yat* refers back to something well-known;
as in: "That formidable and most fierce kṣatriya splendor which belonged to this king—surely even that was lost by him while playing with dice. (193)
In this [verse], there is the word *tat* (that).
Now, one might ask: "How is it that you are the vessel of auspicious splendors, O Universal-formed One? Bestow upon me abundantly the foremost glory; O God, be gracious!
Whatever sin I have committed, O Lord of the World, strike it down from me as I bow before you. Grant me every blessing, O Blessed One, for the sake of supreme welfare. (194)
In this context, having said "whatever," it was then said "that [tell] me.

It is explained as follows: by the phrase "whatever," any entity whatsoever existing in whatever form is implied as being the universal self (*sarvātman*); that very thing, being of such a nature, is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*).
Or, for example: "Was Bharata overcome by greed, by whom this was done toward his mother, who has thus fallen into the frailty of a woman? Or was it my middle mother herself?"

"This thought of mine is false; that he is both the younger brother of my noble elder and my teacher, and that she is my mother and my father's wife—I consider this arrangement made by the Creator to be improper. (195)

In this case, one should say "of the noble one" (*āryasya*) or "of the father" (*tātasya*), but these two should not be made subordinate members within a compound. The same should be illustrated for other types of compounds as well.

An example of that which produces a contradictory notion: "Resorting to patience, their lands reddened [with blood], and their bodies embraced by jackals, they now lie with their lives departed, having abandoned all strife. (196)
In this case, while it is intended to convey that those endowed with qualities such as auspicious moments (kṣaṇa) dwell in happiness, the perception of "slain" (hatāḥ) constitutes a contradiction.

Examples for each part of the word, as applicable, in order: "Enough with this union with a woman, because of its extreme fickleness, its resemblance to a dream or an illusion, and its bitterness at the end.
Even if we contemplate this truth a hundred times over, the inner self still does not forget the deer-eyed one. (197)
In this regard, however, [the Lord says]:
"Or rather, go for the sake of success; perform the work of the gods, for this purpose can only be achieved through another means.
It requires a causal condition for its attainment, just as the sprout of a seed requires water before it can arise. (198)
In this regard, "ddhyai bdhyai"—this is the pungent [note].

And he who, with his peaks, bears a richness of minerals that produces the playful ornaments of the Apsarases, appearing like an untimely twilight whose colors are distributed by scattered fragments of clouds. (199)
In this context, the word *matta* has the sense of "intoxicated," which constitutes the fault of *nihitārtha* (a word used with its meaning suppressed).
At first, their forms were smeared with a mass of collyrium; then, they were scorched by the spreading fire of separation fanned by the gusts of their sighs.

Now, the fawn-eyed maiden freely performs the ritual of "drinking" (*pānakarma*) for the arrows of the god whose mind is the source of desire, using the water of her tears as the consecrating libation.
In this context, the plural number in the word *dṛśām* (of glances) is meaningless,
because only one woman, "the fawn-eyed one," is mentioned.

Nor can the plurality be justified on the basis of a difference in activity— as in the case of the expression *alasavalitaiḥ* (with languidly rolling [glances])— because no such distinct activities are actually presented here.
Furthermore, the word "vision" (dṛk) does not denote an activity here;
in this very context, the middle-voice ending in "kurute" would also be purposeless.
Because when the fruit of the principal action is not connected with the agent, there is an absence of the fruit of the action intended for the agent.

The preceptor of archery is the conqueror of Tripura; Kārttikeya is the one to be conquered; the ocean is your abode when occupied by weapons; and this earth is your abundant sacrificial fee (*hantakāra*).
All this is indeed true; yet, does your sword Candrahāsa feel ashamed before your axe, which has already performed the act of severing the throat of Reṇukā? || 201 ||
In this context, the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya-pratyaya*) in the word *vijeya* is non-expressive (*avācaka*) of the meaning of the past passive participle suffix (*kta-pratyaya*).
