The rogue utters words that are exceedingly thin, extremely limited in syllables, and most insignificant; yet, in reality, he carries within him one who is truly sensitive, as if fashioned from the Kālakūṭa poison.
In this context, the word *pelava* [is used].

He who is purified by bathing in the multitude of holy fords at the mouths of the celestial rivers, and by the firm rooting of the cultivation of the scriptures—he, the noble-born and preeminent among the powerful, falls within the sight of only a rare few men. (203)
In this context, the word "pūya" (pus) [is used].
O dear one, how can he who was always such a unique sanctuary for his devotion to the Vinaya be seen today as being the same, having attained the state intended by that [Vinaya]? 204.
Now follows the word *preta*.
In what action does his capability not shine forth most brightly?
Since he is a follower of the virtuous, let this salutation with joined palms be offered here to him.
In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether "sādhu" comes first, or whether it means "he behaves toward those who are good."
What can be said of this great jewel upon the garland of crowns of kings, whose splendor is perceived even by those who are exceedingly difficult to overcome with the arrows of speech? (206)
Here, by the word *vacaḥ*, the word *gīḥ* is indicated through metaphorical designation (*lakṣyate*).
Indeed, in this case, not only the preceding member of the compound,
but even the subsequent member cannot tolerate a substitution of synonyms.

In cases such as *jaladhi* ("ocean"), it is only the final member [of the compound] that is [accented]; whereas in cases such as *vaḍavānala* ("submarine fire"), it is only the initial member that is [accented].

Although certain varieties such as *aprayukta* (unemployed) and others belong exclusively to the *asamartha* (semantically incompetent), they have nevertheless been demonstrated by other theorists through specific classification; thus, they are stated separately and illustrated by way of showing these distinctions.

(Verse 75) [The defects are: harshness of sound (*pratikūlavākya*), broken euphony (*upahata*), elided pause (*luptāvasarga*), faulty sandhi (*visaṃdhi*), defective meter (*hatavṛtta*), deficient words (*nyūnapada*), redundant words (*adhikapada*), repeated words (*kathitapada*), falling excellence (*patatprakarṣa*), and resuming what has been concluded (*samāptapunarātta*). //53//

(Defects of meaning include: using two words for one sense (*ardhāntaraikavācaka*), employing a compound where it is not prescribed by the rules of the system (*abhavanmatayogamanabihitavācya*), placing a word in the wrong position (*apadasthapada*), a misplaced compound (*apadasthasamāsa*), the confused (*saṃkīrṇa*), the parenthetical (*garbhita*), and that which contradicts established usage (*prasiddhihata*). //54//
A sentence is likewise [defective] when its progression is broken, when it lacks proper sequence, or when it confuses one's own interest with that of another.
(1) The suitability of phonemes to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) will be discussed; the opposite of that is "discordant phonemes" (*pratīkūlavarṇa*).
For example, in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa: "O sweet-voiced one, me who am filled to the throat with unrestrained longing..."
Place [your hand] for a moment upon the conch-like neck of the slender-necked woman and remove her distress of the throat.
This very land, where lakes were filled with the blood of enemies, has become like Raurava; such was the humiliation of my father, the seizing of his hair by the enemy.
Those same resplendent weapons of mine, heavy with the power to devour the arms of my foes, are here; for the wrathful son of Droṇa performs exactly what was done by Rāma.
For in this context, a harshness of syllables (*vikaṭavarṇatva*) and long compounds (*dīrghasamāsatva*) are appropriate.

For example: "May the flaming axe, hurled in an instant by the pillar-like arm of the formidable Bhārgava—impelled by his wrath upon seeing the bow of Śambhu split in two by Niśumbha whom he had never encountered before—become a guest at the base of your neck, so that by this very weapon the Lord Hara may be proclaimed throughout the worlds as 'Khaṇḍaparaśu' (the one with the broken axe). (209)
But where there is no anger, when expressing the fourth quarter, the employment of words is exactly the same.
(2) That in which the *visarga* has become damaged (*upahata*) or (3) has been elided (*lupta*),
such as: "The king here is wise, disciplined, skillful, and handsome."
He whose servants are exultant in their strength, devoted, and distinguished by their intelligence; // 210 //
(4) *Visandhi* is the discordance of euphonic junction (*saṃdhi*), which consists of disjunction, vulgarity, and harshness.
Among these, the first is as follows: "O King, your deeds shine forth—those which possess the luster of the moon even within the netherworld (*rasātala*).
O you who extend your vast power of intellect and your unwearied strength, acting with propriety, you shine having attained the perfection of victory. (211)
Or just as the moon, rising from that [mountain], possesses a lofty, radiant, and golden luster as it emerges from the high peak of the eastern mountain.
Alas! His own lineage, possessing the noble and radiant luster of a pearl, shines forth as something of priceless value, like a precious gem.
"I will not perform the *saṃhitā* even once at my own will"—this is a fault; however, when the cause is *pragṛhya* and so forth, it is a fault repeatedly.
"Having flown up into the sky with a swift and heroic motion, this bird is soaring away;
therefore, take your pleasure right here."
In this case, there is indecorousness due to the intentional ambiguity of the compound.
"O broad one, here this row of trees stands beautifully at the edge;
it is not proper to go straight ahead here—bend your head slightly. (214)

(4) *Hatavṛtta* (defective meter) is that verse where, even when following the formal characteristics, the meter is unpleasant to hear, lacks a heavy syllable at the end where one is required, or is discordant with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Examples in order: "Amṛta is nectar—of this there is no doubt; nor is it otherwise with honey. Even the fruit of the mango is exceedingly sweet and possesses a clear juice.
Yet, let a person who is impartial and ignorant of other tastes say once more: what else could be sweeter than the lip of a beloved? (215)
In this regard, "yadihānyatsvādu syāt" is unpleasing to hear; or as in:
"That which cannot be avoided even slightly by the quality of its beauty..."
However, there is one whose fault has been acknowledged even by his opponents. // 216 //
In this [verse], the second and third *gaṇas* consist of the syllables *sa* and *bha*.

Spring captivates the mind even of the sage—spring, which possesses a swarm of bees humming with the enchanting fragrance of blossoming mango trees, and which bears the beauty of beautiful chowries made of fresh sprouts. (217)
In this context, the word *hāri* [is used];

the reading *hāri-pramudita-saurabha* is appropriate. Or as it is said: "Those other lands are the source-mountain for the jewels of virtues; that soil is indeed different; those constituent materials are truly unique—by which [materials] this youth was created by the Creator."
[It was seen] from the palms of the hands of their enemies—who possessed glorious beauty—and from those of the women. // 218 //
In this context, in the reading "vastrāṇy api," even that which is light acquires heaviness.
Alas, King! Alas, wise one! Alas, friend of poets, O Lord who was the refuge of thousands of brahmins!
O jewel within the assembly of the simple and the learned, where have you gone, and where are we, these followers of yours? (219)
This meter (*vṛtta*) manifests the sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*). An example of a verse with deficient words (*nyūna-pada*) is as follows:

"Having seen the daughter of Pañcāla in such a state in the assembly of kings, having lived for a long time in the forest with hunters while wearing bark garments, and having stayed in Virāṭa’s residence concealing our unaccustomed activities—even now, my elder brother feels grief for me who am exhausted, but not for the Kurus. (220)
In this context, "by us" is placed before "weary," and "thus" is likewise [placed].

(7) How much more so [is he] one who is as stainless as the form of a crystal, who has fully reflected upon the sharp truths of the scriptures, whose speech and reasoning are consistent and endowed with harmony, and who causes his rivals to set while he himself rises—such a person is truly extraordinary. 221.
In this context, there is the word *ākuñci* (contraction).
For example: "Or how strange and out of order it is that men here still experience amorous transformations even in old age;
and furthermore, that the life or the love of broad-hipped women has not been made to end with the sagging of their breasts. (222)
Regarding the phrase "done here" (*atra kṛtam*): on the contrary, such a construction brings about a breach of the intended structure.
And so it is said: "Furthermore, that which [is not done] by those with the eyes of a deer..."
In this reading, the cognition is indeed free from expectancy.

(8) An example of a repeated word (*kathitapada*) is as follows: "O fair-limbed one, tell me, whose royal consecration as the crown prince of the King Smara does this clearly manifest—the pallor of your cheeks that fades away from the friction of feigned sleep upon the surface of your palm? (223)
In this context, "līlā" means play.

(9) An example of *patatprakarṣa* (falling excellence): "Who, who, where, would not grunt with a terrible *ghur-ghur* sound from his snout? Which elephant is not intent on making this lotus-pool devoid of lotuses?
Which wild buffaloes would not uproot which forests? For the lion dwells here, bound by the playful affection of his lioness. (224)

(10) *Samāptapunarātta* (the resumed after completion): May the sound of the bow of Love, the cry of the cuckoos of amorous play, the humming of the bees of the clusters of Rati, the call of the playful cakora birds, the tinkling of bracelets slipping from the tossing arms that cast off the bodice of the slender maiden, and the sound of the flute for the dance of fresh youth—may these extend love unto you! (225)

(11) An example where a single word from the latter half serves as a supplement for the first half: "Walk with gentle steps; the ground is covered in *darbha* grass; place the hem of your garment upon your head; the heat is fierce"—thus was the daughter of Janaka beheld on the road by the wives of travelers with eyes full of tears, and she was thus instructed. // 226 //
(12) That in which a connection (yoga), meaning a relationship (saṃbandha), is considered (mataḥ) or intended (iṣṭaḥ) [is called *abhavadyoga*].
For example: "Those whose heat of valor drank the streams of ichor from the elephants of the gods, and who fashioned pleasure-drinking grounds in the shade of the Nandana groves."
What have those night-stalkers achieved—whose mere roars caused even the Lord of the Gods to tremble—that is worthy of mention or capable of pleasing you? Nothing at all.

In this context, according to the principle stated as "And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality," since the meanings indicated by the word *yat* (which) lack mutual coordination, no specific distinction is perceived in the phrase *yaiḥ*. Therefore,
the reading *kṣapācāribhiḥ* (by those who wander at night) is appropriate, as it provides the necessary coordination.

Or rather, since you possess such beauty and he is the familiar limit of loveliness and the arts, it is by good fortune that you two alone occupy the pinnacle here; O fortunate one, since this pair accords so well with you both, whatever remains thereafter will then be won by your excellence.
In this passage, where "yat" occurs, there is no mention of "tad," and where "tadānīm" occurs, there is no mention of "yadā. The reading "cet syāt" would be more appropriate.
Or, for example: "O King, listen as you have arrived on the battlefield and strung your bow—to see what was suddenly encountered by each [of us]."
From the bow come arrows; from the arrows, the head of the enemy; by that, the circle of the earth; by that, you; by you, incomparable fame; and by that fame, the three worlds.
In this case, if the object of the act of hearing were [the individual items], then "the bow" and "the arrows" would follow as the objects of the sentence-meaning;
however, neither the referent of the word *yat* nor its qualifiers are the bow, the arrows, and so forth.
Nor is there a question such as "by whom? and so on.
Or as in: "The master archer, the conqueror of Tripura... (230).
In such passages, the intended meaning is the censure of Bhārgava;
however, that [censure] is perceived in relation to the axe through the word *kṛtavatā*.
But if the reading were *kṛtavataḥ*, there would be a connection with the mind (*mati*).
Or rather: "We four are the officiating priests, the blessed Hari is the preceptor of the ritual, the king is initiated for the sacrifice of battle, and his wife has taken her vow;

the Kauravas are the sacrificial animals, and the pacification of the suffering caused by the humiliation of our beloved is the fruit—thus does the drum resound loudly, summoning the royal army. (231)
In this case, because the word *adhvara* (sacrifice) has become subordinate within the compound, its meaning is not connected with all [the other members]. For example:

"Victorious is the fresh *daṇḍapāda* (staff-like foot) of Bhavānī during her imitation of her Lord’s dance; it possesses shanks that are like stalks, formidable with rows of filaments shimmering from the rays of her toenails, with young sprouts in the form of the spreading luster of fresh lac-dye, and bees in the form of charming anklets—creating the beauty of a lotus born from the pond of the natural, transparent loveliness of her own body. (232)
Here, Bhavānī’s own body is perceived as resting upon the staff, yet it is intended to be understood as belonging to her [the goddess].
(13) Where something that must necessarily be said has not been mentioned:
For example—though he was captivated by the extraordinary deeds of this extraordinary being, which were witnessed and utterly marvelous, still [the king] had no firm conviction:
"This is some being in the form of a heroic child, yet a reality composed of the very essence of immeasurable beauty. // 233 //
In this context, the injunction regarding the state of being carried away— as in "I have been carried away"— must be expressed;
for even so, the phrase "tathāpi" (nevertheless) is logically justified only as occurring within the second sentence.

Indeed, since I, born from the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, have attained this state which lies far beyond the reach of the desires of gods and asuras, having brought about the daughter of the Asura king—one whose beautiful form was realized in a dream through union with Aniruddha—[I am truly blessed]. (234)
In this context, the meaning "far beyond even the reach of desires" should also be expressed.

Or, for example: "O proud woman, what speck of an offense do you see in me—that I, whose love is fixed upon you, who speak kindly, and whose heart is averse to breaking our intimacy, should abandon your servant? (235)
In this context, it should have been stated as "even a fraction of an offense" (*aparādhasya lavam api*).

(14) An example of misplaced words (*asthānasthapada*) is as follows: "No woman discarded the garland, though soiled by water, which her lover had woven and placed upon her chest over her full breasts; for virtues reside in affection, not in physical objects. (236)

In this case, it should have been stated as "a certain [woman] did not abandon [him]. Or, for example: "May he protect you—he whose curved, copper-hued mark was imprinted upon the surface of Pārvatī’s cheek during the midst of her sleep by the crescent moon on Śiva’s blue neck, which hung down from his matted locks loosened when she playfully seized them; and which was then wiped away by her sprout-like hand, as she felt ashamed by the playful smiles of her friends who suspected it to be a scratch-mark. (237)
In this context, the phrase "kuṭilatāmra-" should be stated before "nakhalakṣmā."

(15) An example of a compound whose placement is improper: "Even now, as this pride (*māna*) desires to dwell within the hearts of women—difficult to traverse like mountains due to their breasts—a curse upon it! As if red with anger, the Moon, stretching forth his rays like hands from afar, instantly draws his sword: the rows of bees emerging from the cups of the blooming night-lilies. (238)
In this case, no compound was formed in the speech of the angry man, but it was formed in the speech of the poet.

(16) *Saṃkīrṇa* (confusion) occurs where the words of one sentence intrude into another sentence. For example: "Why do you not see this foot [of yours], which has fallen [at my feet] and possesses many virtues? Take it!
Indeed, release from your neck this lord of your heart, who is the very embodiment of the darkness of your mind! (239)
In this case, [the speaker says]: "Why do you not look upon the Lord of your heart, who possesses many virtues and resides at your feet?
Take him by the neck and abandon this anger which is the very form of darkness for the mind.
However, the distinction is that in the case of a single sentence (ekavākyatā), it is considered *kliṣṭa* (defective).
(17) *Gārbhita* is where another sentence enters into the middle of a sentence.
For example: "Association with wicked people who delight in harming others—I tell you the truth—should never be entered into. (240)
In this case, the third quarter of the verse has entered into the middle of another sentence:
"By her whose limbs were covered in passion, [the sword] was firmly clung here to the neck of an enemy; she who was seen falling even upon elephants by other men;

he who is attached to her does not take anything into account—let it be known to you that for this reason I have been given away to servants. By the command of His Majesty, his fame has gone to the ocean as if to say: 'I have come. (241)
In this case, the phrase "let it be known to you" has been employed;
however, since prosperity actually departs from him because of it, it constitutes a contradiction of intended meaning (viruddhamatikṛt).
(18) “In the case of anklets and the like, it is primarily *raṇita*; among birds, it is *kūjita* and so forth;
in sexual union, it is *stanita* and *bhaṇita*; and in the case of clouds and the like, it is *garjita* and so on.”

Thus it transcends all established experience: "Whence comes this unprecedented roar today before us from the ocean of battle—resembling the echoes of the fierce thundering of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds agitated by the winds of the great dissolution, repeatedly terrifying to the ears and filling the cavities of heaven and earth? (242)
In this context, "roar" (rava) is well known to refer to frogs and the like, but not to the specific lion's roar as previously described.

(19) *Bhagnaprakrama* (Broken Order): [An instance where] the sequence is broken. For example: "Alas! When the Lord of Night had gone to his setting by the decree of destiny, the night too has departed.
For noble women, indeed, there exists nothing more auspicious than a state of affairs that corresponds to their circumstances. (243)
In this context, when "gone" (*gata*) is introduced, it is understood as "departed" (*yāta*) due to the root meaning; likewise,
"the night has gone" (*gatā niśā*).
This, however, is logical.
But surely it was stated elsewhere that "generally, a single word should not be used twice," and it was also said right here that the repetition of a word (*kathitapada*) is a defect.
How then can there be a double usage of a single word? It is said in reply:

the prohibition against the use of a single word applies to a context other than that of a subject (uddeśya) and its subsequent reference (pratinirdeśya); in a context involving such [subject and reference], on the contrary, there is a fault if that very same word—or a pronoun—is not employed.
For instance: "The sun rises copper-red and sets copper-red;
the greatness of the great remains uniform in both prosperity and adversity. (244)

In this context, if it were stated that "the red one itself sets," then that very same meaning, which was already conveyed by another word, would appear as if it were a different meaning and would obscure the comprehension.

Or just as success approaches those who are free from longing yet devoted to effort—as if eager herself—to enable them to attain fame, or to desire happiness, or even to transcend the ranks of ordinary men. (245)
In this context,
the reading "sukham īhitum vā" for the suffix is appropriate.
Having taken leave of the Himalaya and again gazed upon the wielder of the trident (Śiva),
and having reported the matter accomplished to him, they departed for the sky, dismissed by him.
In this case, instead of using a pronoun,
one should say: "released by him."
Although the king had sons, his gaze found no satiety upon that mountain;
for the swarm of bees, drawn to the mango tree, remains especially attached even when spring possesses flowers in abundance.
In this case, regarding the synonym,
the phrase "though he possessed offspring" (*apatyavataḥ*) is appropriate;
for even though he had a son, his affection was directed toward an offspring in the form of a daughter.
Thus some argue:

"Calamities overcome one who lacks valor; prosperity abandons one who is beset by misfortune; insignificance is certain for one without future prospects; and one who is not great does not attain the station of royal splendor. (248)
In this regard, both misfortune and its reversal [are explained]:
"The overcoming of that [misfortune] brings about expansion;
one who lacks expansion falls into insignificance, and one possessed of insignificance does not attain the station of royal glory."
Thus it was fitting:
some women, their beauty of face and moon dimmed by being covered in dust, imitated the sky; others, with their inner spirits bewildered, bore a burning heat within like the quarters of the horizon;
some wandered like whirlwinds, while others trembled at every step like the earth—thus did these women portend the inauspiciousness that was to come before the departure of the kings. (249)
In this regard, the statement is:
"Some, strewn with dust, following the path of the sky, lacking beauty due to their pale faces, were devoid of splendor"; and [the phrase] "trembling."
In this context, "kampamāpuḥ" (they trembled) should be read [instead of "kampaṃ prāpuḥ"].
Let the buffaloes plunge into the water of the drinking pool, which is repeatedly struck by their horns; let the herd of deer, gathered in groups within the shade, practice rumination.
"Let the lordly boars fearlessly root up the musta-grass in the pond, and let this bow of mine, with its string slackened, find rest. (250)
In this case, regarding the agent (*kāraka*):
"Let the excellent boars confidently make a scar on their temples with *mustā* grass"—
this is not faulty.
As the sage— who possesses a vast majesty of ascetic heat and power beyond measure, who is a treasury of fame, and who is inflated with unfounded pride— approaches in his wrath,
my hand throbs impetuously both for the act of drawing my ever-new bow in a deed worthy of its pride, and for clasping his feet in homage.
In this context, regarding the sequence,
the phrase "for the purpose of clasping the feet" should have been stated first;
other instances should be understood in the same manner.

(20) Where there is no sequence [of time]: "Both that which has gone [to the past] and that which is present have now fallen into a state of lamentation through their longing for union with the Skull-Bearer (Śiva)—both that radiant digit of the Moon and that moonlight which is the eye of this world. (252)
In this case, the particle *ca* (and) would have been more appropriate immediately after the word *tvam* (you).
For example: "O Lord, this sword is the power in your pair of arms; the beauty of the moon resides in your face; likewise, this great procuress, the sword-staff, dwells at your side.
This command of yours pervades everywhere and shines forth before you—what need is there for me, an old woman? Having spoken thus, his fame, white as the rays of the moon, departed in anger. (253)
In this context, it would be more logical to read "having spoken thus" (*itthaṃ procyeva*);
likewise, [the reading] "clung to by her whose face was covered with passion" (*lagnaṃ rāgāvṛtāsyayā*).
In such cases, one should state: "Thus, by the command of the illustrious [Lord]."
(21) *Amata* (the incongruous): where the purpose of another is contrary to the subject at hand.
For example: "Struck in the heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma-Manmatha, that night-stalker woman, sprinkled with fragrant blood-sandalwood, went to the abode of the Lord of Life. (254)
In this context, regarding the intended rasa, there is another meaning that suggests a *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) obstructed by *vīra* (heroic).

He states the defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*) [in Sūtra 76]: "The meaning is: unrefined (*apuṣṭa*), difficult (*kaṣṭa*), contradictory (*vyāhata*), redundant (*punarukta*), ill-ordered (*duṣkrama*), and vulgar (*grāmya*). //55//

The doubtful, the groundless, the contradicted by common knowledge or by science, the unqualified, and those involving the reversal of restriction, non-restriction, particularity, and generality. //56//
Expectant, unconnected with a word, deviating from a common usage, contradicting what has been stated, unfit for affirmation or restatement, abandoned and then re-adopted, and indecent; //57//
The word "defective" (*duṣṭa*) is connected [to each case].
The examples in order are as follows:
(1) "Having abandoned the fatigue of traversing the exceedingly vast path of the sky, [the sun] experiences joy..."
Victorious is the Sun, who causes the laughter of the lotus pond by awakening its fragrance with his rays. // 255 //

In this context, qualities such as "excessive extensiveness" (ativitatatva) and so forth are considered "insignificant" (apuṣṭa) because they do not contradict the meaning being conveyed even when they are not included;
however, they are neither irrelevant nor redundant.

(2) By what great person could these rays of light—the sweet splendors flashing in the sky of the great epics—ever attain clarity? For within them flows this unrestrained Sarasvatī, whose many paths carry the fragrance of nectar-dripping, divine flavor, and who is ever familiar with the dense clouds [of poetic figures]. 256.

In this regard, how can those poetic expressions— which, like the triple-pathed Gaṅgā flowing among the rays of the sun, carry aesthetic wonder amidst the poet’s styles consisting of the delicate (*sukumāra*), the variegated (*vicitra*), and the intermediate (*madhyama*)— be as clear as other types of poetry when they are familiar only to those versed in profound poetry?
Those [expressions] which flow like the triple-pathed river amidst the splendors of the sun...
The concise meaning is: how do those things familiar with clouds become clear?
(3) In this world, there are indeed those victorious things—such as the crescent of the new moon and others—that are naturally sweet and delight the mind.
But for me, that this moonlight for my eyes has come within the range of my vision is the one great festival of my life. 257.

In this case, since the moon’s digit and so forth are merely like mere whispers compared to him, it is contradictory that he alone should be superimposed with the state of being moonlight for the sake of excellence.
(4) "Whatever has been done, or approved," and so forth. // 258 //

In this instance, when you say "O Arjuna, Arjuna" and "by you," the term *kirīṭin* (Arjuna) is redundant in the phrase "of Bhīma and Kirīṭin. Or, for example: "While my father stands here as the commander of the army, acting like the submarine fire (*aurva*) within the ocean of the enemy forces licked by the flames of his weapons—the master of all archers—enough, Karṇa, with your delusion! Go, Kṛpa, leave the battlefield! Hārdikya, cast away your fear! While my father, with his bow as his only companion, bears the burden of war, what room is there for fear? (259)
In this case, the meaning of the fourth quarter-verse is redundant.
(5) O jewel among kings, whose fame rests upon the celebration of unstinting charity, bestow upon me either a horse or an elephant languid with rut. 260.
In this context, it is appropriate for Mātangī to speak first:
(6) "As long as these people nearby are asleep, so long shall I sleep; what is lost to you? Therefore, my dear, now draw back your elbow and quickly straighten your bent thigh. (261)
This one is unskilled.
(7) "Having cast aside stinginess," and so forth. // 262 //

In this case, in the absence of contextual factors and the like, there is doubt; however, when either the *śānta* (tranquil) or the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa is specifically denoted, there is certainty.
(8) You were taken up by him out of fear of humiliation, even though you were not worthy; indeed, through his power, there was no one who was not within your reach.
Yet you have been abandoned by him due to grief for his son, and not out of fear. Therefore, O Weapon, I too shall release you, so that it may be well with you.
In this case, no reason for the discharge of the weapon has been stated.
(9) Tell me, O lotus-eyed one, who told you this, that you should indeed entertain the notion that this is a golden bracelet?
This is that supreme weapon for attacking those difficult to subdue, the discus placed by the God of Love at the base of your lotus-hand out of affection for you.
In this world, the wheel of love is not well-known.

Or rather: "O travelers, as you leave the vicinity of the Godāvarī, look here for another path; for here, by some woman of ruined hopes, a red aśoka tree has been made to wear the bodice of rising fresh sprouts through the placement of her lotus-feet. (265)
In this regard, it is well known among poets that the striking of a foot causes the Ashoka tree to burst into bloom, but not that it causes sprouts to emerge.
"When a beautiful woman, dressed in white garments and ornaments, was walking at will in the moonlight, the moon set;
immediately thereafter, someone sang of your fame, by which she went to her lover’s house free from fear. Where have you not been a bestower of auspiciousness? (266)

In this case, fame, though formless, is described as having the nature of light like moonlight; thus, although it contradicts worldly convention, it is not defective because it conforms to poetic convention (*kaviprasiddhi*).
(10) Having bathed every night, the wise man expounds and listens to various kinds of scriptures throughout the entire day. // 267 //
Bathing at night, except during an eclipse of a planet or similar occasion, is contrary to the Dharmaśāstras.
For one whose strength in the arms is seen to be peerless, the pursuit of the sixfold policy is truly useless. (268)
This is according to the *Arthaśāstra*:
(10a) Having placed her armlet far away, a woman whose limbs were the very playground of the God of Love bore the series of nail-marks made by her lover. (269)
In this matter, it is stated by the *Kāmaśāstra* that a nail-mark was not made upon the place of the armlet; [this is] because,
by means of the firm practice of the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*), he kept the vicinity of the difficult-to-attain supernatural powers (*siddhi*) at a distance.
Now attaining the desired discriminative discernment, he becomes liberated as the crest-jewel of those whose wealth is meditative absorption.

In this system, discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) arises; from that comes cognitive absorption (*saṃprajñāta-samādhi*), followed by non-cognitive absorption (*asaṃprajñāta*), and from that, liberation—not [liberation] directly from discriminative discernment. This is according to the Yoga Śāstra.
In the same way, contradictions with other sciences (*vidyā*) may also be cited.

(11) What is gained from attaining fortunes that grant every desire? What is gained from placing one's foot upon the heads of enemies? What is gained from satisfying friends with riches? And what is gained from the bodies of embodied beings persisting for an eon? // 271 //
Why was it not updated here with "so what?
[The answer is as follows: "If fire burns here, what is the wonder? And if there is weight in mountains, so what?
The water of the great ocean is always salty; indeed, freedom from despondency is the very nature of the virtuous. (272)

(12) For that Being, whose entire creation is such that its purpose remains uncarved [unmanifested], even the conception of a rival for His excellence is the ultimate insult. Since His riches have transcended the very paths of the desires of all living beings, it is only fitting that a gem which reduces other stones to mere semblances of jewels should itself be considered nothing more than a stone. 273.
In this context, the restriction should have been expressed as: "When the mere shadow of that gem has been treated as a gem upon stones, it is only fitting that the stone remains a stone."

(13) Sarasvatī always dwells within your lotus-face; your lower lip is indeed the Śoṇa river; your right arm is the ocean, capable of evoking the memory of the prowess of Rāma; and these armies never leave your side for even a moment. O Lord of the Earth, since this mind of yours is perpetually clear within, how can you have any desire to drink water? 274.
In this case, the restriction "it must be red alone" should not be stated.
(14) O friends, bring forth a dark hue upon the dark-complexioned one with thick brushes of ink; then, having employed spells and rituals, take away the splendor of the white lotuses!
Grind the moon into powder by crushing it into fragments upon a stone slab, so that I may be able to behold the ten directions marked with the seal of her face. // 275 //
In this context, the specific type of Śyāmā referred to as "Jyautsnī" is what ought to be expressed.
(15) O abode of sea-monsters, do not despise these jewels because of the harsh blows from stones tossed about by the surging waves;
was not even Puruṣottama himself made to stretch out his hand in supplication before you because of the Kaustubha gem? 276.
In this context, the general statement "Why was he not appointed by you alone? should be expressed.
(16) Even though his desire was made manifest, the Lord did not obtain the fruit; on the contrary, the son of Daśaratha, acting with hostility and contrary conduct, was joined with that maiden.
How can the ten-faced god, the lord of the world, endure the increase of another's pride and fame, his own loss of honor and glory, and the jewel among women? (277)
In this context, [the word] "strīratnam" (a jewel of a woman) is intended with the sense of "to disregard";
for its connection with the word "parasya" (of another) is not appropriate.

(17) His command is cherished by Śakra as his crest-jewel; the scriptures are his new eyes; his devotion is fixed upon the Pināka-wielding Lord of Beings; his station is the divine city of Laṅkā; his birth is in the lineage of Brahmā. Oh, such a suitor is not easily found! Yet, were he not Rāvaṇa, where indeed could all these virtues be found together? 278.
In this context, [the sentence] should conclude precisely with: "If this were not Rāvaṇa.
(18) Wisdom by learning, foolishness by addiction, a woman by intoxication, and a river by water—[all these flow downward].
The night is adorned by the moon, steadfastness by meditative concentration, and the status of a lord of men by statesmanship. // 279 //
Here, through the excellence of their companions—learning and the like—the distinction between the lowly states of vice and folly is established.
(19) Clinging [to me] with limbs shrouded in passion... // 280 //
In this context, by the phrase "let it be known to you," the contradictory implication is revealed that Śrī departs from him because of that.
(20) Awakened today by our efforts and by hymns of praise, you shall rest at the end of the night; today the world shall be without Keśava and without the Pāṇḍavas;
today this talk of war shall be brought to an end for those devoid of glory; today let the exceedingly heavy burden of the forest of enemies depart from the earth.
In this context, "you are awakened with effort while you were sleeping" is the predicate to be established.

Or, for example: "The world was devoured by venomous serpents after they had been reassured by their subsisting on air alone; those serpents, in turn, were swallowed by peacocks who observe the severe vow of drinking only drops of water from the clouds."
Even they were brought to destruction by hunters clad in the skins of cruel deer; yet even knowing this to be a manifestation of deceit, a fool still strives for virtues.
In this context, the three beginning with "subsisting on air" (*vātāhāra*) should be stated in reverse order.

(21) O ornament for the hands of beautiful women! O refuge for swarms of bees! O dispeller of the shame of amorous play! O subduer of the life-breaths of those separated from their lovers! O crest-jewel of the lake-swans! O blue lotus with trembling petals, my friend! I am distressed; loosen my delusion and tell me, where is that moon-faced one? 283.
In this context, the phrase "the subduer of the life-breaths of those separated from their lovers" is not something to be restated (as a subject).
(22) "She whose limbs are enveloped by passion has become attached," and so forth. // 284 //
In this context, although [the teaching] was concluded with the words "Let it be known to you," it is taken up again by the words "by him" and so forth.
(23) For one who is intent on killing, arrogant, and seeking a vulnerability—just as his downfall occurs, so too shall there be no further rise. 285.
In this case, there is also the perception of the male organ;
however, although other defects exist where one defect has been pointed out, they have not been disclosed because they were not relevant to the context.
In expressions such as *karṇāvataṃsa* ("ear-ornament"), the employment of words like *karṇa* ("ear") is for the purpose of conveying proximity and so forth.

Terms such as *avataṃsa* and others refer specifically to ornaments for the ears and so forth; in this context, words like "ear" (*karṇa*) are used to indicate their location on the ear and other parts.
For example: "By her ear-ornament (*karṇāvataṃsa*), all other decoration has been surpassed; likewise, her ear-pendant (*śravaṇakuṇḍala*) shines exceedingly. (286)
Then there arrived bees, resonant with their humming and adorned with crests upon their heads, gladdening the quarters of the sky with an unprecedentedly sweet fragrance.
In this context, the words "ear," "hearing," and "head" are intended to convey the sense of proximity.
In the midst of that terrifying battle where enemies were torn asunder,
your arm— marked by the calluses of the bowstring— throbbed with power.

In this context, the word "bow" (dhanus) is used for the sake of understanding that it was strung; elsewhere, however, [it is said]: "The Lord of Laṅkā, who had conquered Indra, dwelt in prison until his favor [was obtained], with his arms motionless due to the binding of the bowstring and his rows of heads sighing. (289)
In this instance, the word *jyā* (bowstring) is used alone:

"The two breasts seem to laugh with the shimmering pearl necklace, which, through its mistaken identification as the playful embrace of the Lord of Breath (the neck), [mistakes itself for a bowstring]. (290)
In this context, the word "muktā" (pearl) is used to indicate that those who are liberated are unmixed with other jewels.
O friend, whose beauty, wealth, youth, and amorous graces are such that she—like a garland of flowers—does not attract bees? 291.
In this context, the word "flower" (puṣpa) refers to the finest flowers;
for the word "garland" (mālā), when used without a prefix, denotes specifically a garland of flowers.
(78) This justification applies when [the causes] are present. //58//
Indeed, it is not the case that [the description] "ear-ornament" and so forth is made for the ears, while "hip-girdle" and so forth is made for the hips;
rather, he spoke sweet words distinguished by clear syllables. (292)

In such cases, since the intended meaning is successfully communicated even when [the word] functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it is not logical to maintain that "in some instances, even if the meaning is already established, one must employ the substantive (*viśeṣya*) for the sake of providing its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If it were indeed logical, then consider this: "Even with feet devoid of the protection of sandals, he travels a long distance swiftly and does not grow weary. (293)
Thus it should be cited.
(Verse 79) When the meaning is well-known, a reasonless statement is not faulty, as in: "The qualities of the lotus do not reside in the moon, nor does the moon's splendor reside in the lotus."
But having attained the face of Umā, the fickle Lakṣmī obtained a joy that rested upon two supports. // 294 //
In this context, it is well known in the world that the lotus closes at night and the moon loses its luster during the day; therefore, the reason "he does not eat" does not need to be considered.
(Verse 80) But in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), [there is no fault] for any of them—
that is, for all defects beginning with *śrutikaṭu* (harshness to the ear).
Just as this person says, "I saw the deer-eyed one," and so forth; or as he says, "Look! and "O cow! Sacrifice to Sutrāman! (295)
(Verse 81) Due to the propriety of the speaker and other factors, even a defect may sometimes become a merit; sometimes it is neither. //59//

By virtue of the speaker, the person addressed, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, even a defect may in some cases be a merit, in some cases neither a defect nor a merit.

Among these, when the speaker or the person addressed is a grammarian or the like, and when the suggested meaning is a sentiment such as the Furious (*raudra*), harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) is a merit. The examples in order are as follows: "Someone is equal to the roots *dīdhīṅ* and *vevīṅ*, being unworthy of either *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. (Here, the harshness of the grammatical terminology is a merit because the speaker and the addressee are grammarians.)
There is something resembling the *kvip* suffix, in the presence of which [the suffix] does not apply to you. 296.
When I beheld you, so skilled in the science of words, I then remembered my teacher and experienced a surge of joy. (297)
With the sky resounding with the noise of her many ornaments— chiefly large skulls, arm-bones, and thigh-bones protruding from her entrails and jingling harshly as bracelets—
she runs with arrogant pride, her body terrifying with the weight of her swinging breasts, which shine with a thick mire of blood she has drunk and then vomited.

According to the nature of what is expressed (*vācya-vaśāt*): "O elephants, what is the use of your leaping? O jackals, what is the use of your fruitless displays? O deer, why do you fall into rut? Why, O buffaloes, are there no heroes in the wilderness?
When the roar of the ocean resounds before the enemy's elephant—with its trunk raised high by the swelling of anger and its mane bristling with fierce intensity—that alone is true roaring. (299)
In this case, since "lion" is the intended meaning, the words used are harsh.
O red Aśoka tree with slender trunk, where has she gone, leaving behind us who are devoted to her? Why do you vainly shake your head, tossed by the wind?
For how could this outburst of flowers of yours occur without being struck by her feet—flowers whose petals are bitten by the swarm of bees gathering in their longing? (300)
In this context, it refers to the speech of one who is angry, accompanied by the shaking of the head.

In some cases, where there is no aesthetic flavor (*nīrasa*), there is neither merit nor fault. For example: "May the rays of that Maker of Day—who alone heals and restores to health those whose noses, limbs, and hands are withered, whose bodies are scarred, whose voices are hoarse and indistinct, and who have long been afflicted by floods of sin—grant you swift destruction of your sins. These rays, which bestow offerings upon the hosts of Siddhas and whose activity is unimpeded by the intense, thick compassion within him, [are here invoked]. (301)
The *aprayukta* (unconventional) and *nihata-artha* (suppressed meaning) defects are not considered faults when they occur in contexts such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
For example: "May that Mādhava—who, having destroyed the god of love, formerly turned the body of Bali’s conqueror into a woman; who bore the Ganges and wore a serpent as a necklace and bracelets;
whose praiseworthy name the gods call ‘the Moon-headed Destroyer’; and who himself brought about the destruction of Andhaka—protect you at all times. (302)
In this context, according to the *mādhava* interpretation, the words *śaśimat* and *andhakakṣaya* are respectively unidiomatic (*aprayukta*) and of suppressed meaning (*nihnūtārtha*).
Obscenity (*aślīla*) is sometimes a merit;

for instance, in a conversation at the commencement of amorous play, it is established in the *Kāmaśāstra* that "one should hint at secret matters by means of double-meaning words," as in the verse: "Having entered with the trunk of an elephant into the [vaginal] cavity and stirred within..."
Approaching, the banner of a man shines forth through the excellence of his means. // 303 //
In discourses on tranquility, who—were they not a worm—would develop an attachment to the moist wound of a woman, which resembles the split belly of a frog that has been swollen and then burst? (304)
May the sons of Pāṇḍu, who have extinguished the fire of enmity toward Nirvāṇa through their pacification of enemies, rejoice together with Mādhava;
and may the sons of the Kuru king, their lands adorned by blood and their wounds healed, become healthy once more along with their servants.
In this context, it indicates an auspicious omen that is yet to come to pass.

Even that which is ambiguous may, by virtue of the power of the expression, result in the perception of a fixed meaning in certain cases; this is a merit when it culminates in *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
For example: "O King, now our two residences are equal: yours has vessels of vast gold, all your attendants are adorned, and it is crowded with shining female elephants; mine is likewise. (306)
When both the speaker and the listener possess knowledge [of the subject], that which is not yet perceived becomes a poetic quality (*guṇa*).

For example: "Those who delight in the Self, whose pleasure is established in unwavering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whose knots of darkness are severed by the surge of wisdom, and who are grounded in reality—they behold Him, the indescribable One who stands beyond both darkness and light. How can this man, blinded by delusion, know that ancient God? (307)
Or [the mantra is used] for self-contemplation (*parāmarśa*):

"Victorious is that Lord of Power (*Śaktinātha*), who resides within the center of the wheel of the sixteen channels (*nāḍīcakra*), whose form is established in the heart, who bestows success upon those who know him, and who is sought by practitioners with unwavering minds—he who is embraced by the powers (*śakti*). (308)
In the speech of those of base nature, vulgarity is a merit. For example:

"Those *sindhuvāra* branches which bear clusters of blossoms like boiled rice, which resemble buffalo curds that have been strained, and which possess heaps of buds like fresh *vicailla* flowers—those are dear to me. (309)
In this context, although the words *kāla-maṣṭa-bhaktam*, *mahiṣī*, and *dadhi* are rustic (*grāmya*), they are [appropriate] in the speech of the Vidūṣaka.
An omission of words (*nyūnapada*) is sometimes a merit.
For example: "With her breasts flattened by a tight embrace, the hair on her body bristling, and the garment from her beautiful hips slipping away due to the excess of intense passion;
crying out in faint syllables, 'No, no, O giver of honor! Do not [press] me, enough!'—is she asleep, or is she dead, or has she merged into my mind, or has she dissolved? (310)
In some cases there is neither merit nor fault:
"Perhaps she remains hidden by her power due to the force of anger, yet she does not remain angry for long; perhaps she has ascended to heaven, for her heart is still moist with affection for me.
Even the enemies of the gods would not have been able to carry her off while she was standing before me; yet she has gone entirely beyond the range of my vision—what kind of fate is this? (3.11)

In this context, immediately after the word "pihitā" (concealed), the phrase "naitadyataḥ" (this is not so, because... lacks certain words; since it does not produce a specific cognition, it is not a merit [of the argument].
A subsequent understanding sublates a prior understanding.
Thus, there is no fault;
in some cases, an extra word is a merit.
For example: "When a wicked person, intent on his purpose, speaks with a mind set on deception, uttering many feigned words filled with flattery..."
The virtuous are not unaware of this; they know it well, yet they are unable to fulfill his request in vain.

In this context, the word "vidanti" (they know) is the second [instance] intended to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Or, for example: "Speak, speak! That enemy is conquered; he was not killed while you were saying, 'I am yours, yours.'"
"O Citrā! O Citrā! Alas! Alas! she cried out most piteously when her son died.
In such cases, when the speaker is possessed of joy, fear, and so forth;
A repeated word is sometimes a merit,

as in the case of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), in cases where the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*), and when that which has been previously enjoined is subsequently restated (*vihitasyānuvādyatva*).
The examples in order: O Lord who supports the earth, whose form is like that of the sun, your fame possesses the radiance of the rays of the white-rayed moon;
and Lakṣmī, the goddess of prowess, she too belongs to you alone and to no other. (314)
Those virtues arise which are grasped by those who possess the capacity;
like lotuses, they become truly lotuses when graced by the rays of the sun.

Mastery over the senses is the cause of discipline, and excellence in virtue is attained through discipline. By excellence in virtue, people are won over; for prosperity indeed arises from the affection of the people.
Even an intensification that is falling away may, in certain cases, be a merit;
as, for example, in the previously cited verse beginning with "prāgaprāpta-".
The *samāptapunarātta* (resumption after completion) is sometimes neither a merit nor a fault;
this occurs where the resumption is not for the sake of providing a mere qualification, but rather constitutes a distinct sentence altogether.
For example, in the very same passage, in the verse beginning with *prāgaprāpta* and so forth. // 318 //
In some cases, a compound with a word standing at the end (apadastha) is a merit, as in the example cited, "raktāśoka," and so forth. // 319 //
It is likewise "interwoven" (*garbhita*):
"Just as I am one whose pride is cast aside, who is unrestrained, and even devoid of discernment, yet even in my dreams I do not forget my devotion to you, O Beloved. (320)
In this context, the word "pratīhi" (understand) is used in the middle [of the sentence] to produce a firm conviction;
in the same way, other instances should also be understood from the examples.

(Verse 82) The direct verbal expression of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), and stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), as well as the explicit mention of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*) through laborious conceptualization, [constitute defects]. //60//
The apprehension of contrary excitants and so forth, excessive intensity, repetition, sudden expansion and interruption, and the over-elaboration of subordinate elements; //61//

The non-connection of the possessor of the limbs (the whole), the inversion of the constituent elements (prakṛtis), and the mention of what is not a constituent limb—such are the defects in rasa. //62//

(1) The employment of the word itself [as the reason] is fallacious, as in: "May Pārvatī’s gaze—bashful at the face of her beloved, compassionate toward the elephant-hide garment, terrified of the serpent, filled with wonder at the nectar-dripping moon, envious during the sight of the daughter of Jahnu, and distressed at the hollow of the skull—be for your welfare as she gazes with affection upon him in their first union. (321)
In this regard, there are examples such as those beginning with *vṛjī*:
"She was bowed down before the face of her beloved; she closed her eyes at the garment of the elephant-hide; she trembled at the serpent; she was unblinking at the moon dripping with nectar;
she knit her brows at the sight of the celestial river; and she grew faint at the sight of the interior of the skull."
But such [a view] as this is logical.
(2) The rasa may be expressed by its own name.

Examples in order: "Upon bringing her—who was the auspicious glory of the bodiless Love-god’s victory and who had cast a slight glance toward the root of his slightly raised arm—within the range of his vision, an indescribable and continuous rasa arose within him. (322)

Behold, having cast off childhood, he who possesses a lovely form made beautiful by a manifest passion anointed upon his tender cheeks, now reaches toward the limits of the erotic sentiment and spreads a rippling wave of emotion.
(3) As for the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*): during the combat, as weapons struck against one another with a piercing *ṭhaṇatkāra* sound, an extraordinary enthusiasm arose. 324.
In this regard, [it refers] to the self-conceit.

(4) When the cool-rayed moon, with its flood of light white as camphor dust, had washed the circles of the quarters, that maiden’s breasts became manifest in their fullness and elevation through the particular way she adjusted her playful upper garment. 325.

In this regard, the sixth hypothesis is that the excitants (*vibhāva*) suitable for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), consisting of both the excitants as stimulants (*uddīpana*) and the excitants as objects (*ālambana*), remain present, accompanied by a slight degree of the ensuants (*anubhāva*).
(5) He abandons his delight, his intellect is shattered, he stumbles violently, and turns about again and again.
Alas! Such a wretched state forcibly overcomes his body; what can we do in this matter? 326.

In this context, since the ensuants (anubhāvas) such as the avoidance of sexual pleasure can also occur in the sentiment of pathos (karuṇa) and others, the determinants (vibhāva) in the form of a beloved woman must be specifically established with effort.

(6) Abide in serenity, manifest your joy, and cast away your anger, O beloved; your words sprinkle my withering limbs like nectar. Turn your face toward me for a moment, you who are the treasury of happiness; for the deer of time that has passed cannot be recovered, O charming one. 327.

In this instance, within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the excitant (*vibhāva*) consisting of the manifestation of impermanence—which is contrary to the tranquil sentiment (*śānta*)—and the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of world-weariness (*nirveda*) manifested by it, have been employed.
When her husband has entered the path of her vision while she is in the midst of her elders, the young wife, her heart free from all hesitation,
desires nothing but to go to the forest.
In this case, if there is a journey to the forest accompanied by all [attendants], the two [emotions] are the calm (śānta) and the consequential (anubhāva).
If the journey to the forest under the pretext of fetching fuel and so forth is for the purpose of enjoyment, there is no fault.
(7) Radiance (*dīpti*), moreover, occurs repeatedly, as for example in the *Rativilāpa* section of the *Kumārasambhava*.

(8) Expansion at an inappropriate time, as for example, in the second act of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, when the slaughter of many heroes has already commenced, there is a description of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) between Duḥśāsana and Bhānumatī.

(9) An untimely interruption (*akāṇḍa-ccheda*) is, for example, in the second act of the *Vīracarita*, when the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) has reached its peak between Rāghava and Bhārgava, upon Rāghava’s utterance: "I am going to the bangles' festival."
(10) An excessive description of a subordinate member [of the plot],
such as the description of Hayagrīva in the *Hayagrīvavadha*.
(11) Non-connection of the principal character:
as in the fourth act of the *Ratnāvalī*, Sāgarikā’s forgetfulness upon the arrival of Bābhravya.

(12) The natures (*prakṛti*) are divine, non-divine, and both divine and non-divine; they are primarily characterized by the heroic, the furious, the erotic, and the peaceful sentiments (*rasa*); they are the noble-magnanimous, the noble-proud, the noble-graceful, and the noble-calm; and they are superior, inferior, and middling.
Among these, [the first four] consist of love, laughter, sorrow, and wonder.
The same [rules] that apply to non-divine characters apply to divine ones as well;
however, erotic love (*rati*) in the form of the *saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of union) directed toward supreme deities should not be described.
Indeed, a description of that [act] would be as utterly improper as a description of the sexual union of one's parents.
Even as the words of the gods, "O Lord, restrain your wrath! Restrain it! were still traveling through the sky, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to nothing but ashes. (329)

When this has been said, anger—devoid of such transformations as frowning and so forth—is productive of immediate results; likewise, the enthusiasm for leaping across heaven, the netherworld, the sky, and the ocean exists only among divine beings. Among non-divine beings, however, one should depict only that which is well-known or appropriate according to their specific heroic deeds (*avadāna*). If more than this were depicted, it would appear false, [contradicting the maxim]: "One should behave like the protagonist (*nāyaka*), not like the antagonist (*pratināyaka*)."
Thus, one would not reach a definitive conclusion regarding the teaching concerning divine and non-divine [beings],
in either case.

When propriety has been thus defined, "inversion" (viparyaya) refers to describing even the qualities such as the *dīrghodātta* (lofty-noble) and so forth in a manner contrary to their nature, just as one might do with the *divya* (divine) and other characters.
In this regard, the honorific *tatra-bhavan* or *bhagavan* must not be used by an inferior person for a superior;

nor should *muni-prabhṛti* (sage, etc. be used for a king or similar figure by an inferior; nor should *bhaṭṭāraka* be used for a king or similar figure by a superior; nor should *uttama* (superior) be used by an inferior for a king or similar figure, because such usage results in a perversion of the natural order (*prakṛti-viparyaya*). Thus it should be stated.
In this manner, the dress, conduct, and so forth appropriate to place, time, age, caste, and other such factors must be consistently portrayed.

(13) Description of that which is irrelevant to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*): for example, in the *Karpūramañjarī*, the King’s praise of what was described by the bard, while disregarding the description of the spring season provided by both the heroine and himself.
“‘Such as these’ refers to the description of the hero’s anger and so forth caused by the heroine’s kicking him with her feet and the like.
For it has been stated by the author of the *Dhvani*: ‘There is no cause for the disruption of rasa other than impropriety (*anaucitya*).’”
But the composition of propriety is the supreme secret of rasa.
Thus it is said.
Now, it is said that in certain cases these [reasons] are even faultless.
(Sūtra 83)

There is no fault even when a transitory emotion (*saṃcārībhāva*) is expressed by its own name in certain cases. For example: "May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness—she who, at their first union, was hurried on by longing, turned back by innate modesty, and led forward again by the various words of her female kinswomen; who, seeing her husband before her, was seized by a sense of trepidation; and who was embraced by the laughing Hara with her hair standing on end. (330)
In this case, the word *autsukya* (longing) itself does not produce the same degree of apprehension as its actual effect (*anubhāva*) would;

for this very reason, in such instances as "eager from afar" (*dūrād utsukam*), although there are effects of bashfulness, love, and so forth— such as averting the eyes— the effect of longing, which consists in a sudden forward rush, lacks that same power of producing apprehension, and thus the word *utsuka* was employed.
(Verse 84) The statement of that which is contradictory to the intended emotion (*saṃcārin*) and subject to sublation (*bādhyamāna*) is conducive to poetic excellence. //63//
The mention of something as being sublated (bādhyatvena) is not a supreme defect, provided that it serves to nourish the intended rasa (rasaparipoṣaka).
For example, in such passages as: "Where is the improper act, and where is the lineage of the moon? (kvākāryaṃ śaśalakṣmaṇaḥ kva ca kulam). // 331 //
In this case, although initial thought (vitarka) and other stages arise, the rest remains within reflection alone; thus, there is a full development of the intended aesthetic flavor (rasa).
O friend, your pale and emaciated face, your passionate heart, and your languid body clearly announce within you a deep-seated internal disease.
In such cases, since paleness and the other qualities are common [to both the subject and the object], there is no contradiction.
It is true that women are enchanting; it is true that worldly prosperities are delightful.
But life is indeed as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of an intoxicated woman's eye.
Thus, the first half of this verse is stated precisely as something to be sublated.

Since the instability of a side-glance is even greater than that of life itself, its employment as a comparison with a well-known fragile object nourishes only the *śānta* (tranquil) rasa; there is no perception of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa here, because its constituent elements (*aṅga*) are not apprehended.

However, the objection that this is for the purpose of turning the audience toward the intended theme is not a valid solution, because there is no lack of continuity between the *śānta* (peaceful) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiments.
Nor is it for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the poem, since such enhancement could arise from another sentiment or even from mere alliteration (*anuprāsa*).

(Verse 85) That which is contradictory when residing in the same substratum should be made to reside in different substrata; likewise, a rasa that would otherwise follow immediately [in sequence] should be separated by another rasa. //64//

Since the heroic (*vīra*) and the terrible (*bhayānaka*) are contradictory when residing in a single locus, the terrible must be introduced as belonging to the opposing party. As for the peaceful (*śānta*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), however, they are contradictory by their very proximity; therefore, another rasa must be placed between them. For example, in the *Nāgānanda*, after the peaceful Jīmūtavāhana exclaims, "Oh, what a song! Oh, what music!", the marvelous (*adbhuta*) is inserted within, and then the erotic is established toward Malayavatī.
This contradiction does not cease merely in a long composition, but even within a single sentence when there is an intervention by another sentiment (*rasa*).

For example: "Stained with the dust of the earth, their chests scented by the pollen of fresh *pārijāta* garlands, closely embraced by jackals while the space between their arms was clung to by celestial nymphs... (334)
They were being fanned by the quivering wings of blood-drinking birds,
and they were cooled by the sprinkling of fragrant sandalwood water and by the silken garments of the wish-fulfilling creepers.
Seated upon the couches within their celestial palaces, those heroes, filled with curiosity at that moment,
saw their own fallen bodies being pointed out by others with playful fingers.
In this case, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is placed between the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
Even if it is contradictory [to its neighbors], when it is recalled or intended to be expressed as being equal [to them], there is no fault. (Sūtra 86)
Those two [members] which have attained the status of being members are not mutually defective. //65//
This is that hand which used to pull up the girdle, press against full breasts, touch the navel, thighs, and hips, and loosen the knot of the lower garment.
Beholding this hand of Bhūriśravas fallen upon the field of battle, his wife spoke;
herein, the recollection of former states, though an element of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), further nourishes the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa*).
The tooth-marks and the gashes torn by claws upon your body, where thick horripilation has burst forth,
were bestowed by the lioness with a mind full of passion, and were gazed upon even by sages who felt a surge of longing.
In this context, the intention is to express a similarity: just as the tooth-marks and so forth of a lover cause wonder, so do those of the Jina;
or, just as another person who is erotically impassioned feels longing upon seeing them, so too do these sages regard these [marks]. Thus, there is a desire to convey their equality.
Treading upon the ground strewn with darbha grass with feet whose tender toes are bleeding, as if their soles were stained with red lac, their faces washed by trickling tears,
and their hands grasped by the hands of their husbands in fear— your enemies' wives now wander about the forest fire like brides once again taking up the marriage procession.

In this *cāṭuka* (flattering verse), love directed toward the king is perceived; therein, just as the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) is a subordinate element, so too is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and thus there is no contradiction between them. As it is said: "Come! Go! Fall down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"
In this way, the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the crocodile of hope.

In this regard, there is no contradiction between coming and going when they are viewed in relation to play—as in "Come, let us play" and "Go, let us play. May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortunes—the fire which [consumed] the youth of Tripura like a lover who has committed a fresh offense; for though he was seized by the hand, he was cast off; though struck violently, he grasped the hem of her garment; though seized by the hair, he was pushed away; though falling at her feet, he was not looked upon due to her agitation; and though he embraced her, he was repelled by the young women of Tripura, whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears. (340)

In this passage, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the excellence of the power of the Enemy of Tripura, while the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is a subordinate element to that pathos; nevertheless, since there is no final resolution (*viśrānti*) in the pathos, it remains merely a subordinate element.
Alternatively, just as the lover behaved previously, so does the fire of the arrow; thus, by means of the pathos nourished by the erotic, the primary meaning itself is reinforced.
For it has been said: "A subordinate element that has undergone its own refinement serves the principal;
for in this way, it contributes more extensively to the benefit of the principal."
Thus [it is said].
Since there is no contradiction between one rasa and another previously established rasa, nor does the relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) exist,
the word "rasa" here indicates the underlying stable emotion (sthāyibhāva).
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Kāvyaprakāśa, titled "The Examination of Defects."
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Having thus stated the defects, he speaks of the distinction between qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*): (Sūtra 87) "Those attributes of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is the possessor of the parts, that serve as causes for its excellence—like bravery and so forth in the case of a soul—and which possess an unchanging stability, are qualities (*guṇas*). //66//

For just as bravery and other such qualities belong to the self alone and not to the physical form, so too sweetness and other such qualities belong to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone and not to the phonemes (*varṇa*).

However, because one sometimes observes a large physical stature and other traits appropriate to bravery, there arises the conventional usage, "His very form is brave"; and elsewhere, even in one who is not brave, one may be called "brave" based merely on the fact that his physical build is expansive.

Thus, just as people—whose cognitions do not rest upon the actual fact—apply the designation "not a hero" to someone who is actually a hero merely because of his physical frailty, so too does the application of the designation "sweet" (*mādhurya*) and so forth proceed based on the softness (*saukumārya*) and other qualities of the phonemes that manifest sweetness and the like.

Consequently, for those phonemes that are constituents of non-sweet sentiments (*amadhura-rasa*), there is no sweetness due to their mere lack of softness; and for those phonemes that are accessories to sweet sentiments (*madhura-rasa*), there is no lack of sweetness due to their possession of softness and the like.
People employ [these terms] while being devoid of a comprehension that rests upon the culmination of rasa;
for this very reason, sweetness and the other qualities are attributes of rasa manifested by appropriate phonemes (*varṇa*), and do not reside in the phonemes alone.
How these function as manifestors will be illustrated accordingly.

(Verse 88) Those figures such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*) which, by means of their constituent parts, occasionally assist that [poetic sentiment] which is already present, are ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), like necklaces and other such jewelry. //67//

Those elements which, through the excellence of the characteristics of the expressive words (vācaka) and the expressed meanings (vācya), assist the primary, possible aesthetic flavor (rasa), are called ornaments (alaṃkāra); for they benefit the possessor of the body by means of enhancing the limbs such as the throat, just like necklaces and other ornaments. However, where there is no rasa, they result merely in the variety of expression.
In some cases, however, even existing things do not provide assistance.
The examples follow in order: "Remove the camphor; put the necklace far away; what is the use of lotuses?
Enough, enough with the lotus-stalks, O friend! Thus the young woman speaks day and night. (341)
In such cases, through the medium of the expressive words, the passion of the mind spreads incessantly like fierce poison, all-consuming; it blazes like a smokeless fire once kindled;
it strikes every limb like a grievous fever. Therefore, neither my father, nor my mother, nor you yourself are able to protect me from this. (342)
In such cases, the figures of speech assist the rasa by means of the expressed meaning (vācya).

She is restless in her mind yet not satisfied; she rolls upon her beds and sprawls across the quarters of the sky; she prattles and exerts herself in composing poetry; but through meditation, the youthful woman finally finds long-lasting contentment. 343.
In such cases, it is purely expressive (*vācaka*).

When her friend had gone away somewhere, while the forest of lotuses remained silent and the bees were sighing in distress, the *cakravāka* bird, separated from his mate, saw a *sārasa* crane standing before him near his beloved;
he neither tasted the lotus-stalk nor cast it aside, but merely placed it around his neck like a bolt against his life-breath as it was about to depart. (344)
In such cases, only the literal meaning is intended, not the rasa;
here, the comparison that "a lotus stalk is not capable of obstructing life" is an inappropriate simile for the context.
And this is precisely the distinction between *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras*.

Thus, the assertion that "let there be a difference between *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras* on the grounds that qualities such as heroism (*śaurya*) exist through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*), whereas necklaces (*hāra*) and the like exist through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-vṛtti*), yet since both sets— those beginning with *ojas* and those beginning with alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*)— exist through the relation of inherence, their distinction is merely a 'stream of blind cows' (*gaḍḍulikā-pravāha*)," is incorrect.

As for what was also stated— that "the qualities (guṇas) are those attributes that produce the beauty of poetry, while the ornaments (alaṃkāras) are the causes of its excellence"— that too is not tenable.
For, does the designation of "poetry" apply on account of all the qualities collectively, or only on account of some of them?

If [the *rīti*] consists of all [the qualities], then how can the Gauḍī and Pāñcālī *rītis*, which possess only a limited number of qualities, be the soul of poetry? Therefore, it must consist of only some [of them].
Then, on this mountain, a great fire blazes intensely, and this smoke rises up and spreads.
Thus, when qualities such as *ojas* (vigor) and the rest are present, the designation of "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) is attained.
"The fair-complexioned woman shall attain heaven with this very body; the nectar of her lips utterly surpasses the [celestial] ambrosia. (346)
In such cases, *viśeṣokti* (peculiar cause) and *vyatireka* (contrast) are the factors that initiate the designation of "poetry," independent of the [other] poetic qualities (*guṇas*).
Now he states the classification of the qualities (sūtra 89):
"These are three, known as sweetness (mādhurya), vigor (ojas), and clarity (prasāda), and not ten.
He states their definitions in order (sūtra 90).
Sweetness (mādhurya) is the quality of being delightful; it is the cause of melting in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). //68//
In the erotic sentiment— that is, in the context of sexual union—
there is a state of melting, as it were;
however, the quality of being pleasant to hear belongs to both *ojas* and *prasāda* as well.
(Verse 91) In the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*), in the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*), and in its tranquilized form (*śānta*),
it is endowed with excellence because it is the cause of extreme melting of the heart.
Ojas is the cause for the expansion of the self through radiance; it resides in the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa). (Sūtra 92) /69/
Vigor is that which produces expansion, form, and radiance of the mind.
(Verse 93) There is an increase of that [vigor] respectively in the sentiments of the loathsome and the furious;
from the heroic to the loathsome, and from there to the furious, vigor reaches its highest degree.
(Verse 94) Like a fire upon dry fuel or like clear water, he [the practitioner] [attains it] all at once. //70//
(Verse 95) This clarity pervades the other, its presence established everywhere.
"The other" refers to—
In this context, the mind is the pervader;
"everywhere" means in all flavors and in all compositions.
Furthermore, their operation upon the word and its meaning is considered to occur through the function of secondary qualities (guṇavṛtti). //71//
By way of the function of qualities (*guṇavṛtti*), that is, by metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*);
[it refers] to those qualities,
just as [the word "lion"] applies to the form of bravery.
Why are there exactly three and not ten? To this he says:
(Sūtra 96) "Some are included within these; others are based on the abandonment of faults;
others possess the nature of faults in some respect; therefore, there are not ten. (72)
That *śleṣa* (punning condensation) which consists in the appearance of many words as if they were a single word; that *samādhi* which takes the form of the sequence of ascent and descent;
and that [quality] characterized by ruggedness (*vikaṭatva*).
Elevatedness (*udāratā*) consists of a relaxation infused with vigor (*ojas*),
and thus it is included within *ojas*.
Sweetness (*mādhurya*), characterized by the distinctness of words, is directly mentioned by way of a figurative expression.
The clarity of meaning has been grasped through the favor [of the commentator].
The uniformity consisting in the non-differentiation of the path is, in some cases, a fault; for instance, as in: "What is the use of the leaping of elephants?"
In such instances as the naming of a lion, the avoidance of the smooth (masṛṇa) path is a merit (*guṇa*).

Since harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) and vulgarity (*grāmyatva*) have been declared defects, by their exclusion, the quality of delicacy (*saukumārya*), which consists in the absence of roughness, and the quality of luster (*kānti*), which consists in brilliance, are thereby accepted.
Thus, there are not ten qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇa*).
“Forming a sentence from word-meanings, expressing word-meanings through sentences,
boldness, expansion and contraction, and the intentionality of these— [these constitute poetic power].”

Thus, that maturity which is called *ojas* (vigour) is merely a form of strikingness (*vaicitrya*) and not a true poetic quality (*guṇa*), because the designation of "poetry" still applies even in its absence. Furthermore, by the exclusion of such faults as lack of significance, redundancy, lack of novelty, inauspiciousness, vulgarity, and the vulgar, *ojas*— in the sense of being purposeful— is established.

Lucidity (*prasāda*) consists in the purity of meaning; sweetness (*mādhurya*) takes the form of variety in expression; gentleness (*saukumārya*) consists in the absence of harshness; and nobility (*udāratā*), consisting in the absence of vulgarity, has also been accepted [as a quality].

By means of the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of intrinsic nature) which is about to be discussed, as well as by *rasadhvani* (suggestion of aesthetic flavor) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), the quality of *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning)— consisting in the vividness of the nature of things— and the quality of *kānti* (loveliness)— consisting in the brilliance of aesthetic flavor— are accepted [as being subsumed].
