Even *śleṣa* (conjunction), which consists of the arrangement of forms through the application of propriety characterized by gradualness, curvature, and lack of excess, is merely a form of variety (*vicitratva*).
*Samatā* (evenness), whose nature is the absence of unevenness, is merely the absence of a defect; it is not, however, a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
For what person, unless he were insane, would assert one thing when another has been presented?

If there is no perception of a meaning that is either unoriginated (*ayoni*) or originated from a reflection (*chāyāyoni*), how can it be poetry? Therefore, even the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consisting of the vision of such a meaning is not a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
Therefore, the qualities of the meaning need not be expressed; rather, it is the words that ought to be spoken.
(Verse 98) Furthermore,
those which have been declared to be the qualities of sound— phonemes, compounds, and poetic structure— are said to possess the capacity for manifestation.
To the question "Whose [is it]? he says:

(Sūtra 99) "The stops (sparśa), excluding the sibilants (ṣa-varga) and the liquids (ṭa-varga), when followed by the final letters of their respective classes at the end of a word; the letters *ra* and *ṇa*; a light syllable (*laghu*);
non-repetition (*avṛtti*), or repetition with a moderate interval (*madhyavṛtti*); and likewise a composition (*ghaṭanā*) that is sweet (*mādhurye*). //74//
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, excluding *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*, joined at their head with the final letter of their respective groups;
likewise, the letters *ra* and *ṇa* separated by a short vowel—these are the phonemes. "Absence of compound" (*samāsābhāva*) or "middle compound" (*madhyama-samāsa*) constitutes the compound.
Furthermore, a composition characterized by sweetness through the connection of various words is the manifestor of sweetness (*mādhurya*).
For example: "The limbs of that slender-limbed woman, resembling the stage of the bodiless god [Kāma], have assumed various graceful gestures;
they suddenly cause the hearts of young men to abandon all other thoughts. (347)

In the *ojas* [guṇa], there is conjunction (*yoga*) at the beginning, the third, and the end; the letters *ra* and *ṇa* are equal [in frequency]; the suffixes beginning with *ṭ* are present; the sibilants *ś* and *ṣ* occur; there is a density of compounds (*vṛtti*), protracted vowels (*dairghya*), and a forceful composition (*gumpha*). (75)
The first and third letters of each varga [are joined] with the last two [letters of their respective vargas],
and the second and fourth [letters] are joined with the letter *ra*.
Whether below, above,
or in both places, for any two identical [sounds], there is a connection between them; that is, the *ṭa*-group (excluding the letter *ṇ*), the letters *ś* and *ṣ*, and a long compound.
Vikaṭā-saṃghaṭanā (the rugged arrangement) is [a quality] of *ojas* (vigor).
An example is: "mūrdhnāmudvṛttakṛtta... and so forth. // 348 //

That excellence which is considered the common grace of all [the poetic factors], by the mere hearing of which word there arises a comprehension of the meaning, is known as *prasāda* (clarity). //76//
[This concerns] the combination of all the flavors (*rasas*) and their structural arrangements (*saṃghaṭanā*).

An example: "This bed of lotus leaves, withered on both sides from contact with her full breasts and hips, yet remaining green in the middle because it has not reached the friction of her waist—this disordered arrangement, through the tossing and turning of her limp vine-like arms, speaks of the torment of the slender-limbed woman. (349)

Although composition and other elements are dependent upon the *guṇas*, nevertheless, due to the propriety (*aucitya*) of the speaker, the subject matter, and the literary work, a certain deviation from [the standard] arrangement, meter, and phonemes is also permitted in various instances. (77)
In some cases, the composition and other elements arise solely from the propriety of the speaker, regardless of the subject matter of the work.

For example: "Whose drum is this that has been struck—deep as the roar of Mount Mandara when its hollows are submerged in the waters of the ocean tossed by the churning-stick; fierce like the mutual clashing of thundering masses of clouds at the time of universal dissolution during the beat of the drumstick; the foremost messenger of Kṛṣṇa’s wrath; a cataclysmic whirlwind for the destruction of the Kuru clan; and a companion to the echoes of our own lion-roars? (350)

For here, nothing expressive of anger and the like should be expressed; moreover, since this is poetry intended for dramatic performance (*abhineyārtha*), highly florid compositions and the like are contrary to its purpose,
as is the speaker here, Bhīmasena.
In some cases, the *rasas* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) arise solely from the propriety of the subject matter (*vācyaucitya*), independent of the speaker or the composition.
For example: "Beheld by Aruṇa, who turns his sun-chariot sideways out of fear for the blow of Rāhu—a fear produced by the speed of its upward leap corresponding to the force of its mighty severance;

In some cases, these [stylistic features] are appropriate solely to the composition itself, regardless of the speaker or the subject matter.

For instance: in an *ākhyāyikā*, even when dealing with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), there are no soft-sounding phonemes and the like; in a *kathā*, even when dealing with the furious (*raudra*), they are not excessively harsh; and in dramas (*nāṭaka*) and the like, even when dealing with the furious, there are no long compounds and so forth.
In this manner, other instances of propriety should also be followed accordingly.

And that [poetic figure] is eightfold due to the distinctions of phoneme (*varṇa*), word (*pada*), gender (*liṅga*), dialect (*bhāṣā*), root (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), case-ending (*vibhakti*), and number (*vacana*).

It is said: here, the distinction between defects, merits, and ornaments as pertaining to word and meaning is established solely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For instance, [defects] such as harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) and so forth, [merits] such as intensity (*gāḍhatva*) and so forth, and [ornaments] such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth—

Figures such as simile (upamā) and the like are established as pertaining either to the word or to the meaning precisely because they follow the presence or absence of [qualities] such as futility (vyarthatva) and boldness (prauḍhi). For example:

"The dawn twilight itself, shining with rays as copper-red as young shoots, bestows desired fruits upon those greedy for the reward of sleeplessness"—this is an instance of a *śleṣa* (pun) without a break (*abhaṅga*).

Thus, because both [types] depend solely on words (*śabda*), it is established that both possess the nature of verbal punning (*śabda-śleṣa*), and not that the first possesses the nature of semantic punning (*artha-śleṣa*).

In such cases, simile (*upamā*) occurs when there is equality of qualities, equality of actions, or equality in both; for example:

In such cases, even though there is a mere similarity of words, [the figure] is indeed connected with meaning (sāyukta).
For it has been stated by Rudraṭa: "Clearly, these two—simile and conjunction—are figures of meaning;

Furthermore, in such instances as "Abindusundarī is eternally dripping with drops of loveliness," it is not *śleṣa* (paronomasia) that serves as the cause for the emergence of the semblance of contradiction (*virodhapratibhā*), but rather it is *virodha* (contradiction) that serves as the cause for the emergence of the semblance of *śleṣa*.
For here there is no verbal *śleṣa* (paronomasia) that conveys two distinct meanings,

Nor is it the case that a semblance of *śleṣa* constitutes *śleṣa*, as is the case with the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) being [merely] "contradiction" (*virodha*).
In such sentences as these, the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is indeed another poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).

It is called "verbal paronomasia" (śabda-śleṣa), yet it is classified among the ornaments of meaning (arthālaṃkāra); what kind of principle is this?
Furthermore, as for the claim that "variety is ornament," since variety exists precisely where the poet’s creative intuition and effort operate, that alone is the ground of ornament.

If it is argued that these words possess an inherent capacity to suggest meaning (*arthasūcakatva*), then the same applies to alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like; why, then, are they not also considered ornaments of meaning (*arthālaṃkāra*)?

In cases such as "vidhau vakre mūrdhni," where there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) of phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, one should personally investigate whether the status of *arthaśleṣa* (punning coalescence of meaning) would undesirably follow even when there is a difference in words, provided they are uttered with a single effort of articulation. Thus, and so forth, should be considered by oneself.
That is called *citra* (pictorial poetry), wherein the phonemes serve as the cause for the formation of shapes such as a sword and so forth. //85//

He states the ornaments of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*):

(Sūtra 125) "Similarity (*sādharmya*) is *upamā* (simile), provided there is a distinction between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*); for similarity does not exist between things such as cause and effect. Thus, *upamā* is the connection of those two alone with a common attribute."
The mention of "distinction" (bheda) is for the purpose of excluding non-connection (ananvaya).

(Verse 126) *Pūrṇā* (complete) and *luptā* (elliptical) [simile]. When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the comparison (*upamāpratipādaka*) are all employed, it is *pūrṇā*. When one, two, or three of these are omitted, it is *luptā*.
(Verse 127) The *agrīmā* [type of simile] is the *pūrṇā* (complete).
It may occur in a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), or likewise in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), whether based on the literal meaning (*śrautī*) or the implied sense (*ārthī*).

Just as in the case of words such as *yathā* and *iva*, the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is understood as belonging to that which they refer to; although these are adjectives qualifying the object of comparison (*upameya*), nevertheless, by the power of their own verbal expression, they convey the relationship through direct denotation (*śruti*) itself, like a genitive case-ending.
When these are present, the simile is "based on direct denotation" (*śrautī*). The same applies when the suffix *vati*—prescribed in the sense of *iva* by the rule *tatra tasyeva*—is employed.
In such instances as “his face is equal to that,” the word is used only with respect to the object of comparison (*upameya*),
as in “that is equal to this.”

In such cases where the object of comparison [the upamāna] is expressed by words like *eva*, and where both [the subject and the object] are expressed as "this and that are equal," the words such as *tulya* (equal) find their final rest in both instances;

thus, through the contemplation of similarity (*sāmya*), the cognition of equality arises. Consequently, because the common property (*sādharmya*) is implicit in the meaning, when words such as *tulya* are employed, [the simile is complete].
Similarly, when there is the presence of the suffix *vati* prescribed by the rule "When [something] is equal to that, if it is an action,

the suffix *vati* is used," and when there is a compulsory compound according to the rule "A compulsory compound with *iva*, with non-elision of the case-ending, and the original accent of the preceding member."
When joined with the word *iva*, [the upamā] resides in a compound.

The examples in their respective order are as follows: "Even in dreams, the Goddess of Victory does not forsake you in battles, just as a woman who has her husband under her control does not leave her beloved, the source of her power. (392)

An example: "The speech of that fortunate man, who possesses a preeminent excellence of benevolence unparalleled by others, is to be acted upon; his word is truly like nectar. (397)
With his sword drawn, as he moved about in the heat of battle, that lord was seen by the enemy army to be like Death himself.
His conduct is like a sword, his speech is like nectar, and his mind is like poison; if you know this, my friend, then you live. (399)
(Verse 129) When the standard of comparison is not explicitly mentioned, [the simile] resides either in the sentence or in the compound. //88//
The bestowal of the glory of complete rest upon all constituent parts is not seen in the case of fine poetry;
rather, it is either perceived or heard even in its smallest portion. 400.
If the reading is *kavvasamaṃ* instead of *kavvassa*, and *ṇūṇaṃ* instead of *sarisam*, then this very [type of simile] is one residing in a compound (*samāsagā*).

(Verse 130) When there is elision of the word *vā* and so forth, in a compound, in the suffix *kyac* used in the sense of the object or the locus, in the suffix *kyaṅ*, and in the suffix *ṇamul* used in the sense of the object or the agent.

The word *vā* indicates a comparison (*upamā*). Thus, when the comparative particle *vā* and so forth—which expresses comparison—is elided, there would be [the formation of a compound] in six ways: by means of a compound (*samāsa*), by the suffix *kyac* produced after a word denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) following the word *sarmaṇas*, by the suffix *kyaṅ* after a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), and by the suffix *ṇamul* when words denoting the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*) function as the attendant words (*upapada*).
The example: "Then the eastern quarter was adorned by the moon, the lord of the night-blooming lilies, pale as the cheek of a longing woman, and the delight of the eyes. (401)

Thus, upon seeing the prowess of his rival, he became one whose sword-blade was terrifying like a black serpent, whose movements were swift due to a mind agitated by a longing for combat, whose body was covered in horripilation, and whose cheeks possessed a radiant glow. (402)
This man, skilled in diverse deeds, acts as a father toward his people in the midst of battle; he acts as a woman within his inner apartments;
and upon beholding his exploits, the enemy army acts like a woman before him who holds a sword in hand on the battlefield.
In battle, his enemies behold him as the sun at the height of summer;
yet that lord of the earth moves again with the maneuvers of Arjuna.
(131) When both of these are elided, [the suffix] *kvip* occurs within a compound. //89//

Of these two speakers of dharma, the example is as follows: "The sun acts like the moon, and the moon likewise acts like the sun; nights act like days, and days act like nights, when the mind is brought under the sway of pleasure and pain. (405)
Unassailable even by hundreds of the hostile desires of his enemies,
this elephant among kings shines resplendent as he engages in battle.
(Verse 132) The elision of both the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is observed both in compound (*vṛtti*) and in the sentence (*vākya*). For example:
"Clinging [to them], you will die from the thorns of the *ketaka* groves."
O bee, wandering about, you shall not obtain that which is like the flower of the Māhika tree. // 407 //
In the reading *kusumena samam*, it is a sentence-based [simile]; in the case of *kyac*, when the initial element and the object of comparison are omitted. (Sūtra 133)
Though free from desire, his eyes wide open at the sight of the prowess of his enemies, and with the staff-like arms of his sword raised high, he acts as if he possessed a thousand weapons.
Here, the self (*ātman*) is the object of comparison (*upameya*); and when three [elements] are elided, it is a compound-based (*samāsagā*) [metaphor]. (Sūtra 134) //90//
Of the three types of similes involving the subject (*vādī*), the property (*dharma*), and the object of comparison (*upamāna*):

the example— "With her gaze fixed upon youth, her form bestowed with graceful charms, and her inner being pierced by the multitude of Cupid’s arrows, the deer-eyed woman steals away even the mind of the sage. (409)
In this case, when the compound and the elision occur by means of the rule beginning with "saptamyupamāna" (Pāṇini 2.1.40), then this is the example.
Because of the determination that a cruel conduct is an iron spike (*ayaḥśūla*), one "seeks [the goal] with an iron spike," thus [being called] *āyaḥśūlika*;

this is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), and not a simile (*upamā*) where there is an elision of the three elements—the object of comparison (*upameya*), the common property (*dharmavādin*), and the word of comparison—due to the elision of the common property of sharpness in the cruel conduct.
Thus, there are nineteen types of elliptical similes; together with the complete ones, there are twenty-five.
Then, through that despondency, her royal splendor faded away like a lotus-pond by freezing water— just as sovereignty fades through misrule, or high-mindedness through wretchedness.
Thus, when the common property is non-differentiated:
"Like moonlight, she is a delight to the eyes; like wine, she is a cause of intoxication;
like sovereignty, she attracts all people—the woman of shapely hips. (411)
Thus, when that [distinction] is broken and many points of comparison are employed for a single subject, it is a "garland simile" (mālopamā).
When each subsequent object of comparison serves as the point of comparison for the preceding one, while maintaining the same or different attributes as before—as in the case of:
"whose mass of wealth was rippled by waves of hands holding droplets of water from the incessant giving of gold..."—[it is a garland simile].
Her intellect was like her speech, her conduct was like her intellect, and her fame was as stainless as her conduct. // 412 //

The king’s intellect was as sweet as his personified form, and his assembly, rich in majesty, was like his personified form; likewise, his assembly was like his personified glory of victory—such a king could not be conquered by others.
The "girdle simile" (*raśanopamā*) and others like it have not been specifically defined [as separate figures],
because thousands of such varieties can arise and yet do not transcend the categories already mentioned.
(Verse 135) When both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison belong to one and the same thing within a single sentence, [it is a case of self-comparison].
*Ananvaya* (non-comparison) is the absence of connection with any other object of comparison.
An example: "Not only does that woman of shapely hips shine with extreme beauty, she shines like herself."
As far as they were the abodes of the dance of the weapon of playfulness, so were those playful movements like his own playful movements.
(Verse 136) The reverse of that [is] the simile of mutual comparison (*upameyopamā*) between those two. //91//
Of those two— the object of comparison and the subject of comparison—
there is an exchange,
that is to say, between two sentences.
It is called *upameyopamā* because it consists of a comparison by means of the object compared (*upameya*), with the purpose of excluding other possible standards of comparison.

Example: "Like a lotus is his intellect, like his intellect is the goddess Kamalā; like his body is his radiance, like his radiance is his body; like the earth is his fortitude, like his fortitude is the earth—thus he shines eternally, alas! (415)
(Verse 137) Furthermore,
*utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is the imagining of the subject at hand as being equal to something else; "equal" means by way of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

An example of the *udāra* (noble) style: "O lady of graceful form, I believe that the beauty of the lotus has, out of joy, clung to your feet—thinking, 'The pride of beauty belonging to that enemy by birth who cannot endure my blossoming during the night has been forcibly quelled by the splendor of this woman’s face. (416)
Darkness seems to smear my limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium;
and like service rendered to a wicked man, my vision has become fruitless.
In such passages, pervasion and so forth are conceived in the form of anointing and so forth.
(Sūtra 138) But *sasaṃdeha* [simile] consists of doubt when there is either an explicit statement of difference or no such statement. //92//
As an example of the expression of doubt (*bhedokti*), [consider this]: "Is this the sun? But he has only seven horses. Is it fire? But it does not spread in all directions with certainty.
Is it Death himself? But his vehicle is a buffalo. Having gazed at you for a long time on the battlefield, your opponents entertain such doubts. (418)

By the phrase "when there is a statement of distinction" (*bhedhoktau*), it is not only this doubt characterized by certainty (*niścayagarbha*) that is accepted, but also the doubt that culminates in certainty (*niścayānta*).
For example: "Is it the moon? Where is the spot? Is this a lotus? Where has the water gone?
O deer-eyed one, through her charming and playful words, [the observer] finally concluded, 'It is her face. (419)

However, because no certainty is perceived here—despite the presence of what seems to be an internal certainty—it was disregarded by Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa. For example, in the absence of such a statement [of certainty], [we have]: "In the creation of this woman, was the Creator the Moon, the bestower of luster? Or was he Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was he the month of spring, the source of flowers?"
How indeed could that ancient sage, rendered dull by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sensory objects, have been capable of creating this enchanting form? (420)
(Verse 139) That is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), which is the non-difference between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*),
due to extreme similarity, wherein the difference is not denied; it is non-difference.
(Verse 140) When the words heard [in the text] denote all things as superimposed [upon one another], [the resulting cognition is called "verbal" (śābda)]. //93//
When those things being superimposed are as if they were the objects of superimposition and are expressed by words,
then, because all things constitute its object, it is called "having all things as its object" (*samastavastuviṣaya*).
The plural number in the word *āropitā* (placed upon) is not intended to be significant. For example:

"This night-wandering female ascetic (*kāpālikī*), pale as if smeared with the ashes of moonlight, bearing the bones of stars, and delighting in the passion for the art of invisibility, wanders from island to island, carrying within the skull-cup of the moon the fragrance of the *siddhāñjana* ointment under the guise of its dark spot. (421)

In these three quarters, since the state of being intent on the calamity of invisibility is indeed an imposed attribute (āropitadharma), there is sufficient evidence for accepting it as a metaphor (rūpaka); therefore, one should not entertain a doubt regarding its commingling (saṃkara).
(Verse 141) That [type of metaphor] in which some [elements] are expressed by words and others are understood through the force of the sense is called *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest).
Some of the things being superimposed are conveyed by the words themselves, while others are to be inferred from the power of the meaning.
Because it turns out only one part [of the intended meaning], it is called "partial development" (*ekadeśavivarti*).
For example: "In the battle-field of his harem, as he brandishes the tip of his sword, the army of his enemies, though facing him with passion, suddenly turns its back. (422)

Here, while the nature of an inner apartment (*antaḥpura*) is being superimposed upon the battlefield, the status of the heroine (*nāyikā*) for the sword-blade creeper and the status of the rival heroine (*pratināyikā*) for the enemy army are understood through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*). Thus, because it functions specifically with respect to a single part [of the whole], it is called "partially developed" (*ekadeśavivartin*).
(Sūtra 142)
This [type of inference] is "with its members" (sāṅga),
meaning it possesses the two aforementioned divisions and consists of constituent parts (sāvayava).
(Verse 143) But the pure [love] is without limbs,
as when she makes the limbs of a doe motionless during the sounds of song, and when she asks her friend again about news of her beloved even though it has already been heard.
And that she sleeps within herself without slumbering—oh, I know this: the Mind-born has begun to water the fresh creeper of love in her heart.
The garland, however, is as before. (Sūtra 144) //94//
In a *mālōpamā* (garland simile), as it were, many attributes are superimposed upon a single object:

"She is a river of beauty, an outburst of joy from the excellence of youth, a magical spell for loveliness, the dwelling place for the manifestation of the secrets of dalliance, the science of crooked speech, the realization of the Creator’s boundless mastery, the arrows of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], and the crest-jewel of all women—she is my beloved. (424)
(Verse 145) That superimposition upon another which serves as a means for a fixed superimposition is *paraṃparita* (transferred metaphor);
it occurs when the expressive word is either based on a double entendre (*śliṣṭa*) or possesses distinct meanings (*bhedabhājin*). //95//

O Swan of the minds of the wise, O You of radiant splendor who causes the lotuses of Your enemies to close, O Nīlalohita (Śiva) to those seeking the path to the fortress, O Vaiśvānara (Fire) to those offering fuel in the form of their vows, O Expert in bestowing love for the Truth, O Terrifying One through the preeminence of Your victory—O Lord, O Excellent Hero, may You perform the imperial rule of Brahmā for a hundred years! 425.

In this case, the very closing of the mind is the closing of the lotuses; the non-seeking of difficulties is the seeking of Durgā; the acceptance of fuel is the acceptance of sacrificial wood; affection for truth is the lack of affection for Satī;
and victory over others is the victory of Arjuna.
Thus, the superimposition of a swan and so forth is based on the cause of superimposition (*āropaṇanimitta*).

Although it has been stated—and will be further explained—that this is a figure of speech belonging to both word and meaning (*śabdārthālaṃkāra*), it is nevertheless mentioned here in accordance with common usage; for others designate this as "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*).

O King, your arm—which bestows widowhood upon the wives of enemy heroes—shines forth as a pillar for the elephant of victory, a stone dam against the ocean of calamity, the eastern mountain for the fierce-rayed sun of your sword, a playful pillow for the Goddess of Fortune, and Mount Mandara for the sport of churning the nectar-ocean of battle. (426)

In this context, when the elephanthood and so forth are superimposed upon Jayodarbhi— who is denoted by a distinct word— the superimposition of "tethering post" and so forth upon his arm is appropriate.
[He is] one who has illuminated the three worlds with a supermundane, great light.
O Lord, by whom is your jewel-like pearl from a noble lineage not praised? 427

Victorious is Your first manifestation here in the form of the Tortoise— the root-stalk for the creeper of the fourteen worlds— whose state is boundless and independent, and who has not ceased the manifold display of His wondrous play.
And thus, even a *amālā-rūpaka* (non-series metaphor) should be understood as being *paraṃparita* (transferred).

Love conquers the minds of lovers with the sprout-like hands of creepers and the lotus-hands of passionate men; it conquers them with the lotus-faces of water-lilies and the moon-like faces of women. 429.
Such instances of the *raśanā* (girdle) metaphor do not possess sufficient variety and have therefore not been defined [as a distinct figure].
(Verse 146) When one thing is negated so that another may be established, that is *apahnuti* (concealment).
That is *apahnuti* wherein the object of comparison (*upameya*) is rendered unreal and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is established as real.
Example: "O Daughter of the Mountain, this is not a blemish that has attained boldness upon the body of the moon, whose luster is now mature;
rather, I think it is the Night, the beloved of Love, who, exhausted from dalliance, lies deeply upon his chest, which is cool with trickling nectar. (430)
"O friend, look! Alas, how great indeed is this enmity of Smara toward this world of lovers emaciated by separation from their beloveds!
For, under the guise of bees shimmering upon the mango trees in the grove, he has engraved deadly *kālakūṭa* poison upon every one of his arrows. (431)
For here the understanding is not that there are mango trees with bees, but rather that these are arrows accompanied by the *kālakūṭa* poison.
Or again: "In this lake of the nectar of beauty belonging to that fawn-eyed woman, the God of Love—surely burnt by Śiva—has surely fallen upon her broad hips."
When this crest of smoke, a foreboding omen for the embers within the limbs, transforms into the form of a line of hair in the hollow of the navel. // 432 //
In this case, there is no line of body hair; rather, the cognition is that "this is a column of smoke.
In this same manner, it should be inferred through other modes as well.
(Verse 147) *Śleṣa* (punning connection) occurs in a single sentence where there is a multiplicity of meanings. //96//

*Śleṣa* (punning) is that figure where multiple meanings are conveyed by words intended to express a single meaning. An example: "He causes the rising [of the sun]; he utterly dispels the darkness of the quarters; he brings to an end the seal of sleep; he sets all activities in motion; he thoroughly cuts short the practice of unrestrained conduct—alas, alas! the mass of radiant splendor, the maker of light, shines forth. (433)
In this case, because there is no restriction on the primary denotative function (abhidhā), both the sun and the king are expressed as the literal meaning (vācya).

(Verse 148) *Samāsokti* (Indirect Description) is the expression of a non-contextual meaning by means of a sentence that conveys the contextual meaning through the power of its punning adjectives— not through the power of the substantive itself— by means of words that are "punned" (*śliṣṭa*) with respect to their differentiating features (*bhedaka*). It is called *samāsa* because it expresses two meanings in a concise manner (*saṃkṣepa*).
*Samāsokti* (Abridged Expression).
Example: "Having obtained the touch of your arms, she experienced a certain indescribable joy; now, in your absence, O Goddess of Victory, she is neither radiant nor even weak. (434)
In this case, the word *jayalakṣmī* does not denote merely a beloved woman.
(Verse 149) Illustration (*nidarśanā*):
A connection with an unreal thing that brings about a conceptualized simile. //97//
*Nidarśana* is the act of providing an illustration;
it is an *udāharaṇa* (example): "Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?
Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean, so difficult to traverse, by means of a small raft. (435)

In this case, the description of the Solar dynasty through my intellect culminates in a simile, like crossing the ocean by means of a small boat (*uḍupa*). Or, for example: "When the sun rises with its cord-like rays extended upward, and the moon sets, this mountain bears the grace of a lordly elephant attended by two hanging bells. (436)
In this case, how can one person bear the playfulness of another? Thus, it culminates in a simile: "resembling that.

"O King, he who exerts himself to recount your virtues surely wishes to cross the ocean with his two arms, desires to seize the moon’s orb in his hand, and seeks to leap over Mount Meru—just as one might wish to catch a serpent amidst the waves. (437)
In such cases as these, this [type of simile] should be understood as occurring when the form of a string (mālā) is absent.
(Verse 150) Furthermore,
there is another [type of inference] which is the statement of the connection between its own [subject] and its own cause through the action itself.
That is, when the relationship between its own nature and its own cause is understood through the action itself, that is [the second type].

Another illustration: Just as one who, having attained a high position, is bound to fall with ease if he is light—so too does a fragment of stone atop a mountain peak fall downward when shaken by a gentle breeze. (438)
In this case, when there is lightness resulting from the act of falling, the connection with the attainment of a high position is made manifest.
(Verse 151) That which is the praise of the irrelevant (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) is itself [a form of] *aprastutapraśaṃsā* when it has the relevant (*prastuta*) as its basis. //98//
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant) is the implication of the relevant subject through the mention of something irrelevant.
(Sūtra 152) When the effect, the cause, the general, or the particular is the subject under discussion, [the description of something else serves as its indication].
"Of one different from that," "of the same as the word," and "of the same as [the object]"—thus it is fivefold. (99)

This refers to causes and so forth other than that [the actual cause]. Here are examples in sequence: "O beautiful one, do those who have departed not return? You should not worry for my sake; you are exceedingly thin. While I was speaking thus with tears, she looked at me with eyes whose pupils were languid with shame and whose falling tears had been drunk up, and by her smile, she signaled her resolve for an imminent death. (439)
When asked the reason for his return from this journey, he stated the cause:
"O King! The princess does not teach me; the queens also remain silent. O hunchback, feed me! Why is nothing being eaten yet by the prince’s ministers?
Thus, O Lord, the parrot released from its cage by travelers in the enemy's palace speaks one by one to those standing in the paintings, as he gazes upon the empty balconies.
In this instance, having learned that you were about to set out on your expedition, your enemies fled in haste;
thus, while the cause was intended to be stated, the effect has been mentioned.
How much more so than this must one hear from his own mouth: that fool who, upon a lotus leaf, mistook a drop of water for a pearl!
When it is being slowly taken up, vanishing upon the light touch of the fingertips, he does not sleep day after day with inner grief, wondering, "Where has it flown away from me? (441)

In this context, while the general principle that "the dull-witted harbor a sense of ownership toward what is inappropriate" was intended to be introduced, a specific instance has been stated instead:

"He who wipes away the tears of his friends' wives by avenging their enmity—he alone is worthy of honor, he is a true man, he is possessed of statesmanship; his life is well-lived, and he is the vessel of prosperity. (442)

In this instance, while a specific case is under discussion— namely, "If you pacify the grief of the wives of the demon Naraka by slaying Kṛṣṇa, then you alone are praiseworthy"— a general statement has been made. When an equal [subject] is introduced and an equal is expressed, there are three varieties.
Pun (*śleṣa*), *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), or mere similarity (*sādṛśyamātra*) are indeed the causes for the implication (*ākṣepa*) of one thing by another similar thing.

The examples follow in order: "Even if he were to deviate from his manhood, even if he were to go below, even if he were not great in granting favors—even so, he would uplift the entire universe; such is the direction revealed by this Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). (443)
O Moon, since you were reduced to exhaustion by the Sun when he had risen, it would have been fitting for you to retaliate against him, rather than grasping at his very feet.
If this was performed by you while you were waning, why are you not even slightly ashamed? Indeed, your dullness of nature is evident in that you merely shine in the sky.
Having gathered water from all around the mouths of the rivers, what has been achieved by this wicked ocean?
It has been rendered salty, offered as a libation into the submarine fire, and deposited within the hollow depths of the netherworld.
And this [type of suggestion] occurs in certain cases where the suggested meaning exists without being superimposed upon the expressed meaning, as for example:
"The waters of the ocean, which conceal the expanse of the world and the depths of the netherworld in its belly—indeed, many here possess the means of ships capable of crossing it.
But if by some stroke of fate it were ever to become empty, who indeed would be able even to look into its cavernous abyss? (446)

In some cases, it occurs through superimposition alone. For example: "Who are you, sir? "I am a wretched man, cursed by fate; know me to be a *śākhoṭaka* tree. "You speak as if out of world-weariness (*vairāgya*). "Well said! I understand. "Why is this being said? "Here on my left is a *vaṭa* tree, which travelers serve with their whole being. "But even though I stand right on the path, I do not provide even a shadow for the benefit of others. (447)
In some parts [of the meaning], it is through superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

For example: "That unprecedented method of reversing the tongue; that fickleness of his ears; that gaze which, intoxicated, has forgotten the distinction between self and other—what more need be said?
O bee, you have forgotten everything! Why, brother, do you still serve this elephant whose trunk is empty within? What kind of obsession is this? (448)

In this case, the perversion of taste and the state of being rendered empty are not the causes for the bee's indulgence; rather, the fickleness of the ear is the cause, while intoxication, on the contrary, is the motive for its indulgence.

(Verse 153) But [the figure] *nigīryādhyavasāna* (swallowing and then identifying) is that where the subject at hand is identified with another; where there is the attribution of something else to the topic under discussion; and where there is a conceptualization upon the statement of a condition (*yadyartha*). //100//

The reversal of the sequence between cause and effect is also to be understood as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). One type of this consists in the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the object of comparison (*upameya*), which has been internally swallowed by the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Just as a lotus grows not in water but upon a lotus, and blue lilies grow upon that lotus, and they all grow upon a golden creeper, and that creeper is itself delicate and beautiful—what is this succession of marvels? 449.

In this case, the face and so forth are determined (adhyavasita) as having the form of a lotus and so forth; and that very thing which is determined as something else—that is the other [type of metaphor]. For example: "Another loveliness, another indescribable grace of movement."
The moon does not even possess the splendor of the moonlight of the Lord of the World. // 450 //
“If it concerns the object”: the conceptualization (i.e., of an impossible object) expressed by the word *yadi* or the word *cet* is the third [type of impossibility].
If the body of the moon were to become free from blemish on the night of the full moon,
only then would her face attain a state of surpassing similarity to it.
The fourth [type of *pūrva*] is used when the effect is mentioned before the cause in order to express the swiftness of the cause's action.
For example: "O beloved of women, it was first that Mālatī’s heart was struck by the arrow of the flower-bowed god, and only afterwards did you come within the range of her eyes. (452)
But that is *prativastūpamā* (the simile of corresponding objects). //101//
Where a single common property resides in two sentences,
that is the shared attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) in the sentence concerning the object of comparison (*upameyavākye*).

In a sentence of comparison (*upamāna*), since the repetition of a word is considered a defect, when something is introduced through a different word because the actual object (*vastu*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the sentence-meaning, that is *prativastūpamā* (comparison by parallelism). For example:
"Having been elevated to the status of a queen, how can she occupy the position of a mere attendant?
Indeed, a jewel marked with the form of a deity is not fit for common use. (453)
If fire burns here, what is the wonder? And if there is weight in mountains, what of it?
The water of the great ocean is always salty; indeed, freedom from dejection is the very nature of the virtuous.
Thus, this *mālā-prativastūpamā* (chain simile) is to be understood;
in the same way, it should be followed in other instances as well.
(Verse 155) Furthermore, the illustration for all of these is their reflection. //102//
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is that wherein the end—that is, the certainty—of these common properties and so forth is observed.
"Upon seeing you alone, her mind, inflamed by the god of love, is extinguished;
for indeed, at the sight of the moon, the flower of the night-lily blossoms. (455)
This is by way of similarity;
but by way of dissimilarity: "In your battle, while you—finding joy in acts of audacity—were bringing your hand near the sword, the soldiers of your enemies went to ruin."
For dust particles indeed attain stability when there is no wind. // 456 //

The simultaneous occurrence of a single attribute belonging to both the relevant and the irrelevant subjects across many actions is the figure of speech known as *dīpaka* (the illuminator). (Sūtra 156)

When the attribute—such as an action or the like—of both relevant and irrelevant subjects (that is, the objects of comparison and the objects compared) is employed only once, it is called *dīpaka* because, by being situated in a single place, it illuminates the entire sentence.
For example: "The wealth of the miserly, the hood-jewels of serpents, the manes of lions..."
How could the breasts of young women from noble families swell when they are not suckled? // 457 //
And *dīpaka* (the illuminator) is the single occurrence of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) across many actions.
For example: "She perspires, shrinks, trembles, quivers, blinks, and casts sidelong glances;
she rejoices within and desires to kiss—thus does the newlywed bride behave upon the bed. (458)
(Verse 157) If the first [type] is the Garland-Lamp (*mālādīpaka*), it brings about successive qualities; that is,
by means of each preceding subject.
When each subsequent element is further assisted by the preceding one, that is *mālādīpaka* (the lamp-in-a-garland).
For example: "O King, listen as you have arrived on the battlefield and strung your bow—listen to what has been suddenly attained by each thing:

by the bow, arrows; by the arrows, the enemy's head; by that [head], the circle of the earth; by that, you; by you, incomparable fame; and by that fame, the three worlds; and by that [fame], you; and by you, incomparable fame; and by that fame... [The structure repeats].
And the three worlds. // 459 //
(Verse 158) The simultaneous occurrence of attributes among things that are restricted [to a single category] is, moreover, the figure of speech called *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). //104//
[This occurs] only for those that are restricted [to a specific context], whether they belong to the subject matter at hand (*prākaraṇika*) or not (*aprākaraṇika*).

The examples in order are as follows: "O friend, your pale and emaciated face, your passionate heart, and your languid body clearly announce a deep-seated consumption (*kṣetriya-roga*) within your breast. (460)
Before your eyes, which possess such charming grace, what are the rows of white, red, and blue lotuses?
Nectar, the moon, and the water-born lotus are all simultaneously surpassed by your face.

(Sūtra 159) That which is the excellence of one thing over another is indeed that [vyatireka]. The excellence (*vyatireka*) of another, namely the object of comparison (*upameya*), is its superiority.
It is true that even when the moon has waned, it waxes again and again;
but desist, O beautiful one, and be gracious, for youth once gone does not return.

Regarding this, the claim made by some that in such cases the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) possesses superiority over the object of comparison (*upameya*) is incorrect; for what is intended here is the superiority of the instability inherent in youth.
(Sūtra 160) When the two causes are mentioned or not mentioned, there are three [varieties]; when the similarity is expressed... //105//
When [the excellence] is suggested by both the word and the meaning, or when it is based on a pun (*śliṣṭa*), that same [figure] is eighteenfold.

It is the cause of *vyatireka* (distinction), which consists in the statement of two things: the ground for the superiority residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the ground for the inferiority residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Whether of one or of two [elements],

there is non-statement; thus, these three types of non-statement, together with the fourfold division when the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is expressed by word (*śabda*),
and by meaning (*artha*) respectively, constitute exactly four varieties.
When the simile is explicitly stated (*ākṣipta*), there are likewise [twelve];
thus, there are twelve [in this case].
Since these also occur in the presence of *śleṣa* (punning), there are twenty-four varieties in total.
The examples in order: "Though he has overcome a multitude of enemies with nothing but his sword as his companion, this man of great fortitude feels no pride, unlike other insignificant people. (463)
In this very context, when the terms *tuccha* (insignificant) and *mahādhṛti* (of great fortitude) are not employed either alternately or simultaneously, there is another threefold division.
This should be understood in the same way for other cases as well.
Here, because of the presence of the word *iva*, there is a verbal comparison (*śābdamaupamyam*).
Even though he has only a sword as his companion and faces the defeat of many enemies, this man of great fortitude is not at all arrogant like other insignificant people. (464)

In this context, since the suffix *vat* is used in the sense of equality, the comparison is implicit in the meaning: "This fair-eyed woman, with her face that has eclipsed the beauty of the lotus and is free from blemish, triumphs over the moon which is possessed of a spot. (465)
Even in the absence of words such as "atīva" (exceedingly) or "tulya" (equal),
the simile is indeed implied:
[of one] who, through mastery over the senses, properly serves those advanced in knowledge.
The virtues of this one, whose qualities are exceedingly profound, are not fragile like the fibers of a lotus.
In this sense, the suffix *vati* is used;
the word "guṇa" is a pun (*śliṣṭa*), and the comparison is expressed through words (*śābda*).
Behold this illustrious lord of the earth, whose circle [of dominion] is unbroken!
He never undergoes a deficiency in his qualities, like the moon. // 467 //
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "equality," and the word *kalā* is employed with double meaning (*śliṣṭa*).
Just as there is a "garland simile" (*mālōpamā*), a "garland contrast" (*mālāvyatireka*) is also possible;
its varieties should likewise be inferred in this manner.
A mere illustration is provided:
"O Lord, you are never like Hara, whose vision is partial; nor like Hari, who has shaken off his vast bovine nature; nor like Ravi, who scorches the earth with his unbearable rays. (468)
In this verse, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "equality," and the words such as *viṣama* (uneven/difficult) are *śliṣṭa* (punned).
"With its ever-risen majesty, this king, possessing solar brilliance, has utterly conquered that sun whose light is closed up during the three watches of the night. (469)

For here, the simile "shining" (*bhāsvatā*) is indeed implied and thus constitutes a *śliṣṭa* (pun). Or, for example: "In that place, the wine—which possessed the reflection of the moon shining forth due to the quality of its own clarity, which bore the luster of [the wine's] own form, and which had a natural, pleasing fragrance—removed the thirst of young men drinking it excessively during the nights, whereas the faces of the women did not. (470)
Even in the absence of words such as *atireka* ("excess") or *tulya* ("equal"), the simile (*upamā*) is understood as being implied by the punning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*).
Other varieties of this same type are also possible when a word capable of double entendre (*śliṣṭokti*) is employed separately;
these too should be observed by this same method.
(Verse 161) A negation [is that which is employed] with the desire to express a specific qualification of that which one intends to state. //106//
That *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), whose objects are both what is yet to be said and what has already been said, is considered to be of two kinds.
It is a negation—or rather, a negation in appearance—of that which is intended to be expressed because it is the primary subject matter and should not be treated as subordinate;

this negation serves to state a distinction, namely either the impossibility of being spoken or its extreme well-knownness. Thus, *ākṣepa* is twofold: having as its object what is yet to be said (*vakṣyamāṇaviṣaya*) and having as its object what has already been said (*uktaviṣaya*).

Examples in order: "Come here! For some reason, for someone's sake, I say something—enough of it! Or rather, let her who undertakes the commencement of an unconsidered task die; I will not speak. (471)

Moonlight, strings of pearls, sandalwood paste, the liquid from the moonstone, camphor, plantains, bracelets of lotus stalks, lotus leaves, and other things equal to the mind—alas, alas! when you, O Lord, are present, these serve only to produce a mass of sparks for her; what need is there to say more? We shall not even speak of it.
Even when an action is negated, the manifestation of its result is *vibhāvanā*. (Sūtra 162) //107//
Vibhāvanā is the manifestation of the effect even when its cause and the action [leading to it] are negated; for example:
"Though not struck by blossoming creepers, she bore pain; though not stung by swarms of bees..."
She was whirled about, and though not stirred by the waves of the lotus pond, she reeled.

(Verse 163) *Viśeṣokti* (the description of distinction) is the non-statement of the effect when the causes are unimpaired. *Viśeṣokti* consists in the failure to mention the result even though the causes have all come together.
Those with unspoken causes, those with spoken causes, and those with inconceivable causes.

An illustration in sequence: When sleep had ceased, when the jewel of the day had risen, when her companions had reached the threshold of the door, and when the lover’s passion for the embrace had slackened, that woman moved away from the embrace.
Salutations to that Makarakeṭu (the god of love), whose power remains effective among every person even when he is like burnt camphor; salutations to him of irresistible valor!
That god of the flowery arrows alone conquers the three worlds;
for although Śambhu took away his body, he did not take away his power.
(Verse 164) There is a correspondence between successive [factors] according to their respective order, precisely in sequence. //108//

O Lord, just as you dwell threefold within the minds of these—of your enemies, of the learned, and of the fawn-eyed women—you nourish, respectively, torment, the essence of joy, and passion, through the heat of your valor, through discipline, and through grace. (477)
Whether it be a general rule or a particular instance, that which is supported by something else—
either through similarity or otherwise— is *arthāntaranyāsa*. //109//

When a general principle is supported by a particular instance, or a particular instance by a general principle, either through similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), that is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).
The examples in order are as follows: "To those whose minds are shrouded by their own defects, even that which is exceedingly beautiful appears otherwise.
One afflicted by bile sees even a conch shell, white as the moon, as yellow. (478)
Once, while a beautiful woman, adorned with white garments and ornaments, was walking at her leisure in the moonlight of the Kaumudī festival, the moon set.
Immediately thereafter, your fame was sung by someone, whereby she went to the house of her beloved, free from all apprehension; for where are you not the bestower of auspiciousness?
It is solely due to the wickedness of his own virtues that a draft ox is yoked to the burden;
the barren cow, whose shoulder has not yet developed calluses, sleeps in comfort.
Alas! I have indeed committed a great offense against my long-lived friend, in that such unpleasant words as these must be spoken by me.
Blessed are those friends who, never having witnessed defeat in this world, have passed away before seeing such ruin.
(Verse 166) Contradiction (*virodha*) is that speech which, despite there being no contradiction, is expressed as if it were contradictory.
Even when there is no contradiction according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*), the expression of two things as if they were contradictory constitutes contradiction.
A genus is opposed by four [categories], beginning with genus itself; a quality is opposed by three. (110)
Action arises from two [substances], and substance arises from substance alone; thus, there are ten [types of causes].

The examples in their respective order are as follows: "O fortunate one, for this deer-eyed woman, by the power of fate, the fresh lotus leaf, the lotus stalk bracelet, and so forth, have become a mass of forest fire upon the fall of the thunderbolt of separation from you. (482)
O Lord of Men, in your presence, even the mountains are surely devoid of loftiness, even the wind is motionless, even the oceans are not deep, and even the earth is exceedingly light. 483.

O King, it is a marvel that for those monarchs whose minds are intent on the joy of battle, even the sharp rain-cloud, having attained the state of being embraced by their necks, becomes impassioned and attains a certain affection; yet for them, you perform the rite of cleansing with masses of dust. 484.

That Janārdana, who by his very nature invariably creates, protects, and destroys this world with effortless ease, even when he becomes a mere minnow according to the exigency of the occasion—this too is a marvel! (485)
O King, because of their constant engagement in numerous household chores, the hands of the wives of the twice-born—which were once as delicate as lotuses—become calloused. (486)
Indeed, even the sweet words of a villain burn the hearts of those who know the truth;
yet even the harsh speech of a virtuous person brings joy like sandalwood oil.

Since that Krauñca mountain— firm with its formidable boulders— became as soft as the petals of a fresh lotus under the unobstructed fall of the showers of his arrows, it is true that Bhārgava was a creation of unprecedented origin.

Beyond all demarcation and outside the scope of every word, that which has never yet entered the path of experience in this birth—some inexplicable transformation, dense with great delusion accumulated through the destruction of discernment, both stupefies the inner self and brings forth torment. (489)
"This ocean is the sole abode of waters, a mine of jewels"—thus did we, our minds agitated by thirst, take refuge in the sea.
Who could have known that this Sage would, in a single moment, drink it up along with its gasping whales and sea-monsters, as if it were contained within the hollow of his own cupped palms?

O ornament of the earth, when you dwell upon its banks, even the river that is the crest-jewel of Śiva becomes the Kālindī through its embrace by the river-like flow of the ichor from the temples of his subdued elephant.
(Verse 168) *Svabhāvokti* (Description of Nature), however, is the depiction of the form and action of infants and the like. //111//
"Of its own [two] which have that as their single support":
"form" (*rūpa*) refers to both color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*).

An example: Having stretched out his two hind legs, having extended his body high by bending his back, having lowered his head with his neck curved, and having shaken his mane grey with dust against his chest—[the lion roars].
Desiring a mouthful of grass, the horse, its muzzle constantly flickering, rises from its bed and, making a low sound, scratches the earth with its hoof.
(Verse 169) *Vyājastuti* (ironical praise) is either censure or praise expressed on the surface that is otherwise established [as its opposite].
It is praise in the form of a pretext, or praise by means of a pretext.

Examples in order: I believe that for those whose minds are weary of restraint, there is no other crest-jewel [of excellence] than you, except perhaps for the Goddess Ramā, who is seen nowhere else apart from the casting aside of shame.
She who, having been sought by hundreds of suitors, utterly abandoned her resort to you; yet even after receiving the humiliation of being forsaken, her abode remains with you alone. (493)

O Ocean, you who have effortlessly conquered the Bodhisattvas by your very speech, what is the use of further elaborations? There is no one else like you who has taken a vow to bestow benefit upon others;
for out of compassion, you provide assistance to the desert, bearing the heavy burden of ill-repute acquired from turning away from helping thirsty travelers. 494.
(Verse 170) That is *sahokti* (joint description), wherein, by the force of the meaning of "together," a single word expresses two things. //112//

*Sahokti* (concomitance) is that [figure of speech] which, although expressing a single object, makes both [the primary and secondary objects] understood through the power of the sense of "together" (*saha*).
For example: "With the days and nights, her long sighs; with the jeweled bracelets, the streams of tears fall.
O fortunate one, in your separation, the hope for life has become as weak as her trembling body. (495)

Length and so forth residing in the breath, the staff, and the like are verbal [cognitions]; however, that which resides in the day, night, and so forth is understood through the force of the meaning (sahārthasāmarthyāt).
(Verse 171) *Vinokti* (the figure of speech of "without") is that where one thing, being absent another, is either non-existent or not otherwise;
in some cases it is inauspicious, and in others it is auspicious.
The examples in order: "Without the night there is no luster for the moon; without the moon, even that [night] is utter darkness.
Without both, the throbbing of love does not shine at all for the two lovers. (496)

Without that deer-eyed woman, this son of the king—once so confident in the brilliance of his eloquence regarding diverse worldly affairs, and whose heart was as beautiful as the moon—is [now] without that friend. (497)
(Verse 172) Parivṛtti is the exchange of objects for those that are either equal or unequal. //113//
*Parivṛtti* (Exchange) is an ornament.
An example:— "Having bestowed upon these creepers, now blossoming with flowers, the wind grants them an incomparable joy through its dance;
yet, alas, having suddenly seized the gaze of the travelers, it bestows upon them a confluence of mental anguish, physical disease, dizziness, and rising delusion. (498)

In this battle, O King, having received the blows accompanied by terrible sounds with various weapons, he equalized the equal in the first half [of the engagement] and the inferior with the superior in the second.
By the multitude of Dṛpta’s enemy heroes, this earth was granted the practice of an embrace free from deception.
In this case, [the comparison is made] of the superior by means of the inferior.
(Verse 173) That in which past and future entities are made to appear as if they were directly perceived is *bhāvikam*.
"Bhūta" means past and "bhāvin" means future; this is a *dvandva* compound.
Since the poet's intention (*bhāva*) is present here, it is called *bhāvika*. An example: "I see that there was collyrium here in your eyes."
I behold your form, already adorned with the full array of future ornaments.
In the first case there is the perception of what has already come to be; in the second, the perception of what is yet to be.
(Verse 174) Poetic Figure of Reason (*kāvyaliṅga*) consists in the fact that a reason is expressed as either the meaning of a sentence or the meaning of a word. //114//

Regarding the meaning of the sentence as a whole (*vākyārthatā*), for example: "O Destroyer of Tripura, from the manifestation of this body, I infer that in my previous births I likely never bowed to you at any time.
Having bowed now, I am liberated; in the future, I shall be bodiless and thus incapable of bowing. O Great Lord, these two offenses must be forgiven. (501)

Regarding the quality of multiple meanings (*anekapadārthatā*): This arm of mine—by which even delicate blows from *śirīṣa* flowers, obtained through the playful jests of affectionate friends, cause her body to suffer—shall fall upon the head of one who raises a weapon against that very body to slay her, like the sudden staff of Yama’s rod. (502)

The state of being a single referent (*ekapadārthatā*) is as follows: "O you who smear yourself with ashes, may it be well with you! O auspicious rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads! Alas! By the Lord, now gratified by our worship, we are today cast into that great delusion called liberation—which destroys the vision of the bliss of serving you—[a delusion] which is the staircase leading to the abode of the Consort of the Mountain’s Daughter. (503)

Regarding these two offenses, the causes are, respectively, as previously described: for the first offense, the failure to bow in former and later births; for the second, the hurling of weapons when one's arm falls [in battle]; and for the third, the severance of the vision of bliss during a state of great delusion.

(Sūtra 175) *Paryāyokta* (Indirect Expression) is that speech which occurs without the relationship of signifier and signified; that is, when there is a presentation by means of a process of comprehension distinct from the relationship of signifier and signified, it is [called] *paryāya*.
Paryāyokta (Indirect Description) consists in expressing something by means of a different turn of phrase.
An example: "Upon seeing whom, even the long-established affection for their dwelling was abandoned—by Airāvaṇa’s pride in his face, and by Indra’s pride in his heart. (504)

In this case, although it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) that Airāvaṇa and Śakra have become free from intoxication and pride, it is also expressed by words; thus, what is expressed is itself the suggested.
However, it is not expressed in the same manner as it is suggested.
For example, when one sees a white cow moving, [one does not say] "the white cow moves," but rather "the cow, which is white, moves."
Such is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
One conceptualizes exactly what has been perceived, but not in the manner in which it was perceived;
for it was perceived as undifferentiated and unassociated.
One conceptualizes by means of differentiation and conjunction.
(Verse 176) *Udātta* is the excellence of a subject;
excellence is the possession of prosperity.

Just as play-parrots, suspecting them to be pomegranate seeds, pull from afar those pearls that have slipped from necklaces whose strings were undone during sport, been swept up by brooms, and lie at the edge of the courtyard in the morning, reddened by the lac from the slowly moving feet of young girls— such, O King Bhoja, is the playful display of generosity found in the palaces of the learned.
(177) And it is also an indicative mark of great beings. //115//

Indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) is a subordinate element (*aṅgabhāva*), by implication, with respect to the object to be indicated. An example: "This is that very forest, wherein [lived] he who was devoted to fulfilling the command of Daśaratha."
Dwelling there with only his arm as his companion, Rāma brought about the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
And the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is not present here, because it serves merely as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in this context.
(Verse 178) When there is a single means for accomplishing a certain end, and another [means] also serves to accomplish that same end,
this is conjunction (*samuccaya*).
*Samuccaya* (Accumulation) is that where, while one means for accomplishing the matter at hand is already present, other means are also possible.

An example: "The arrows of Love are irresistible; the beloved is far away; the mind is exceedingly restless; love is intense; youth is fresh; the vital breaths are very firm; and the family is stainless."
Femininity is opposed to fortitude, time is a friend to the god of love, Death is inexorable, and my friends are clever; how indeed shall this cruel separation be endured? 507.
In this case, it is the arrows of Love alone that cause the inability to endure separation; upon that, factors such as the beloved being situated at a distance are added.
This very *samuccaya* (cumulative conjunction) results in the combination of good things, bad things, or both good and bad things, and thus is not defined separately.
For example: "A stainless lineage, an auspicious form, an intellect adorned with sacred learning, sufficient strength of arm, abundant prosperity, and unimpeded sovereignty."
For these states of being are naturally charming; O King, it is by means of them that people fall into even greater arrogance, yet they themselves are your goads.
In this case, there is the conjunction of things that exist;
however, in the example just mentioned, there is the conjunction of things that do not exist:
"The moon is grey as day, the loving woman has lost her youth, the lake is devoid of lotuses, and the face of one with a fine form is without letters."
A lord devoted solely to wealth, a virtuous person who is perpetually destitute, and a wicked man who has gained access to the royal court—these seven are thorns in my heart.
In this case, "while the moon is pale, there are other thorns within the thorn," is an instance of the conjunction of the beautiful and the ugly;
however, that which consists of qualities and actions occurring simultaneously is another [type]. (Sūtra 179) //116//
"Qualities" (*guṇa*), "actions" (*kriyā*), and "both qualities and actions" (*guṇakriyā*); these are the [three types].
Here are the examples in order: "O King, this army of yours, having shattered the entire host of enemies, quickly became pure;
and those faces of the wicked, O Lord of Men, have become soiled. (510)
On one hand, this separation from my beloved, suddenly brought upon me, is unbearably difficult for me;
on the other, the days must become delightful, free from the heat of the sun due to the rising of fresh rain-clouds.

O Lord of Kings, your eye, which possesses a splendor like that of a white lotus, has suddenly become turbid toward your enemies; and clearly, by its side-long glances, calamities have fallen upon their bodies.

From the observation of such instances as "He shakes off the sword and spreads his fame," and "You, with sword in hand on the battlefield, and the gods in the abode of the gods with shouts of 'Bravo!'," [the figure] occurs when there is a difference of substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Thus, it should not be said that [it exists] "in one place."
(180) One in succession among many is a "paryāya.
When a single entity comes into being or is produced in succession within many [states], that is a *paryāya*.
Examples in order: "O Kālakūṭa poison, by whom was this successive progression of your residence taught?
First in the heart of the ocean, then in the throat of the bull-bannered Śiva, and now you dwell in the speech of the wicked. (513)
O slender one, this very passion was previously seen only on your bimba-like lips;
now, O fawn-eyed one, it is observed even in your heart. (514)
Although passion is in fact diverse, its oneness is not contradictory because it is determined as a single unity.
"The flower-arrowed god [Kāma], having placed their hearts—whose sole essence was the joy shared with their own splendor—upon the bimba-like lips of their beloveds. (515)
(Verse 181) The other is otherwise than that:
when many [things] occur or are produced in a single [locus] sequentially, that is the other.

Examples in order: "Ah, the speech of the wicked, charming with sweetness, first spreads forth as nectar; then, alas, that very same speech reveals itself as the internal *hālāhala* poison, the cause of delusion. (516)
That house with its curved walls has become this palace; that cow has gained space in the heavens; those lowing, aged elephants have become these masses of clouds dark as rain-clouds;
that wretched, broken sound has become this sweet singing of women—what a wonder that in a few days this twice-born man has been raised to such a state!
In this case, because the abandonment and the acquisition of one and the same thing are not intended to be expressed, there is no *parivṛtti* (exchange).
(Verse 182) That which is stated as the statement of the probandum and the probans is called inference. //117//

The means of proof (*sādhana*) is a reason (*hetu*) possessing three characteristics by virtue of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

The state of being the probandum (*sādhyatva*) consists in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*). For example: "Wherever these women with eyes as tremulous as waves direct their eyebrows, there these arrows that pierce the vitals fall incessantly."
With his bow drawn into a circle and his hand brandishing uplifted arrows, the wrathful Smara, the bearer of their command, truly always runs right at the front of them.
Since there is no distinction whatsoever in the conceptual alternatives regarding the priority or posteriority of the probandum and the probans, it has not been shown in that manner.

(Verse 183) When there is a statement of the subject (*viśeṣya*) through significant epithets (*viśeṣaṇa*), that is *parikara* (the "pregnant" ornament). [The subject is understood] by implication (*arthāt*).

Example: "The great-spirited, those whose wealth is honor, honored for their riches, wielders of the bow who have won fame in battle—neither united nor acting with dissension, they desire to accomplish what is pleasing to him even at the cost of their lives. (519)
Although the acceptance of "fullness of meaning" (*puṣṭārthatva*) was achieved by refuting its opposite through the statement that "deficiency of meaning" (*apuṣṭārthatva*) is a fault,
nevertheless, because such a presentation of many qualifiers as residing in a single locus possesses aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*), it is classified among the figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*).
(Verse 184) *Vyājokti* (Artful Concealment) is the hiding of the true nature of a thing by means of a pretext. //118//
*Vyājokti* (Artful Concealment) is that wherein the nature of an object, though hidden, is somehow revealed and then denied under some pretext.
Nor is this *Apahnuti* (Denial), because here there is no possibility of a similarity residing in both the subject at hand and something else not at hand.

An example: "Agitated by the disruption of his entire ritual engagement—distraught due to the breaking of the sequence caused by the bristling of his hair and other symptoms as he was embraced by the hand of the Mountain-Daughter (Pārvatī) while being presented to the Lord of Mountains..."

"Alas! How cool are the hands of the Snowy Mountain!"—may that Śiva, who spoke thus with a smile while being gazed upon by the circles of mothers in the mountain's inner apartments, protect you all. (520)

In this case, horripilation and trembling, having manifested as the nature of a symptom (sāttvikabhāva), cause a *vyājokti* (artful concealment) because their true nature is denied by being presented as having coldness as their cause.
Whether something is asked or unasked, when that which is stated serves to exclude other such possibilities, it is traditionally known as *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). //119//

When an object already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is expressed by a word and—due to the absence of any other purpose—results in the exclusion of other similar objects, that is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). In this case, the statement is observed to be either preceded by a question or otherwise; likewise, in both instances, there is the manifestation of the excluded object and its status as being directly denoted (*vācyatva*). Thus, there are four varieties.

The examples in sequence are as follows: "What is to be resorted to by men? The faultless vicinity of the celestial river (Gaṅgā). What is to be meditated upon in solitude? The pair of feet of the wearer of the Kaustubha gem (Viṣṇu).
What is to be worshipped? Merit. And what is to be desired? Compassion; for through attachment to which the mind becomes capable of attaining boundless liberation. (521)

What is the most enduring ornament here? Fame, not jewels. What is the task to be performed? Noble conduct and virtuous deeds, not vice. What is the unimpeded eye? Intellect, not the physical organ. Who other than you knows how to distinguish between the real and the unreal?
Curls reside in her mass of hair; redness dwells in her hands, feet, and lips;
hardness abides in her pair of breasts; and tremulousness lives in her two eyes. (523)

The great-souled generally display devotion toward existence, not toward worldly prosperity; attachment to scripture, not to the weapon of youthful passion; and concern for their reputation, not for their physical bodies. (524)
(Verse 186) If each subsequent [member] serves as the cause for each preceding meaning,
then it would be a "garland of causes" (kāraṇamālā).
*Yathottaram* (progressive) refers to each subsequent [statement] being superior to the preceding one.
An example: "Control of the senses is the cause of modesty; excellence of virtue is attained through modesty.
By excellence of virtue, people are won over; for prosperity indeed originates from the affection of the people. (525)
“The statement of a cause together with that which possesses the cause, by way of non-difference, is the ‘cause’ [figure of speech].
Thus, the figure of speech called *hetu* has not been defined [here],
for a form such as “clarified butter is life” can never deserve the status of an ornament due to the absence of any striking variety (*vaicitrya*).
This delightful season has now arrived, causing longing in the hearts of people—a time of the continuous blooming of lotuses, the intoxication of all the bees, and the joy of the cuckoos. (526)

In this instance, the status of being poetry was established solely through the power of soft alliteration (komalānuprāsa), and not by the postulation of the figure of speech "causation" (hetu); thus, the very "poetic cause" (kāvyaliṅga) mentioned previously is the actual reason [for its poetic quality].
But [the relationship] between [words] is mutual through action. //120//
When two things arise through mutual causality by means of a single action,
there exists the ornament named *anyonya* (mutuality).
Example: "The beauty of swans is enhanced by lotuses, and that of lotuses by swans;
these two seem to weigh themselves against one another. (527)
In this case, both [factors] are mutually productive by way of accomplishing their mutual essence of glory.
(Verse 188) Where the inference of a question is made from the mere hearing of a subsequent statement, or where such a question actually exists; //121//
That which serves as a reply when an impossible response has been repeated is a *uttara*.
First, there is one type of *uttara* where a prior statement is inferred solely from the perception of a rejoinder.
An example: "O merchant, whence could we have ivory, or tiger-skins?"
Meanwhile, the daughter-in-law, her face disheveled with bees, wanders about the house. // 528 //
The statement of the buyer, "I desire those elephant tusks and tiger skins; give them to me for a price," is inferred from this sentence.
Nor is this a *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication), because the subsequent [response] cannot logically possess that same nature.

A reply is not the cause of a question, nor is this an inference, because the probandum and the probans are not indicated as residing in a single locus; therefore, a more excellent answer is indeed another type of ornament (*alaṅkāra*). An answer that follows a question and takes a form so inconceivable due to its transcending the sphere of worldly experience is what constitutes another kind of reply.

Furthermore, since the perception of beauty does not arise when these two are employed only once, it is stated that they must be used "repeatedly. An example follows: "What is an uneven course? The way of the gods. What is gained? That people appreciate virtue. What is happiness? A good wife. What is suffering? That the world is wicked. (529)

In the case of an exhaustive enumeration of questions (*praśnaparisaṃkhyā*), the intention (*tātparya*) lies solely in the exclusion of other [possibilities]; but here, it lies in that which is directly expressed (*vācya*).
Thus is the distinction between these two: [the former is] repose, while [the latter is] such-and-such.
Even a subtle object, once perceived from some source, can be made manifest to another. (Sūtra 189, Verse 122)
Whereby it is indicated as subtle through some characteristic (*dharma*),
whether from some gesture, facial expression, or sign— subtle, to be perceived by one of sharp intellect—
for example: "A certain woman, seeing the saffron [on her body] broken by a continuous stream of sweat-drops trickling from her face upon the floor..."
Manifesting masculinity, her female friend smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon the slender girl's hand.

In this instance, having observed his physical form, a certain woman imagined he was acting like a man; through her ingenuity, she made this manifest by drawing a sword-blade [upon him], for it is appropriate that men alone should hold swords in their hands.
Or, as in the case of a clever woman who, knowing the paramour to be thinking of the time of their tryst, [acted accordingly].
