The playful lotus, its intention slightly directed toward her eyes, was closed.

Here, the time for the rendezvous, which was desired by a certain woman, was understood through a mere gesture and gracefully indicated by the closing of the lotus, which betokens the arrival of night.
(Verse 190) There should be a progressive excellence, reaching its ultimate limit in the *sāra*. //123//
The "limit" (paraḥ) is the ultimate boundary, which serves as the horizon for excellence because its culmination comes to rest right there through a process of progressive ascent.
An example: "In a kingdom, the essence is the earth; in the earth, a city; in a city, a palace."
In the palace was a couch, and upon the couch was a beautiful woman, the very essence of the god of love.
When two properties that stand in the relation of cause and effect appear simultaneously at entirely different locations, that is the figure of speech known as *asaṃgati* (incongruity). //124//
In this world, it is observed that an effect arises in the very same location as its cause, as in the case of smoke and so forth.

However, when two phenomena, though existing as cause and effect, appear simultaneously in different locations due to some particular excellence, that constitutes "inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*), because of their abandonment of the mutual connection naturally arising from their essential nature.
An example is: "The person who says, 'The wound is where the arrow is,' speaks falsely."
One should not speak of the injury to the teeth, for it causes great pain to one's co-wives. // 533 //
And this [reason] is a sublater of contradiction, not a contradiction itself; for here, the contradictoriness of the two [properties] appears precisely as residing in different loci.

In the case of actual contradiction, however, the state of being a contradictor is established as residing in a single locus even if it is not explicitly stated, because a general rule (utsarga) is determined by excluding its exceptions (apavāda).
And thus it has been illustrated as follows:
(192) Concentration (*samādhi*) is a task easily accomplished through the application of other auxiliary causes.
When an agent, assisted by other means of accomplishment, undertakes a task and completes it without difficulty, that is what is called concentration.
Example: "To dispel her pride, as I was about to fall at her feet, by good fortune this thundering of clouds has arisen for my benefit. (534)
(193) If a union based on mutual compatibility is possible in some instance, //125//

If there is a determination that this particular relationship is appropriate because it is praiseworthy for these two, then that is *sama* (the Equal), whether the union is between the good and the good (*sadyoga*) or the bad and the bad (*asadyoga*). An example: "This deer-eyed woman is the touchstone for the excellence of the Creator’s craftsmanship; and this god-like man is the peerless recipient of the Goddess of Beauty’s favor. By fate, a union worthy of both has come to pass; thus, the kingdom of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) has now been established under a single umbrella. (535)
How wonderful, how truly wonderful, oh, how very wonderful is this marvel! By fate, the Creator has been born as a designer of a most fitting arrangement:
that the abundance of the ripened fruits of the *nimba* trees is fit for tasting, and that the world of crows is skilled in the art of devouring them. (536)

(Verse 194) In some cases, because of extreme disparity, no connection can be established; furthermore, there may be the attainment of the fruit of action by the agent, or even the occurrence of misfortune. //126//
When the quality and action of the effect are respectively opposed to the quality and action of the cause, this is considered the "uneven" (viṣama) figure of speech. //127//

Because the two are absolutely dissimilar, their connection is perceived as being logically untenable; furthermore, when an agent undertakes some action, due to the failure of that action, he not only fails to obtain the desired result, but may even encounter an undesired calamity. This remains true even though the effect conforms to the nature of its cause.
In that [type of *viṣama*], the qualities and actions of those two proceed to mutual contradiction. That *viṣama* consists of four forms, including the "equal-opposite" (*samaviṣayaviparyaya*).
The examples in order: "Where is this long-eyed woman, whose limbs are softer even than the *śirīṣa* flower?
And where is this fire of love, harsh as the fire of chaff? (537)
Terrified by the son of Siṃhikā, the hare took refuge with the cool-rayed moon;
there, another son of Siṃhikā swallowed him along with his refuge.
Immediately upon receiving the touch of his hand, the blade of his sword— dark as a tamāla tree in every battle—
has brought forth a fame white as the autumn moon, which serves as an ornament for the three worlds.
O lady with eyes like blue lotus petals, you bestow this intense bliss upon me;
yet it is by you alone that this separation has been produced, which now torments my body most severely.
In this case, the granting of bliss is contradicted by the heat of her body.

Thus, he whose belly, vast as the ocean, swallowed the worlds at the end of an eon, was in turn drunk up by the gaze of a certain city woman, which was entirely intent on the intoxication of amorous play. (541)
In such cases as well, the state of inequality should be understood according to the specific circumstances.

(Verse 195) When there is a greater magnitude between the two, namely the supported and the support, respectively, the support and the supported may exist even when [the former] is minute; however, that [magnitude] is indeed superior. //128//
The dependent is that which is supported, and the support is its substratum;
even when both of these are large in scale, they become relatively minute in comparison to it.
Yet, when there is a desire to express the excellence of the subject at hand, the support and the supported respectively attain a state of greater magnitude.
This aforementioned [figure] is of two kinds, called *adhika* (excess).
The examples in order are as follows: "O King, how vast is the interior of the three worlds!
For even the mass of your fame, which cannot be contained, finds room within it. (542)

The joys arising from the arrival of the ascetic could not find room within the body of the Enemy of Kaiṭabha, even though the worlds themselves— whose selves were withdrawn at the time of the end of the eon— dwelt within it with full expansion.

(Verse 196) When one is unable to retaliate against an adversary, the disparagement of something belonging to that person for the sake of praising him is called *pratyanīka* (the counter-attack). //129//

When someone, being unable to directly refute an adversary who is intent on humiliation, instead disparages that very person upon whom the adversary relies in order to exalt the adversary himself— that is called *pratyanīka* (counter-attack), because it is equivalent to attacking the enemy's army (*anīka*).
For example, as in the case of an army (*anīke*):

The meaning is as follows: when someone, out of delusion, brings a lawsuit against another who has become a representative of the actual defendant, so too here, when the counter-positive (the object to be conquered) is to be defeated, another person belonging to him is defeated instead.
An example: "O handsome one, you have completely conquered the form of the Mind-born (Kāma), and she is in love with you;
yet Kāma torments her all at once with his five arrows, as if out of resentment. (544)
Or as Rāhu, unable to do anything else to harm him, having undertaken a conflict by seizing his body, even now afflicts the moon with a form resembling his beloved’s face. (545)
Indra's ownership here [is established] through a connection with that which is connected to him.
(Verse 197) When an object is concealed by another object through similarity— whether that [concealing] object is inherent or adventitious— that is known as *mīlita* (the hidden). //130//

Whatever common characteristic—whether innate or adventitious—exists, by means of which some object is concealed by another object through its very nature of being more powerful, that is remembered as *mīlita* (the concealed), and it is considered to be of two kinds.
The examples follow in order: "The eyes are tremulous at the corners; the words are sweet with curved syllables; the gait is slow with an abundance of grace; and the face is exceedingly lovely."
Thus, these tremors in the limbs of the deer-eyed one arise spontaneously through her own playful charm; herein, the onset of passion, even though it has taken root, is not perceived.
In this case, the trembling of the eyes and other such symptoms of the body are both natural and common; for they are observed even in Mahodaya.

As for those enemies who dwell constantly in the caves of the Himalayas, their minds rendered helpless by the fear of your descent—their bodies bearing horripilation and trembling—alas, even a wise man would not recognize these as signs of fear! (547)

But here, since coolness is understood through implication, the trembling and horripilation produced by it also possess that same nature and share its quality, because both are observed even in states of fear.

Where an object is either established or excluded, each subsequent one following the preceding in its capacity as a qualifier, that is the two-fold *ekāvalī* (string of ornaments). (Sūtra 198) //131//

When, by means of repetition (*vīpsā*), there occurs either an establishment or a negation of each subsequent object in relation to each preceding one as its qualifier, that is called *ekāvalī* (the single-string necklace) by the wise; it is of two kinds.
The examples in order are: "In that city, the towns were filled with excellent women; the excellent women had limbs graced by beauty;
the beauty possessed manifest, true charm; and that charm was the very weapon of the flower-armed god [Kāma]. (548)

That was no water which did not contain beautiful lotuses; that was no lotus which did not have bees alighting upon it; those were no bees which did not hum sweetly; and that was no humming which did not captivate the mind. (549)

In the preceding [verse], excellent women are mentioned first; by way of qualifying their limbs, their beauty is described; then their graceful charms; and finally, their weapons—thus, in this sequence, the qualification is established. In the subsequent [verse], the same logic should be applied even regarding the negation.
Just as there is a recollection of an object upon seeing something similar to it, according to how it was previously experienced—
that is memory (*smṛti*).

When an object that has been determined by some specific form and experienced at some time or other is later remembered exactly as it was upon seeing a similar thing that awakens the memory, that is *smaraṇa* (recollection).
An example: "The water that was splashed by the waves into the deep hollows of the navels of those with tremulous eyes..."
By those cooing sounds produced therein, the celestial women were reminded of the throat-murmurs of amorous play.
Or, salutations to the horripilation of Kṛṣṇa, who has remembered Pañcajana and whose hand is grasped by the hand [of Rukmiṇī], while his lower lip is pressed against the mouth of her breast. 551.
(Verse 200) One who possesses error [perceives] another's consciousness when seeing what is similar to it. // 132 //
The word "that" (tad) refers to something else that is non-contextual;
by means of it, what is similar to it—namely, the contextual [object] such as meaning—is here taken as the basis.
When there is a perception of such a thing, that cognition which occurs by way of its being non-contextual is "the mistaken" (bhrāntimān).

This is neither a *rūpaka* (metaphor) nor a *prathamātiśayokti* (hyperbole of the first kind), because in those cases there is no actual delusion, whereas here, since the designation functions by following the literal meaning of the object, that delusion is clearly perceived. An example: "A cat licks at the rays of the moon from a skull-cup, thinking them to be milk; an elephant gathers the rays as they pass through the gaps in a tree, imagining them to be lotus stalks."
Even a woman steals the garment from those lying on the bed at the end of lovemaking; alas, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, throws this entire world into confusion! 552.

(Verse 201) *Pratīpa* consists in the subordination of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or rather, if that very [standard] is conceived as the object of comparison (*upameya*), based on the grounds of its disparagement. //133//

When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is discarded through the rhetorical device of *kaimarthya* (uselessness), on the grounds that the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone is sufficiently capable of bearing the burden;

or when, for the sake of expressing a desire for another standard of comparison, the status of being the object of comparison is attributed even to that which is already well-known as a standard of comparison for the purpose of showing disregard—these two forms constitute *pratīpa* (the inverse), because the object of comparison acts in opposition to the standard of comparison.

Examples in order: "O King, since the Creator has fashioned you—the abode of beauty, possessed of the majesty of valor, the foremost among the generous, and with arms capable of bearing the weight of the earth—"
Was the moon fashioned? Was this sun created? Was the wish-fulfilling gem produced? And were these mountain ranges created in vain? // 553 //
Come here, O beautiful one; lend me your ear and listen to this reproach:
"O slender-waisted one, people are comparing the moon to your face. (554)

In this case, because the moon—which is being compared by means of the face—possesses inferior qualities, the simile is not fully realized; thus, there is a sense of disparagement conveyed by the word *vacanīyam* ("blameworthy").
However, in some instances, the act of comparison is indeed fully accomplished.
An example of the basis for disregard:
"O charming girl, why do you carry this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes?
Surely there are such blue lotuses in the lakes in every direction. (555)
In this case, the very act of making the lotuses the object of comparison (*upameya*) constitutes their disregard.

Following this same principle, it should be understood that when— due to the possession of extraordinary qualities— the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) has never been experienced before, even the mere conceptualization of such a state constitutes *pratīpa* (the inverse).
"O Hālāhala, my dear, do not be arrogant, thinking, 'I alone am the teacher of the most terrible things.
For are there not many more words like yours among the wicked in this world? (556)
In this case, the state of being a point of comparison for the *hālāhata* (the white water-lily) has been presented as something entirely impossible.

(Verse 202) When the subject at hand is joined with something else through a desire to express equality of qualities, such that their identity is established, that is known as *sāmānya* (commonality). //134//

When something that is not of such a nature is intended to be expressed as being so, and it is described as being of one essence with an unrelated subject while still retaining its own qualities— this, because it is based on common attributes, is the *sāmānya* (commonality) type of illustration (*udāharaṇa*): "Those whose bodies were anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with fresh strings of pearls, whose faces shone with exceptionally white ivory ear-ornaments, and who wore beautiful, spotless garments,
became indistinguishable when the moon, spreading its light, whitened the earth."
The women going to meet their lovers, their fears dispelled, proceed happily indeed to their beloved's dwelling.
In this case, the whiteness, described as being neither less nor more in the subject at hand and its counterpart, is the cause of their identity;
for this very reason, they are not perceived as distinct entities.
Or, for example: "The lotus stalks, possessing a luster equal to that of the young women, have come to rest upon the surface of their cheeks from the tips of their ears."
If the bees had not alighted sportively, who would have known of the fresh campaka flowers?

In this case, even a cognition of diversity produced by another cause is not able to subvert the non-difference first apprehended, because that [non-difference] has been cognized, and it is impossible for a cognition to be sublated once it has been cognized.

(Verse 203) Without a well-established substratum, there can be no persistence of that which is supported; [otherwise] a single entity would exist simultaneously in multiple locations, which is a contradiction. //135//

The threefold distinction is traditionally taught as follows: performing a different task while one is unable to perform the intended one, and likewise, performing that very same task [in an impossible manner]. //136//
The first variety of excellence (*viśeṣa*) is that which expresses the distinguished state of the substratum (*ādheya*) by means of the exclusion of its well-known substratum (*prasiddhādhāra*).

An example: "How could those poets not be worthy of homage here, whose words—possessing a multitude of no small virtues—delight the worlds even for as long as the aeon (*ākalpa*), even after they have ascended to heaven? (559)
The second [type of contradiction] is when a single object exists simultaneously in multiple locations by means of a single nature.
An example: "She dwells in your heart, she alone is in your eyes, and she is in your words;
O handsome one, where else can there be room for sinners such as these? (560)
Furthermore, whatever one might hastily undertake, if while beginning it one starts another task that cannot be accomplished with that same effort, that is another variety [of the fault].
An example: "By him who created you—whose form is throbbing with wonder, whose fire of majesty blazes upward, and whose knowledge is flawless..."
By the prescribed rite, the Mind-born [God of Love] was truly created anew upon the earth, as were Savitṛ and Bṛhaspati. // 561 //

Or rather, since you—my wife, my counselor, my intimate friend, and my dear pupil in the practice of graceful arts—have been snatched away by death, which is indifferent to compassion, alas, what of mine has not been destroyed? (562)
In all such cases, it is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) alone that stands as the vital essence, for without it, there is generally no possibility of being a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
Therefore it has been said: "This very *vakrokti* (curved speech) prevails everywhere; by means of this, the meaning is brought to light.
The poet must exert effort toward this; what poetic figure could exist without it?"
Thus [it is said].

(Verse 204) When an object, by virtue of its conjunction with something possessing exceedingly brilliant qualities, abandons its own quality and assumes the quality of that other thing, it is called *tadguṇa* (the "quality of that"). //137//
When an object whose own form is obscured by something else nearby attains the very appearance of that other thing due to being colored by its excellence of qualities, that is "Guṇa" (the Quality);
for here there exists the quality (*guṇa*) of that extraneous thing (*aprakṛta*).
An example: The horses of the Sun, of diverse colors, are surrounded on all sides by the radiance of the elder brother of Garuḍa.
Moreover, there, by means of jewels as dark as bamboo shoots, they brought their own luster back to its natural brilliance.
Here, the color of the elder brother of Garuḍa is superior to that of the sun’s horses, and the color of emeralds is superior to his.
(Sūtra 205) If this [object] does not conform to the form of that [original], it would be "non-partaking of its qualities" (*atadguṇa*).
However, if it were to fail to apprehend the color of that [original] even though the capacity [for apprehension] exists, then it would be what is called "non-partaking of its qualities."
Example: "O handsome one, although you are white, my heart has been colored red by you; yet, O happy one, though placed upon a heart saturated with passion, you have not become red. (564)
In this case, even though he is conjoined with a mind that is intensely red, he does not attain the state of being red; thus, it is *atadguṇa* (non-attainment of the quality).
Furthermore, here "that" (*tat*) refers to the non-contextual (the mind), and "this" (*asya*) refers to the contextual (the person).
Therefore, it should also be understood that when the form of the non-contextual does not conform to the contextual due to some cause, that is *atadguṇa*.
Just as when you, O royal swan, bathe in both the water of the Ganges and the soot-colored water of the Yamunā, that same whiteness of yours is neither increased nor diminished. (565)
Whatever has been established by someone in a certain way, another person may establish it otherwise. (Sūtra 206) / 131 //

In the same way, that which is performed as a contradiction is known as *vyāghāta* (contradiction). When a certain means is employed by one person and another person, desiring to conquer him, employs that very same means but in a contrary manner, it is called *vyāghāta* because it is the cause of obstructing the established object.
An example: "Those women who, with their very eyes, revive the God of Love whom they had burnt with their eyes..."
I praise those victorious, beautiful-eyed women of Virūpākṣa.
The commingling of these is considered desirable when they exist here in a state of distinction. //139//

Immediately following these [factors], whose natures have just been described, there occurs— in accordance with the circumstances— either in the verbal component alone, in the objective domain alone, or in both, an [understanding] that is independent of one another.
That state is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling), which has the nature of co-inherence in a single object.

Among these, an example of the commingling of verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) is as follows: "By her whose beauty was enhanced by the agitation of bees wandering about, lured by the fragrance of her face..."
Another woman, her eyes flickering with long curls, produced a sweet jingling from her moving girdle.
The commingling of figures of sense (arthālaṃkāra) is as follows: "Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium;
like service rendered to a wicked man, my sight has become fruitless. (568)
In the former case, alliteration and rhyme, being independent of one another, bring about *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling); in the latter case, however, it is simile and poetic fancy that do so.
As for the coexistence of verbal and semantic ornaments, there is this:
"There is no one in this village who can restrain her as she wanders about, a mass of great and intoxicating beauty, plundering the hearts of young men. (569)
Here, alliteration and metaphor are independent of one another;
yet their conjunction occurs because they are both present together in a single sentence or verse.

(Sūtra 208) But when these very [figures] exist within themselves without resting [independently], there is *saṃkara* (commixture), characterized by the relationship of primary and subordinate members (*aṅga-aṅgitva*).

When entities that have not attained independent existence assume the roles of benefactor and beneficiary toward one another, this is called *saṃkara* (commixture), because their essential natures become intermingled.

An example: "O King, when the crest-jewel has been taken, the emerald ear-leaf stolen, the golden earrings seized, the girdle snatched away, and the pair of jeweled anklets quickly grasped; when the redness of the moving forest-dwelling deer-eyed wives of your enemies is [mistaken] for the luster of their bimba-like lips, the Śabaras do not take their necklaces, thinking them to be strings of *guñjā* berries. (570)

In this case, the quality [of the moon] arises through the presence of the illusion (bhrāntimat), and by depending upon that [illusion], it becomes for sensitive readers the cause of great aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*); thus, there exists a relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between these two. Or, for example: "With the luster of matted locks, holding in his hand the dark spot as a rosary of seeds, appearing pure through a renunciation born as if from the calamity of separation from his beloved, the moon—white as ashes, with its surface marked by the skulls of the shimmering stars—wanders in the sky as if in a cremation ground. (571) [In this verse, the figure of *Rūpaka* (Metaphor) is the subordinate element (*aṅga*), while the *Bhrāntimat* (Illusion) is the predominant element (*aṅgin*).]

In this [verse], four figures—simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), poetic fancy (utprekṣā), and paronomasia (śleṣa)—are perceived as related to one another as primary and subordinate elements, as before. When the metaphor "the spot itself is a rosary" (kalaṅka evākṣavalayam) is accepted, the very fact of its being held in the hand serves as the decisive proof. For if this is a metaphor, it is understood primarily as a rosary whose form as a "spot" is concealed; and it is universally well-known that only such a [rosary] is fit to be grasped by the hand.

However, through the shadow of a pun (*śleṣacchāyayā*), the holding of the moon by the hand—though non-existent—is figuratively attributed due to proximity; for the moon merely carries the spot by its very form.
As for the phrase "the spot is like a rosary,"...
In the case of an illusion, there is a perception of a stain due to its intensity;
yet, since its being held in the hand does not exist in reality, even in the primary sense, one would have to resort solely to metaphorical usage.

Such a commingling (saṃkara) of verbal figures of speech is also observed, as for example: "This bank shines, where the torrents of the best of Dānavas have been struck down, and where the forests have their essence destroyed; and there is a herd of elephants, which incessantly exudes ichor (dāna), is excellent (vara), protects its own (sāti-pāti), and possesses strength (sāra) that destroys the forest. (572)

In this case, there is a variety of *citra* consisting of *yamaka* and *anulomapratiloma* occurring in two feet that are mutually dependent; because there is neither a logical reason (*nyāya*) nor a fault (*doṣa*) for accepting one over the other, there is no certainty [as to which is correct]. (Sūtra 209) //140//

Even when two or more ornaments enter into a single [poetic] unit in succession, there is no contradiction such that they cannot coexist simultaneously; nor is there any proof for the acceptance of one,
or any sublation against the exclusion of the other, by which only one would be accepted.
This second type of *saṃkara* (commixture), consisting in the absence of certainty, arises because the commixture itself is implied by the conjunction [of the figures].
An example: "Just as it is deep, just as it is filled with jewels, and just as it has a stainless luster—why was this ocean not made by Fate to possess a voice full of poetic sentiment? (573)

Since the ocean is the subject under discussion here, there arises a doubt: is this *samāsokti* (condensed expression), because an unstated matter is perceived through the similarity of qualifiers; or is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), wherein some relevant subject is praised by means of the irrelevant ocean due to their shared qualities?
Or rather, just as this orb of the moon, which bestows delight upon the eyes,
now shines clear, so too has this darkness been dispelled, even though its quarters were previously obstructed.

In this case, is it *paryāyokta* (circumlocution), because it is expressed by means of another figure that "the time which kindles desire is present"? Or is it *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because they speak [of the moon] as being the lunar disc through the process of identification (*adhyavasāna*)? Or what else?

Pointing to the face with the word "this" (*etad*), there is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) by virtue of superimposing its form upon it; or, if there is an intention to express their conjunction, a *dīpaka* (illustrative lamp); or, if there is a perception of the face through the similarity of qualifiers at the time of expressing censure, a *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing);
or, if it is due to the context of the face’s purity, an *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
Since there is doubt among these many possibilities, this is indeed a *saṃkara* (blending of figures).
But where either a valid reason (*nyāya*) or a fallacy (*doṣa*) applies,
there is no doubt, because one of the two is ascertained.
Logic consists of proof, which is favorability; likewise, a defect consists of sublation, which is unfavorability.
In this regard, the radiance of her smile spreads auspiciousness like moonlight from the moon of her face. (575)
In this context, the radiance of laughter, being perceived primarily in the face,
conforms to that very location.

Thus, while that [simile] establishes the comparison, it is not contrary to the metaphor; therefore, it does not subvert it: "While this moon of your face exists, what other cool-rayed moon has risen? (576)

In this case, the fact that the "inferiority" (aparatva) of the moon is consistent with [the face] and not contradictory to the mouth serves as a means of establishing the metaphor (rūpaka), rather than being a sublater of the simile (upamā).
"O King-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī embraces you intensely. (577)
In this context, the embrace once again sets aside the simile, because an embrace directed toward someone merely similar [to one's beloved] by a woman who loves another is impossible.
"May the lotus-foot of Ambikā, charming with the tinkling of beautiful anklets, lead us to victory! (578)

In this context, it is stated that "the tinkling of anklets is incompatible with a lotus because of its impossibility"—this is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), but not a prover (*sādhaka*) of the simile (*upamā*) on the grounds that "it is compatible with a foot. This is because a sublater, which obstructs a [potential] injunction, is perceived as more forceful than that [simile].
The same should be examined by the wise in other cases as well.
(Verse 210) It is clearly established that two [types of] word-ornament and meaning-ornament reside together in a single subject matter.

When both a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṃkāra*) and a semantic ornament (*arthālaṃkāra*) clearly attain their established positions within a single, indivisible word, that too is another type of *saṃkara* (commixture).

An example: "Then the day-lotus—its broad pericarp being the sun’s orb with its filaments of clearly shimmering rays, its mass of petals being the cluster of the eight joined directions, and the swarm of bees being the darkness descending upon its surface—contracted. (579)
In this case, simile and alliteration enter into a single word.
Therefore, it is proclaimed as being threefold in form. (141)

Thus, this *saṃkara* (commixture) has been explained as being of only three types, because it is established through the relationship of the favored and the favorer, through doubt, and through being expressed by a single word.

However, it cannot be explained by any other method due to the infinity of its subdivisions. Thus have been presented the figures of speech (*alaṃkāras*) which possess a threefold nature by virtue of residing in the word, the meaning, or both.

But why this restriction—that although these are equal in being causes for the excellence of poetic beauty (*kāvyasobhātiśaya*), some figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) belongs to the word, some to the meaning, and some to both? To this it has been said: in poetry, with respect to the distinction between defects, merits, and figures of speech as belonging to the word, the meaning, or both, only positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are effective, because there is no other cause [for such a distinction]. Therefore, whichever figure of speech follows the positive and negative concomitance of a particular element, that figure is established as belonging to that element.

And thus, just as the *punaruktavad-ābhāsa* (appearance of tautology) and the *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor of succession) are both figures of speech because they follow the presence or absence of both [word and meaning], so too should the *śabda-hetuka-artha-antara-nyāsa* (verbal-based corroborative instance) and others be regarded.
However, in those cases, it is the variety (*vaicitrya*) of the meaning that appears with greater prominence.
Thus, among the ornaments of speech (*vācyālaṃkāra*), these have been defined regardless of the actual state of things.

Even if one were to maintain the conceptualization that "an ornament is that which depends upon something else, and therefore belongs to that [thing]," one must nevertheless rely solely upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

This is because, without relying on those two, there can be no specific relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). Therefore, the cause of the ornaments is as previously stated.
Thus, mutual exclusion is superior.

(Verse 212) Although some of these faults may occur according to their respective applications, they are included within those already mentioned; therefore, they have not been explained separately. //142//

To explain: the three defects of alliteration—lack of convention, futility, and conflict with the poetic style (vṛtti)—do not transcend, respectively, contradiction of convention, lack of nourishment for the meaning, and discordance of phonemes, because they are of that very nature. The examples in order are as follows: "The Discus-bearer [Viṣṇu] holds the row of spokes of his discus; Hari [Indra] also seizes the tips of the banners of Dhūrjaṭi [Śiva];"
May that chariot of the sun, which the moon praises as its constellation, Varuṇa as its pole, Kubera as the tip of its shaft,
and the host of gods as its speed— for the sake of benefiting the world— protect you, it being ever-yoked and pleased with affection day after day.

In this case, the praise is based on a specific restriction of agent and object; it was composed merely for the sake of alliteration, as it is not perceived as such in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other traditional texts, and thus there is a contradiction with established tradition.
Speak, O young woman with a beautiful moon-like face that distills bliss, you who utter playful and charming words: if you are going to the lover’s abode, then what of yours belongs to me? (581)
With its jeweled girdle vibrating incessantly and its lovely anklets chiming without ceasing,
her movement at the time of death produces an uncaused longing for life.

In this case, no beauty whatsoever is perceived upon reflection regarding the expressed meaning; thus, the deficiency of the alliteration consists precisely in its lack of significant meaning (apuṣṭārthatā).
Regarding the phrase "akuṇṭhotkaṇṭhayā" (582a):

here, in the context of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment, the ostentation of harsh phonemes contradicts [the sentiment] according to the method previously stated; thus, the alliteration (*anuprāsa*) of harsh sounds constitutes "contrariety of phonemes," which is a contradiction of the poetic style (*vṛtti*).
The fault of "lack of application" (*aprayuktatva*) consists in the lack of symmetry when a *yamaka* occurs across three quarters of a verse.
Like a jewel on a serpent, like a river infested with crocodiles, those who are full of deceit forcibly drag away the mind of a person, even one who has determined their ultimate wickedness. (583)

In a simile (*upamā*), when there is a deficiency or excess regarding the genus (*jāti*) or the measure (*pramāṇa*) of the object of comparison (*upamāna*), such a state constitutes the defect of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatva*). However,

in the case of the substratum of the quality (*dharma*), deficiency or excess respectively does not deviate from [the defects of] "omission of a word" (*hīnapadatva*) and "redundancy of a word" (*adhikapadatva*).
Examples in order: "A most reckless deed has been committed by you, as if you were outcasts. (584)
This sun shines like a spark of fire. // 585 //
Seated upon this lotus throne, this cakravāka bird shines resplendent,
like the Lord Creator at the beginning of the aeon, desiring to bring forth all living beings.
Your navel is like the netherworld (pātāla), your breasts are like mountains,
and this braid of yours is like the descent of the Yamunā river.
And here, because the subject at hand is excessively degraded by comparisons such as "outcastes" (caṇḍāla) and so forth, there is the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (anucitārthatā).
Marked by his girdle of muñja grass and wearing a garment of black antelope skin, that sage shone like the sun embraced by a portion of dark clouds.

In this case, the attribute corresponding to the girdle of Muñja grass—namely, the characteristic of lightning—is not expressed by any word; thus, there is the defect of "deficiency of words" (hīnapadatva).
Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa assumed a charming form,
like a cloud at night possessed of lightning and Indra’s bow when it is joined with the moon.

In this case, since the object of comparison (upameya), such as the conch and so forth, is not mentioned, the mention of the moon is superfluous; thus, there is the fault of "superfluous words" (adhikapadatva).
Even regarding differences in gender and number,

if the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) were to take a different form, then, because the possession of that attribute would be understood for only one of the two, its status as either the standard or the object of comparison would be perceived— along with its respective qualifier— by means of the attribute as it is implied.
Thus, because the matter introduced is not clearly carried through to its conclusion, this constitutes the fault of "Broken Uniformity" (*bhagnaprakrama*).
For example: "Alas! You have fallen from my hand like a wish-fulfilling gem; fie upon my wretched fortune! (590)
"O King, the roasted barley flour has been eaten by me, pure as a virtuous wife. (591)
However, where a word denoting a universal does not undergo a change in its own form despite a difference in gender and number, this objection does not apply in either case.
Because its nature is capable of following [the truth], it is renowned for its priceless qualities, just as the great ocean is for its jewels. // 592 //
Clad in that attire, which was unlike that of other women and possessed a sweetness of its own,
they displayed a supreme beauty, like her own graceful charms personified.

Even when there is a difference in tense, person, mood, and so forth, the cognition does not attain a state of rest because it lacks an unimpeded form; thus, this too is pervaded by the fault of broken uniformity (*bhagnaprakrama*).
For example: "Kumudvatī obtained from the descendant of Kakutstha a son named Atithi, just as consciousness obtains clarity from the last watch of the night. (594)
In this matter, consciousness attains clarity and does not lose it again; such is the distinction of time.

With a form purified by the excellence of a fresh bath, with the lovely ends of your garments shimmering with the beautiful safflower dye, you shine resplendent while worshipping the god whose banner is the sea-monster, like a creeper born from a branch of young coral leaves. (595)

In this case, there is a difference of person (*puruṣabheda*) due to the transposition of the predicate (*parabhāga*), which resides in the person being addressed— namely, "the creeper shines here, but you do not shine"— by making it the object of one who is not being addressed.
May your fame flow forever like the Ganges.
And in such cases as "the Gaṅgā flows" (gaṅgā pravahati), rather than "let the Gaṅgā flow" (pravahatu), there is an injunction whose nature is to impel that which has not yet begun to act;
and of other meanings of this same kind.
The distinction between injunctions and so forth arises from the impossibility [of those things] existing within the scope of an analogy.

Now, it may be argued that when a comparison is completed by resorting to some other attribute—whether explicitly uttered or merely implied—the object of comparison (upameya) is connected with its own contextual attribute; thus, there is no discrepancy regarding time and so forth.
This is true even in cases where the comparison is established solely through a common attribute that has been explicitly mentioned.
It is understood, for example, in the case of the statement: "This person speaks the truth like Yudhiṣṭhira.
In that context, we shall understand it to mean: "Like Yudhiṣṭhira, this speaker of truth speaks the truth.

Nor should one suspect tautology in the expression "a speaker of truth speaks the truth," just as in the case of "he nourishes his prosperity"; for the meaning understood there is: "By speaking the truth, like Yudhiṣṭhira, he is a speaker of truth."

This is true; however, while this justification holds for established usages, it is not entirely faultless because it obstructs the comprehension of the subject matter at hand—of this, only those possessed of discernment are the authority.
Even the lack of similarity and the impossibility [of comparison] in a simile result ultimately in the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatā*).
For example: "I string together the moon of poetry, with its rays of extensive meanings. (597)
In this case, there is the fault of "inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārthatva*), because no similarity whatsoever is perceived between the king and the moon, nor between his arrows and the rays.
[For example: "From his mouth, as it were, there fell blazing arrows situated within the circle of his bow."
Like streams of water blazing as they fall from the sun that reaches midday and is surrounded by a halo. // 598 //
In this case as well, the meaning being depicted—that blazing streams of water issuing from the solar disc do not exist—merely nourishes impropriety.

Even in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), only words such as *dhruvam*, *iva*, and so forth are capable of expressing the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), whereas the word *yathā* is not; for this [word *yathā*] alone is sufficient only to convey similarity (*sādharmya*), and since that [similarity] is not intended to be expressed here,
its inability [to express the required sense] constitutes the fault of non-expressiveness (*avācakatva*).
Just as a dark blue lotus bud emerged from the heart of a pond,
appearing as if it had shrunk out of fear of the cleverness of a woman's eyes.

Since even that which is imagined is devoid of any real form, it resembles something non-existent (*nirupākhya*); therefore, the employment of a corroborative *arthāntaranyāsa* to justify it is as utterly improper as searching for light in the sky—this is precisely the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatā*).
For example: "He who protects from the sun the darkness hidden in caves, as if it were afraid of the day..."
Surely, even when a lowly being has sought refuge, those of lofty mind feel an exceedingly great sense of "mine" toward them.

In this case, since it is impossible for insentient darkness to experience fear of the sun, how could there be any protection from the mountain prompted by that fear? However, since this [protection] appears through the power of a suggested meaning (*vyañjanā*), no inconsistency arises; thus, any effort to justify it is entirely futile.
Indeed, by the force of common epithets alone, the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* (condensed expression) occurs even when not explicitly stated.

Since it reveals a specific quality of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), there is no purpose in its further inclusion here; thus, its non-inclusion constitutes the fault of "lack of nourishment" (*apuṣṭārthatva*) or "redundancy" (*punarukta*). For example: "When the sun touches the quarters with its rays, as if with a beloved woman whose heat has increased, the splendor of the day remains for a long time, beautiful yet possessing a state of intense indignation. (601)

Just as here the sun and the directions are manifested as the hero and the heroine respectively through the force of their shared adjectives and the selection of specific individuals, so too will the beauty of the summer day be understood as the heroine; therefore, what is the purpose of employing its own word, "dayitā" (beloved)?

But that is the domain of the simile based on double entendre (*śleṣopamā*), where, even when common attributes are employed, there is no such perception [of similarity] without the explicit mention of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
For example: "And she herself was resplendent with hands shining like copper-colored sprouts..."
Like the morning twilight, she bestows the desired fruits upon those who long for them.
Thus it is said.

In the figure of Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) as well, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood through this very same method; it should not be subjected to the indignity of being explicitly stated again. For example: "When birds are summoned, the gnat is not warded off even when it comes before them; a piece of glass, though resting in the midst of the ocean, possesses the luster of gems; even a firefly does not tremble to move among the luminous bodies. Fie upon that common, insentient thing which, like a master who has not grasped the inner essence, [remains indifferent to its own kind]! (603)
Since the insentient Lord is manifested through the medium of a relevantly unconnected specific universal, it is certainly not appropriate to state it again.
Thus, these faults of ornamentation,
as well as others of this kind that may possibly occur, are included within the very categories of faults previously mentioned.
Since they do not deserve to be explained separately, this definition of poetry is complete.

Thus, although this path is distinct for various learned scholars, it appears as if non-distinct; this is not surprising, for in that case, the sole cause is the perfectly executed composition itself. //1//
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Kāvyaprakāśa, titled "The Determination of Figures of Sense."
And thus this Kāvyaprakāśa is completed.
